#6055. easyJet Launches 34 New UK Routes: See Full List Now

Several airlines have started announcing their schedules for next summer, and easyJet is among them. According to schedule data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, the British low-cost carrier is set to launch 34 new routes from the UK in 2027.

In fact, seven of those were announced just recently. Note that the 34 routes are based on what the airline has planned for next year so far, and more could be announced in the coming months.

Five of the seven recently announced routes are international, three of which are to Greece. Starting in May, easyJet will launch flights between London Southend Airport (SEN) and Corfu International Airport (CFU). It will also introduce services from London Luton Airport (LTN) to Kefalonia International Airport (EFL) and Skiathos International Airport (JSI).

The budget airline is also expanding its network to Paris Orly Airport (ORY) in France. On March 28, it will launch twice-weekly flights from London Gatwick Airport (LGW), followed by another twice-weekly service from Jersey Airport (JER) on March 30. Note that while Jersey is a self-governing British Crown Dependency and not part of the UK, it has been included here as part of easyJet's wider UK and Channel Islands network.

As for the domestic additions, the low-cost carrier will begin twice-weekly flights between Newcastle International Airport (NCL) and Southampton Airport (SOU) on February 26. Another addition is technically a returning route between Gatwick and Cornwall Airport Newquay (NQY), which the airline served in 2026 but later withdrew its flights. Tickets for the service are now back on sale.

Previously operated by Loganair, although that airline flew to Paris Charles de Gaulle

Operated from June to August (2x weekly); flights back on sale

Looking back at its previous announcements, easyJet is adding seven routes to Spain alone for the summer 2027 season. This includes a brand-new destination on its network, Girona. From March 28, when airlines switch to their summer schedules, the UK budget airline will commence a twice-weekly service between Liverpool John Lennon Airport (LPL) and Girona–Costa Brava Airport (GRO).

In June, it will also start serving the Catalan gateway from London Gatwick three times a week. As noted below in the table, France is another country seeing several new additions. Apart from the Paris Orly services, easyJet is adding five more routes to the country.

Among these are flights from Gatwick to Ajaccio Napoleon Bonaparte Airport (AJA) and from Bristol Airport (BRS) to Montpellier–Méditerranée Airport (MPL), both of which will be solely operated by easyJet.

easyJet’s 13-route winter expansion highlights Newcastle’s rapid growth and renewed investor attention.

Furthermore, there are some winter additions as well. In January, the low-cost carrier will launch a new service between London Southend and Sharm El Sheikh International Airport (SSH) in Egypt. According to Cirium data, the service is scheduled to operate until May 8. It will initially run twice a week, but following a two-week break in March, the airline will increase the frequency to three weekly flights from April.

This will be easyJet's 11th route to Sharm El Sheikh from the country. Interestingly, the airline has added four routes to the Egyptian resort city this year alone. Two of these commenced last month at the start of the Northern Hemisphere winter season, from Edinburgh Airport (EDI) and Belfast International Airport (BFS), both of which are served twice weekly. The other two were launched in August from Glasgow Airport (GLA) and Newcastle.

#6054. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6053. Global Entry Renewal: My Step-By-Step Experience, Cost, And Timeline

Global Entry is an incredibly useful program for anyone who travels internationally with any frequency. I’ve had Global Entry for nearly 15 years now. Several weeks ago, I received an email reminding me that I was within six months of my Global Entry expiring, so I just went through the process of renewing it.

In this post, I’d like to outline the process of renewing a Global Entry membership, since it’s something that frequent travelers have to do periodically. I’ll include a step-by-step guide, the cost, and the timeline. I’ve separately written about how to apply for Global Entry.

For those not familiar, Global Entry is a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) program that allows expedited clearance for pre-approved, low-risk travelers upon arrival in the United States (or at CBP Preclearance facilities). With this program, approved members can enter the United States using their biometric data at virtually all international airports.

The exact way that biometric data is verified varies by airport. It used to be that you’d have to go up to one of the Global Entry kiosks and answer a few questions. Then they updated the technology, and you just had to stand in front of one of those kiosks for a few seconds. Now many airports just have a camera in the Global Entry lane that automatically verifies your identity as you walk through. It’s pretty awesome.

You do still typically have to walk past an immigration officer and verify that you don’t have anything to declare. You can then proceed to the baggage claim area and exit (unless you’re selected for additional screening).

Over the years, Global Entry has probably saved me dozens of hours. Back in the day I’d be stressed when landing back in the United States, wondering if I’d be stuck in an hour-long immigration queue. Nowadays I can just breeze right through.

Before I share a step-by-step guide of my Global Entry renewal experience, let me share some basics about the timeline, how much it costs, etc.

Global Entry is valid for roughly five years after you’re approved. The reason I say “roughly” is because it’s valid for five years from your next birthday. In other words, if your birthday is December 1, and you apply January 1, 2027, your membership would be valid through December 1, 2032.

If you strategically apply for Global Entry, you can get it for almost six years with one membership. Just apply shortly after your birthday.

Generally speaking you’ll get an email six months before your Global Entry expires informing you of the upcoming expiration. If you want to look for it in your email, that usually comes from [email protected].

Alternatively you can log into your Trusted Traveler Program dashboard, and go to the section that lists your program status. You’ll see the expiration date listed there.

You can apply to have your Global Entry renewed up to a year before the expiration date. There’s no penalty for renewing early, in the sense that it will still be valid for five years from when your membership currently expires, and not five years from when you’re approved. So you might as well renew early.

You won’t want to let your membership lapse, since the process is more complicated for a lapsed membership. Be sure to apply for renewal well before your Global Entry is set to expire.

There is a grace period for Global Entry renewal, as long as you submit your renewal application before your membership expires. Specifically, there’s a grace period of up to 24 months, which is super long. Back in the day, the grace period was only six months, but that has been increased considerably over time.

If you do submit your application but aren’t approved before the expiration, you’ll continue to be able to use Global Entry the same way as before during that period.

It costs $120 for adults to renew Global Entry (Global Entry is free for kids under the age of 18). Fortunately, many credit cards offer a fee credit toward Global Entry renewal. Note that in all cases, you can use your credit for anyone — so if you have extra credits, you can use them for friends and family to renew their Global Entry.

When you first apply for Global Entry you have to be interviewed, either in-person or virtually. Do you need to be interviewed when you renew? It depends:

While only tangentially related, what happens if you have to renew your passport before your Global Entry expires? The good news is that it’s a really easy process.

You just have to log into your account on the Trusted Traveler Programs website and update your passport number there. Your Global Entry will then continue to apply with the new passport up until the Global Entry expiration date. See this post for more details on how that works.

On November 15, 2026, I submitted my application to renew Global Entry. My current membership expires on April 20, 2027, though as long as the application is submitted before then, there’s a grace period of two years.

To renew your Global Entry membership, you’ll want to go to the Trusted Traveler Programs website, and click “LOG IN” at the top right under the “Returning GE/NEXUS/SENTRI/FAST Member/Applicants” heading.

Note that back in 2017 the government migrated from the Global Online Enrollment System (GOES). So if you don’t yet have a new Trusted Traveler Programs profile, you’ll have to set that up first, which is a quick process (though at this point I imagine that virtually everyone has transitioned).

Once logged in you’ll see your current Global Entry membership, and underneath that you should see a “Renew Membership” option listed, assuming you’re within the renewal period.

There you’ll be able to select the program you want to apply for or renew, which in this case would be Global Entry.

Essentially the Global Entry renewal application contains all the information you submitted the last time around, so you just have to confirm that it’s correct, and update any outdated information.

This includes reviewing your personal information, documents, driver’s license, address, employment info, travel history, and more.

You do have to upload a copy of your passport during the process (assuming your passport number changed since your last application, which will likely be the case half of the time for adults, since passports are usually valid for 10 years, while Global Entry is valid for five or so years).

The only slightly complicated part of this process is having to update your travel history, as you have to list all of the countries that you’ve been to since the last time that you applied. So yeah, that can take a second, if you’re a frequent traveler.

At some points the process of reviewing info isn’t very intuitive, as you have to click a lot of unnecessary buttons confirming that nothing has changed. But it’s pretty self explanatory. I’d say the whole process up until this point took me about 15 minutes, and that includes having to recall all the countries from the past five years (which is quite a few).

To finish off the process you just have to certify that all of the information that you’re providing is accurate, and then you have to pay.

When you pay, make sure you use a credit card that has a Global Entry fee credit, assuming you have one.

I used my Amex Business Platinum, and the fee reimbursed within two days.

As mentioned above, I submitted the Global Entry renewal application on November 15, 2026. Then on November 25, 2026 — 10 days later — I received an email indicating that there had been an application status change on the renewal. The email came from [email protected] with the subject line “TTP Application Status Change.”

The email as such doesn’t tell you a whole lot, so you have to log into your account again to see the status. There I found out that the application was approved, meaning that there was no need to take part in an interview.

Experiences seem to be mixed as to whether an interview is required for renewals. For example, during my last renewal, I did need to get an interview, while during my renewal before that, I didn’t need to get an interview.

The good news is that if you do need to be interviewed, you can typically just do so when you return from an international trip. When I did it, it took less than a minute.

I just went through the process of renewing Global Entry, and it was pretty easy. You basically just have to confirm that all the information during your last application is still accurate, add all the countries you’ve been to since then, and pay a fee.

This time around, the application was processed in 10 days, and there was a full approval, so no interview was required. However, don’t be surprised if you do need an interview, as that happened to me during my last renewal.

Hopefully this is useful for anyone else who has a Global Entry renewal coming up soon.

#6052. Amex Blue Business Card Bonus: As High As 50K Points Or $500 Cash Back Welcome Offer

At the moment, we’re seeing increased welcome offers on two of Amex’s most lucrative business cards — The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card. Ordinarily these cards have really unremarkable bonuses, but at the moment the offers have been improved very nicely — we’re talking doubled on one card, and more than tripled on the other card. If you don’t yet have either card, this is absolutely the time to apply.

I’ll cover the welcome offer on the Amex Blue Business Plus, which I’d argue is one of Amex’s most lucrative and most approachable business cards, especially for those looking to accrue points. I’ll also talk about the Amex Blue Business Cash, which is essentially the cash back version of the card.

Link: Learn more about The Blue Business® Plus Credit Card from American Express and The American Express Blue Business Cash® Card

The Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus is currently as high as 50,000 Membership Rewards points after spending $5,000 on purchases within the first three months of card membership. Apply and find out your welcome offer. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Amex Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, potentially making this offer worth $850. As a point of comparison, previously the publicly available welcome offer was just 15,000 points after spending $3,000 within the first three months, so this offer is potentially worth more than three times as much. For a no annual fee card (Rates & Fees), this is pretty incredible. This is absolutely the time to apply if you’re interested.

However, as I’ll explain below, the reason you get the card isn’t just because of the welcome offer, but also because of the long term value that it offers. There are lots of great uses of Amex Membership Rewards points, as they can be transferred to all kinds of useful airline and hotel partners, ranging from Air Canada Aeroplan, to Air France-KLM Flying Club, to Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, to Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. Just to give some examples of how points could be redeemed:

In line with Amex’s “once in a lifetime” rule, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card bonus isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card (or previous versions of the card) in the past. On top of that, Amex’s general card restrictions apply. There are a few additional things to note:

Anecdotally, I find Amex business cards to generally be among the easiest to get approved for. I also want to emphasize that Amex business cards not counting toward the 5/24 limit really makes the opportunity cost of picking up this card pretty low, for those of us into maximizing our rewards.

The first thing to love about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is that it has no annual fee (Rates & Fees)… you can’t beat that!

But really what makes this card unrivaled within the Amex ecosystem is its return on spending, up to a certain limit. Specifically, the Amex Blue Business Plus offers 2x Membership Rewards points on the first $50,000 spent every calendar year, and then 1x points. It’s that straightforward. So $50,000 in spending per year would earn you 100,000 Membership Rewards points.

This is the only no annual fee credit card on the market that earns 2x transferable points that can be moved to the full list of airline and hotel partners at the “premium” ratio. There’s literally not another card like that. The one caveat is that the card does have foreign transaction fees, so I wouldn’t recommend using it for purchases abroad (Rates & Fees).

Speaking of the ability to move points to partners, I think that gets at the other thing that’s awesome about the Amex Blue Business Plus Card — in the event that you want to close other Amex cards (with annual fees) that accrue Membership Rewards points, this is a great card to have, so that you can maintain your points balance, given the ability to pool points.

So I view this as a very low risk card to apply for, especially with it not counting toward Chase’s 5/24 limit. The only reason I wouldn’t get this card is if I’m otherwise at the Amex five credit card limit.

Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Plus Card here.

In the Blue Business portfolio, the Amex Blue Business Plus Card is the standout card for me. However, I should also mention the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which is essentially the cash back equivalent:

Personally, I get more excited by the Amex Blue Business Plus Card than the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, simply because I value Amex points at well over one cent each. That’s why I’d rather earn 2x points rather than 2% cash back. Admittedly, not everyone will feel the same, especially those who don’t actually want to put the effort into maximizing points.

The Amex Blue Business Cash bonus is also greatly improved, though, as it was previously for a $250 statement credit. So this is twice as good.

Read a full review of the Amex Blue Business Cash Card here.

The Amex Blue Business Plus Card is a product that often flies under the radar. Ordinarily the card doesn’t have a very exciting bonus, but at the moment, we’re seeing a much better opportunity than usual. The card has a welcome offer as high as 50,000 bonus Membership Rewards points. Getting a no annual fee card that earns 2x transferable points (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1x points) that can be moved directly to airline and hotel partners at the most favorable ratio is something you won’t find on any other card. That’s why this card is in my wallet, and the welcome offer is just the icing on the cake.

Meanwhile if you’re looking for the cash back equivalent, it’s at least worth mentioning the Amex Blue Business Cash Card, which has a bonus as high as $500 cash back as a statement credit. That no annual fee card earns 2% cash back (on the first $50,000 spent annually, then 1% cash back), also with no annual fee.

These are both really lucrative cards that can be worth holding onto in the long run, so if you’re eligible, I’d absolutely recommend applying.

#6050. How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly The Airbus A380?

A typical Airbus A380 flight takes around 20–30 crew members in total on a standard long-haul commercial flight, with the statutory minimum being 16 based on the exit doors. The exact crew numbers are typically not published by airlines, although there are Reddit users who do provide insights.

For example, one British Airways crew member writes that there are "22 on our 380s and 8-13 on the rest of the wide bodies (787/777/350)." Contextually, this excludes the pilots. Another user comments that there are a maximum of 12 cabin crew for Boeing 777s, presumably with British Airways, or around ten more than typically staff an Airbus A380.

Let's examine how many pilots and cabin crew it takes to fly an A380 and why it varies by the airline's quality of service, the duration of the flight, and the specific applicable laws. While FAA regulations are typically the go-to, none of the world's A380s are actually based in the United States. Additionally, in practical terms, union agreements also dictate how many flight attendants the airline provides.

Exactly how many crew members it takes to fly an Airbus A380 is highly contingent on the mission and the quality of service of the airline. Strictly speaking, it only takes two crew to legally fly and ferry an A380. Not all flights need to have passengers onboard: there are test flights and ferry flights these aircraft perform.

At times, A380 flights will appear on flight tracker websites that will have fewer crew on board than an A320 operating a scheduled passenger flight. However, airlines are legally required to carry flight attendants whenever passengers are onboard an aircraft with more than 19 passenger seats.

This is true for both FAA and EASA rules. One of the reasons why cabin crew is required is to manage emergency evacuations within the 90-second exit rule. This regulation is about the number of seats, not the number of tickets sold or the number of passengers actually onboard.

All of the world's A380s have 379 (found on Singapore's fleet) or more seats onboard. On the other end, Emirates' densest configuration, with 615 seats, requires at least 13 cabin crew. Theoretically, an A380 could be configured with 853 seats, which would require 18 cabin crew (explained below).

The standard minimum number of pilots needed to fly an A380 is two: the Captain and First Officer. The superjumbo was designed after the Flight Engineer's position was abolished and so was designed as a two-crew fly-by-wire aircraft, much like other Airbus aircraft. The size of the aircraft is not particularly important in determining how many pilots the aircraft needs to fly.

The age of the aircraft is also no longer a factor, with the position of Flight Engineer largely phased out around the world. Instead, the determining factor for how many pilots an aircraft needs to have is the duration of the flight. For example, the ultra-long-haul route between New Delhi and New York JFK is classified as a 13+ hour flight and so requires a minimum of three pilots under both the US's FAA and India's Directorate General of Civil Aviation.

In this case, the FAA allows for one fully qualified Captain and three First Officers, whereas India's flights under DGCA rules are required to have at least two fully qualified Captains. In practice, A380s don't fly that route, but they do fly other long- and ultra-long-haul routes where they are required to have three or four pilots.

This is to ensure crew members can rotate into dedicated crew rest facilities when flight time and duty limits require in-flight rest. Generally, flights with two pilots are capped under FAA rules at eight hours, one relief pilot is required for flights between eight and 13 hours, and flights between 13 and 17 hours need four pilots (two relief pilots).

Differences from crew dynamics to safety procedures changes the work experience between aircraft types.

Under FAA regulations, aircraft with 20–50 installed seats must have at least one flight attendant, those with 51-100 need two, and then another for every threshold of 50 seats installed. EASA rules are similar, although somewhat different. Note that there are some specific rules not mentioned here that can create exceptions, but this is the base underlying rule.

Based purely on this, Singapore Airlines' A380 with 379 seats (the lowest superjumbo seat count) needs at least eight cabin crew, although the door count sets the minimum to 16. Notably, an airline can't meet the minimum number of flight attendants and then stack them in its premium cabins, leaving the crowded economy cabin most deserted.

Governing threshold/trigger (per FAA, EASA)

Greater than 13 and up to 17+ hours (FAA)

FAA regulations explicitly state that flight attendants must be "uniformly distributed throughout the airplane" to provide the most effective egress of passengers in an emergency. Regulators also treat each deck of a double-decked aircraft such as the A380 and 747 as an independent cabin zone.

This means that the back-of-the-envelope math above of the minimum flight attendants may actually be an undercount. Flight attendants are permitted to move about and serve meals. This means they can move from economy to business to serve meals, but if the seat belt sign goes on, they must return to their assigned door station.

Flight duration governs Flight Duty Period limits, which are the maximum time a flight attendant is permitted to work from pre-flight check-in to post-flight release. This is somewhat similar to the relief pilot requirement above, but for flight attendants. When flights exceed standard duty limits, airlines must add augmented (relief) cabin crew and include rest facilities for flight attendants to sleep and rotate.

The regulations for flight attendants are more relaxed than for pilots. Under FAA rules (14 CFR § 121.467), the standard scheduled duty cap for flight attendants is 14 hours. Longer than that, airlines must add extra flight attendants. Between 14 and 16 hours requires at least one more flight attendant, between 16 and 18 hours requires at least two more, and 18 to 20 hours requires at least three more.

Fortunately for the airline, long-haul flights don't require a doubling of the cabin crew. EASA regulations state that "to protect an eight-hour sleep opportunity, the operator rosters a period of eight hours, taking into account fatigue management principles, for each reserve day during which a crew member on reserve is not contacted by the operator."

It is worth noting that countries do not generally vary much in the basic one flight attendant per 50 passenger seat rule. However, they do meaningfully differ around seated vs. passenger-headcount ratios, fatigue and duty-time limits, and national labor/union rules. That is too much to explain here.

The world's largest airliner has plenty of space for crew rest.

There is something of an irony in this article so far. Much of the attention is on the FAA, which is essentially the gold standard for global aviation. However, none of the world's A380s are based in the United States, and only a few are based in Europe (where EASA rules apply).

For the A380, the United Arab Emirates' specific rules are more pertinent, as it is home to more than half of the world's superjumbo fleet. These regulations are set by the nation's General Civil Aviation Authority, which operates in the context of Dubai and Abu Dhabi being massive long-haul and ultra-long-haul hubs.

Firstly, the 50-seat rule is retained. Secondly, in the UAE, airlines rely directly on GCAA regulatory minimums plus their own commercial service standards and not on unions. In the US and Europe, union rules can add to base FAA or EASA rules. The GCAA's long-haul provisions potentially allow airlines such as Emirates to make more intensive use of their cabin-crew workforce than an equivalent EASA-regulated airline.

However, it is not possible to get into the weeds of the nuances of the regulations here. The UAE's baseline cabin safety ratio matches global norms, but its rules are heavily tailored to 24/7 hub-and-spoke waves, late-night departures, and ultra-long-haul rest/recovery cycles across vast time-zone jumps. Generally, UAE operators would likely have a lower minimum cabin crew requirement than airlines operating under FAA and EASA rules.

All Airbus A380 operators are mainline carriers with high numbers of premium seats. Consequently, none are operating at the bare minimum number of cabin crew in the way an ultra-low-cost carrier like Ryanair would be expected to. With their hands tied and forced to have their flight attendants allocated to the economy cabin, they need to add flight attendants for the premium cabins.

Generally speaking, a mainline carrier will have a flight attendant per 35–50 economy class passengers. It would likely have a flight attendant per 12–18 business class passengers and perhaps one per 3–6 first-class passengers. Etihad even advertises a personal flight attendant for its The Residence apartment. Emirates' A380 staffing, meanwhile, is unusually well documented compared with other airlines.

Figures suggest it typically operates its A380s with around 26 cabin personnel (two pilots and 24 cabin crew), with the exact number varying by configuration and sector. On an ultra-long-haul route to Sydney, it would add two relief pilots, but the cabin crew may remain constant. So the count would increase to around 28 crew. As stated, British Airways tends to operate its long-haul A380 flights with 22 cabin crew plus 2-4 pilots.

#6049. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

#6048. Hyatt Credit Cards Compared: Is The Personal Or Business Card Better?

Chase and Hyatt have a pretty straightforward co-brand card portfolio, as there’s one personal card and one business card. Specifically, I’m talking about the World of Hyatt Credit Card and the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card.

In this post, I’d like to compare the two cards, and talk about which is better. First let’s cover the details of both products, and then I’ll share my take on which is worth applying for. This is an especially good time to pick them up, given the current welcome offers.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card or World of Hyatt Business Credit Card

To start, let’s cover the details of Hyatt’s two co-branded credit cards. Below is a chart with the basics, and I’ll go into a bit more detail below.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s personal credit card, with a $95 annual fee. Hyatt’s personal credit card offers a variety of perks, including the following:

The World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more) is Hyatt’s business credit card, with a $199 annual fee. Hyatt’s business credit card offers many benefits, including the following:

If you’re considering applying for a Hyatt credit card and would be eligible for a business or personal card, which should you apply for?

The first thing to understand is that the World of Hyatt Card and World of Hyatt Business Card aren’t mutually exclusive. You could apply for both cards, and also earn the welcome bonus on each. So in some ways, it’s worth assessing the value of the cards independently, since you don’t actually have to decide between them.

If you ask me, the World of Hyatt Card is a slam dunk if you stay at Hyatts with any frequency. The card has a reasonable annual fee, and it’s worth holding onto even if you don’t spend a dime on it.

The annual free night award alone more than justifies the annual fee, and the five nights toward elite status with no spending requirement is a great perk as well. On top of that, I think there’s merit to spending $15,000 on the card per year, to earn a second annual free night award, plus to earn an additional six elite nights toward status.

The math on the World of Hyatt Business Card isn’t quite as straightforward. The card has a different welcome bonus than on the personal card, so there’s merit to picking up the card for that. But beyond that, the main reason you’ll want to get this card is because it offers the best rate of return on spending in terms of earning elite nights.

With the business card, you can earn one elite night for every $2,000 spent, while with the personal card, you can get one elite night for every $2,500 spent (though the increments for earning elite nights differ).

So my best consolidated advice would be that the World of Hyatt Card is more valuable and is easier to justify, and is the best for the first $15,000 in spending annually. Beyond that, though, the World of Hyatt Business Card is best for helping to earn Hyatt status, especially if you’re a big spender. Furthermore, it can be worth picking up the card in part for the huge bonus.

Hyatt has both a personal and business co-branded credit cards. The products are totally different, and there’s potentially merit to both. The World of Hyatt Card is much easier to justify — the card has a lower annual fee, offers an annual free night award, provides five nights toward status without a spending requirement, and more.

That being said, you don’t have to decide between the two cards, and there’s also merit to getting the World of Hyatt Business Card. The card has a better welcome bonus, and has the potential to be more rewarding for spending.

What’s your take on the value proposition of Hyatt’s personal vs. business card?

#6047. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 737 Review: Good For A Short Hop

To kick off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 737-800 business class on the 45-minute flight from Malaga (AGP) to Casablanca (CMN).

I must admit, Royal Air Maroc has a really solid short haul product. While there’s no Wi-Fi or seat back entertainment, I appreciate that the airline has “proper” business class seats, the inflight meal service was outright generous for such a short flight, and I also appreciated the dedicated business class bus upon arrival.

Admittedly the flight attendant serving us didn’t have much personality, and the cabin wasn’t in great condition. But still, those are hardly huge issues. For that matter, it has to be acknowledged how the airlines of northern Africa really lower the bar when it comes to the quality of the inflight experience (hi, Air Algerie!), so on a relative basis, this was rather excellent.

Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

We arrived at Malaga Airport at around 11:30AM, plenty early for our 2:15PM flight. We headed through security and then cleared passport control… only then did I realize that the non-Schengen lounge is currently closed, so we had no lounge option there.

I guess we could’ve exited passport control again to access the lounge in the Schengen area of the terminal, but we figured that wasn’t worth it, so we just decided to grab a seat. I have to say, the non-Schengen portion of the Malaga Airport had quite the scene. Virtually every other flight departing around the same time was on Jet2, and it was definitely a “festive” spirit in the terminal. Based on the passengers, you’d think the airport had banned close-toed shoes.

Boarding for our flight was scheduled for 1:30PM, 45 minutes before departure, from gate B16. Sure enough, that’s exactly when boarding started, with business class passengers being invited to board first.

We boarded the Royal Air Maroc Boeing 737-800 through the forward door, and then turned right into the business class cabin. Royal Air Maroc’s 737s have 12 business class seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2 configuration.

Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class seats are particularly spacious, as they boast 43″ of pitch and 21″ of width, with 6″ of recline. So this is significantly more spacious than what you’d find in domestic first class within the United States, where pitch is more commonly around 37-38″ — an extra 5-6″ is definitely noticeable!

These seats have little foot bars that fold down from the seat in front, for extra support while inflight. These were also old style seats, in terms of having large, deep, leather pockets on the seat back.

The tray table folded out from the side of the seat, and had to be flipped over to be fully extended. It was a bit flimsy, as the cabin definitely felt a bit past its prime.

There was a center console where drinks could be placed during the flight, along with additional little drink trays that could be extended, acting as “wings” to the center console.

On the front side of the center console were the AC charging outlets, which were the extent of the charging options there — there were no USB-A or USB-C charging options.

There were also little channel and volume controls, along with a headphone jack, for tuning into the inflight entertainment.

Perhaps the most modern part of the cabin was the overhead consoles, which had the more modern Boeing overhead lights and air nozzles.

While the cabin definitely felt tired and wasn’t in great shape, the comfort was otherwise great, when compared to what you’ll otherwise find in the region. I mean, my previous two regional flights on airlines from northern Africa were on junky wet leased planes, so this was luxurious by comparison.

Unfortunately this Royal Air Maroc 737 didn’t have any sort of Wi-Fi or streaming entertainment. Instead, there were monitors that folded down from the overhead consoles, which had some programming during the flight — on this flight, there were cartoons.

So the entertainment situation was disappointing, but of course on a flight of this length, it wasn’t an issue. But if I were on a three or four hour flight on one of these 737s, I’d of course have a different impression.

During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of water or lemon mint juice, and we got one of each. They were served in proper glassware — I love the branding!

One thing I have to mention is that the cabin was insanely hot during boarding — I imagine the APU wasn’t working, or something, so we were sweating our you-know-whats off.

Airlines of northern Africa are always a bit funny when it comes to safety. At 1:55PM the safety video was screened, while the door was still open, and before all passengers had boarded.

At 2:05PM the main cabin door closed, with seven of the 12 business class seats occupied. At 2:10PM we began our pushback, and at 2:15PM we began our taxi. There were zero security checks during the taxi out, and a couple of people in business class had their seats reclined.

The captain sure was a good multi-tasker, or at least so I assume — he made his welcome aboard announcement while also taxiing us out and making some turns (at least I assume that at Royal Air Maroc taxiing is a captain-only function, but maybe that’s not the case?).

It was just a quick taxi out to runway 13, where we were second in line for takeoff, behind a Ryanair 737. We were cleared for takeoff at 2:20PM, with some nice views on the climb out.

The seatbelt sign was turned off just five minutes after takeoff, at which point the crew sprung into action, starting by closing the curtain between the cabin and the galley.

After takeoff, the crew distributed some warm towels, which had a nice scent to them.

A few minutes later, the inflight meal was brought out. For a flight of this length, I was impressed. The main dish had some prawns, burrata, and veggies. Then there was a cheese plate, a slice of cake, and a piece of bread. Unlike on Air Algerie, a little thought was also put into presentation.

The crew passed through with water, while other drinks had to specifically be requested. I asked for a cup of tea, which was also promptly served. By the time I finished my snack, we were already well into our descent.

For a flight of this length, this kind of snack is really tough to beat.

Just before landing, I checked out the business class lavatory on the Royal Air Maroc 737. It was a pretty standard previous generation 737 lavatory, and had definitely seen better days. Among other things, the toilet seat just wouldn’t stay up unless you held it open the entire time.

There were no special amenities, other than Royal Air Maroc branded hand lotion.

The lead flight attendant on this flight was a nice older guy. We didn’t interact with him much, but he seemed generally charming. For example, I saw him kindly bring some toys to a kid seated in business class, and engage nicely with him.

The primary flight attendant working in business class was a younger lady. She wasn’t rude, but had zero outward personality. She didn’t smile, and if we exchanged five words, that would’ve been a lot. But at least she was efficient and on top of things, and compared to Air Algerie, she was basically a Singapore Airlines flight attendant.

At 1:50PM Casablanca time (there was a one-hour time change from Malaga, so this was 30 minutes after takeoff), the seatbelt sign was turned on, as we were well into our descent to Casablanca. At that point the pre-landing announcement was made, but again, there was nothing in the way of safety checks, and the person seated in front of me even still had a glass at their seat.

The views on the approach were lovely — Morocco really is a beautiful country.

We ended up landing at Casablanca Airport at 1:05PM, on runway 35L.

From there we had a short five-minute taxi to our arrival stand, where we’d have to get on a bus to get to the terminal.

On the plus side, this gave us a great view of the 737 we had just flown, which was in the special oneworld livery.

As we deplaned, the lead flight attendant and captain kindly bid farewell to everyone. The airline did have a special bus for business class passengers, which is at least a nice aspect of the passenger experience, as it shows some effort.

It was a roughly five-minute ride to the terminal, then we cleared security, and then we boarded our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight to Miami a short while later.

I had a pleasant flight in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class. For a 45-minute flight, it sure is nice to get real business class seats and a proper, tasty snack. The flight also operated on schedule, so I really have no complaints, especially when you consider the typical airline experience in the northern part of Africa.

To be fair, though, the cabin was definitely a bit tired, and the lack of Wi-Fi and streaming entertainment would prove more frustrating on a longer journey. Furthermore, the primary flight attendant working business class just didn’t have any personality.

What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class?

#6045. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6044. Premium Economy Vs. Business Class: What The Extra Money Really Buys On Long-Haul

An aviation writer, pilot, and flight operations professional who sees aviation from both sides of the cockpit door. With a background in aeronautics, safety, and human factors, she brings curiosity, firsthand experience, and a love of the details that turn aircraft and airports into stories worth telling.

Paying several times more for a business class ticket can seem difficult to justify when the difference in seat width is relatively small. Yet the comparison changes when the cabin lights dim on an overnight flight. One passenger can stretch out on a fully flat bed, while another remains in a reclining seat, even with extra legroom and a more generous cabin environment. Both have upgraded from economy, but only one has a seat designed to become a sleeping surface. For anyone facing a long flight followed by a demanding day, that difference can be more valuable than the additional inches suggest.

Premium economy has become an appealing middle ground for travelers who want more comfort without paying business class prices. However, the two cabins serve different purposes, and their value depends on much more than the seat itself. United Airlines' Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner offers a useful example of how the products differ, from cabin layouts and sleeping space to the services associated with each cabin. Understanding what passengers receive, how airlines package those benefits, and when they matter most makes it easier to decide whether business class is a worthwhile investment or an expensive upgrade that may not be necessary.

The most important distinction between premium economy and business class on many long-haul aircraft is the ability to lie flat. Premium economy offers a more spacious version of an economy seat, generally with additional legroom, greater recline and improved personal space. Business class takes the experience further by providing a seat that converts into a horizontal sleeping surface on aircraft equipped with lie-flat seating. That changes how passengers can spend several hours in the air, particularly when a flight crosses time zones overnight.

United's 787-9 illustrates the difference in one configuration, which has 48 Polaris business class seats and 21 Premium Plus seats. In this configuration, the Polaris seat offers approximately 78 inches of flat sleeping space and is about 20.5 inches wide. Premium Plus provides 38 inches of seat pitch, a seat width of approximately 19 inches and around six inches of recline. These measurements describe different things. Sleeping space is the length available when the business class seat is converted into a bed, while seat pitch measures the distance between corresponding points on consecutive seats. The figures are specific to this configuration, not universal specifications for every United 787-9.

The extra room in premium economy matters, but the distinction between reclining and lying flat becomes especially relevant on overnight flights. A premium economy passenger can lean back and potentially rest more comfortably than in standard economy, but the seat remains angled. A flat bed does not guarantee uninterrupted sleep, yet it gives passengers the opportunity to rest horizontally. For travelers arriving in the morning with a full day ahead, that can be a compelling reason to consider business class. The next question is how such a substantial difference in the onboard experience translates into ticket prices.

Business class is not simply premium economy with a larger seat. Airlines allocate more cabin space to each business class passenger, often install more complex seating, and provide a different combination of onboard service and airport benefits. A lie-flat seat also has to function in two modes, accommodating passengers during meals, entertainment and other activities before converting into a sleeping surface. The resulting product is designed around a different level of personal space and comfort.

The price difference, however, is not fixed. Premium economy and business class fares vary with the route, travel dates, demand, booking lead time and ticket restrictions. A business class fare purchased during a sale may be relatively competitive, while a flight with strong demand for overnight travel can carry a substantial premium. Comparing the cabins using a single price multiplier can therefore be misleading. The more useful comparison is the actual fare difference for the same itinerary, purchased at the same time and under comparable conditions.

Larger reclining seat than standard economy

Often a lie-flat seat on long-haul aircraft

Often designed to provide direct aisle access

Typically more extensive dining and service

Lounge access and priority services may be included

Usually more expensive, sometimes substantially so

These differences help explain why the two cabins appeal to different travelers. Premium economy offers a way to make a long flight more comfortable without paying for every feature associated with business class. Business class offers a more comprehensive experience, but its additional benefits may not be equally useful to everyone. The real value depends on which features a passenger will use, rather than the cabin label alone.

American Airlines has really improved its premium economy product on the 787-9P, but is it actually too much of an improvement?

Seat layout can affect the journey as much as the seat's dimensions. In the United 787-9 configuration, Polaris uses a 1-2-1 arrangement, giving every passenger direct aisle access. Premium Plus uses a 2-3-2 arrangement. A traveler seated beside the window or in the middle of the center group may have to coordinate with a seatmate to reach the aisle. That inconvenience can become more noticeable during an overnight flight, particularly when one passenger wants to move while another is sleeping. Travelers should check the aircraft and seat map for their specific flight because airlines operate aircraft with different cabin configurations.

The strongest argument for business class often comes down to what happens after landing. A passenger traveling overnight from the United States to Europe may arrive in the morning with meetings, connecting travel or sightseeing ahead. In that situation, a lie-flat bed provides an opportunity to rest in a position that premium economy cannot replicate. It may be particularly valuable when the traveler has little time to recover before the next commitment.

On a daytime flight, the calculation can be very different. Someone planning to read, watch films, work on a laptop or enjoy the view may find that premium economy provides most of the comfort they need. The wider seat and additional legroom can make several hours more pleasant without paying for a sleeping surface that may see little use. Flight duration matters, but so do departure time, arrival time and the traveler's plans. An eight-hour daytime journey followed by an evening at a hotel presents a different challenge from an overnight flight landing shortly before a working day.

There is no universal price threshold at which business class becomes worthwhile for every traveler. Someone paying personally may view a substantial fare difference very differently from a passenger traveling on an employer-funded ticket. The purpose of the journey matters, too. A special occasion may make comfort part of the experience, while a routine daytime trip may not justify the same expenditure. Once passengers identify which benefits matter most, the next step is to compare the complete cost of obtaining them.

Why premium economy is becoming more important to airlines by the day.

The cheapest fare displayed for a premium cabin is not always the best value. Airlines can attach different conditions to tickets within the same cabin, and those conditions may affect seat selection, baggage, changes, refunds, and access to airport lounges. United announced a tiered fare structure for eligible Polaris and Premium Plus services on April 3, with Base, Standard and Flexible options planned for rollout across selected markets during the year. The airline described the categories as a way for customers to choose between a lower entry price, additional benefits and greater flexibility. The exact availability and conditions must be checked for the flight being booked.

That distinction matters when comparing the cost of a lie-flat bed with the cost of a more comfortable reclining seat. A passenger who wants to sleep during the flight may prioritize the business class seat above other benefits. Another traveler may place greater value on lounge access, baggage allowances or the ability to change plans. A lower fare may be attractive if its restrictions are acceptable, but it should not be compared with a more inclusive ticket without accounting for the differences in benefits.

Aircraft assignments can change, and different versions of the same aircraft may have different cabin layouts. Seat maps and fare conditions are therefore more useful than relying on a general description of an airline's product. With those details established, the final decision becomes less about which cabin sounds more luxurious and more about which benefits justify the additional expenditure.

Premium economy and business class are best understood as different solutions to the demands of long-distance travel. Premium economy improves the experience of sitting, with more personal space and a more comfortable reclining position than standard economy. Business class, when equipped with lie-flat seating, changes the experience by allowing passengers to sleep horizontally. That difference becomes particularly relevant on overnight journeys when a traveler needs to be ready for work or other commitments soon after landing. On a daytime flight, the additional room in premium economy may be sufficient.

United's 787-9 provides a useful example of how those products differ. In the configuration with 48 Polaris seats and 21 Premium Plus seats, the business class cabin offers direct aisle access from every seat, while Premium Plus uses a 2-3-2 arrangement. The comparison is not universal across United's fleet, and the specific aircraft assigned to a flight should always be checked. The airline's tiered-fare announcement also illustrates why travelers should examine the benefits attached to a ticket rather than assume every fare in a premium cabin includes the same services.

Ultimately, the right choice depends on what the passenger needs from the journey. A lie-flat bed can be a compelling reason to pay more when a night's rest could influence the day ahead. When the priority is simply to sit more comfortably, premium economy may offer a better balance of comfort and cost. The most useful comparison is not between two cabin names, but between the extra money required and the benefit a traveler will genuinely use. On a long-haul flight, the difference between a more comfortable seat and a bed can shape not only the hours spent in the air, but also how prepared a passenger feels when the aircraft reaches the gate.

#6042. Air France Economy Class: Impressions From A Flight Across The Atlantic

In the spirit of trying out new ideas and topics here at OMAAT, and having learned that many of you are interested in reading about economy, here are some thoughts about how well Air France does the job.

I’ll focus on the daytime return flight from Dublin (DUB) back to Rio (GIG) via Paris (CDG), as I slept through as much of the outbound overnight as I could. This is not a full review — rather, it’s some general comments on the seats, food, and tech, in Air France’s economy offering.

After completing this trip, I’ve flown back and forth between Brazil and France in all four of Air France’s cabin classes. Yes, including La Première – I do fly in the pointy end sometimes. 😉

Having transited through Paris Charles de Gaulle so many times now, I’m actually starting to learn my way around the crazy maze of terminals.

On this occasion, the transfer was on the simpler side, as both flights used gates in Terminal 2E. That said, I still had to catch the light rail transit from Hall K to Hall L and pass through a full security screening before entering the departures area. Not all airports in Europe require this, and I hope it’s taken into account when CDG simplifies its terminal numbering, which is expected in March 2027.

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I had access to Air France’s Hall L Lounge, which is currently undergoing some refurbishments.

Getting a post- or pre-flight facial would have been amazing, but, like my five previous visits to Air France’s lounges in Paris, I’ve had no luck at getting a slot.

Either there were simply no slots left, or, as on this visit, the remaining slot(s) were after my departure time.

Speaking of lounges, I took this photo from Air France’s lounge in Terminal 2E, Hall K, on a previous trip. According to a staffer I spoke with, the construction outside will eventually be a huge new flagship Air France lounge for Terminal 2E.

I sent this photo to Ben before I boarded, and he was surprised to see that the board specifically referenced pre-boarding for Flying Blue Ultimate members. In case you didn’t know either, now you do.

Here’s one final pic for the AvGeeks: even though Air France’s version of the A380 wasn’t particularly loved, the elevated jetbridge above the Boeing 777-300ER in this pic was a nostalgic reminder of the airline’s former superjumbos.

If you’re locking in for 10+ hour flight in economy, there’s only a limited level of comfort that any airline would be able to offer. I wasn’t envious at all walking through the premium economy cabin during boarding…

Thanks to my Flying Blue Gold status, I was able to choose any seat in the cabin from 72 hours before departure. Contrary to my avoidance of bulkhead/exit row seats and their fixed armrests on night flights, I picked bulkhead window seat 21L in the front row of the economy cabin.

The legroom here was more than I needed for this day flight. My plan was to spend most of the flight working, so this seat also avoided anyone reclining into my laptop.

Of Air France’s three Airbus A350-900 configurations, this was the newest 292-seater version that has been rolling out since 2023. The economy cabin has 212 seats in a 3-3-3 layout, which I know isn’t usually a favorite of families of four. Non-bulkhead/exit row seats have a pitch of around 31 inches.

I didn’t move the four-way adjustable headrest at all during the flight, and the recline is listed as being around 118 degrees.

No matter where I’m sitting, I can’t help but marvel at that wingtip.

Of the 29 flights I’ve taken with Air France, I can only remember one meal that wasn’t good. In fact, it was terrible, and was actually when I was flying premium economy from Paris to Zanzibar (ZNZ) in 2024.

Of the two meal choices, I went for the chicken pasta (I didn’t note down the second option as I only decided to write about this after the flight).

I thoroughly enjoyed the main dish. It had lots of protein, the sauce was flavorful, and the little mini pasta pieces weren’t dry at all. Given the several accompaniments, I consider this a generous helping of food. The Président camembert cheese was a nice premium touch, and the bread roll was quite the opposite of stale. I can’t tell you how good the mini apple tart was, as I’m intolerant to apples.

I wish there had been a menu so I could know for sure what was in this really tasty salad. I’m pretty sure it was a mix of mainly carrots, potato, and barley, in what I guess was a honey mustard sauce.

For those who don’t know, Air France differentiates itself by serving Champagne in economy. Partial though I can be, I stuck to Coke Zero for the caffeine.

I like the intention of using wood instead of plastic for cutlery; I just wish the knife could actually cut!

Despite the hefty lunch serving, I got very hungry midway through the flight as I didn’t eat a proper breakfast. I went to raid the snack baskets at the rear-most galley. The area very busy with lots of passengers lingering, and there was some kerfuffle over a medical issue, so I didn’t take any pictures.

I did, however, get a snap of my snack haul. A mini ice cream, a couple of chocolate truffles, a packet of savory biscuits, and half a cheese sandwich. While the snacks might have lacked in nutrition, it’s nice to know that you won’t go hungry on Air France’s economy flights.

I was so tired after the 3:30 a.m. alarm that I skipped the pre-landing light meal on the return flight in favor of a nap.

Neither did I touch the box containing a very beige selection of a bread roll and a pastry on the flight to Paris from Rio. Craving caffeine after a patchy night of sleep, I attempted the drip-style coffee, but a sip was enough to turn my nose up. Yes, I am a coffee snob, and I’m proud of it.

Air France made a great choice to mount the IFE screens on the bulkhead. Only the screen in the aisle seat in my row of three was in that annoying underseat position that needs to be folded away for takeoff and landing.

I could just about reach the very tactile screen when leaning forward. Otherwise, there was a mousepad-style remote.

The 13.3-inch screens are among the largest in the industry, and are the same size as those in the premium economy cabin on this plane.

I counted four charging outlets: a USB-C and a USB-A port in the IFE screen, and, under the seat, a regular power outlet and a second USB-C port.

As for Wi-Fi connectivity, there were no disruptions to the complimentary Starlink for the duration of the flight. However, the whole IFE system had to be reset shortly after we took off. Then, a few hours into the flight, the vast majority of the movies disappeared from the system, including the one I was halfway through. I was able to connect my AirPods to the screen with no issue.

Other amenities, so to speak, were a rather coarse pillow, a blanket, and over-the-head headphones.

One of my favorite things about flying and traveling is meeting new people, including cabin crew, though due to the busyness of economy cabins, that can be tough.

If I have time, I also try to bring a sweet treat on board for the crew to enjoy during the flight, no matter which cabin I’m flying in, as it is usually a great way to build rapport. It worked on this flight, as several crew members came to thank me for the mince pies. Mattieu, to whom I handed them during boarding, brought me a little note to say thanks for both the pies and my Flying Blue loyalty.

Over the course of the flight, I noticed crew in the economy cabin engaging enthusiastically with passengers. At the start of interactions during meal service, I even heard crew asking passengers whether their preferred language was English or French. On at least three occasions, I noticed crew walking through the cabin offering water.

After being spoiled with lots of lie-flat beds over the years, I’ll admit the pre-flight excitement isn’t quite the same when boarding a long-haul flight in economy. This return trip in Air France economy was perfectly fine, with the pros certainly outweighing the cons.

Whether you only fly business class, or a frequent economy class flier, I hope you gained some insights into the Air France economy experience.

When was the last time you flew long-haul in economy, and how was the experience?
