#6041. These incoming members of Congress have been here before

Rep.-elect Chris Rabb, D-Pa., greets current members of Congress in the Capitol on Nov. 11. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

When Rep.-elect Chris Rabb first worked on Capitol Hill in the 1990s, it didn’t exactly inspire him to want to go into politics.

“I said, ‘Oh, this is how the sausage is made? I should be a vegan,’” the Pennsylvania Democrat recalled.

Working for Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman elected as a U.S. senator, Rabb saw threats and “just vile things” directed at her.

“My entrée to service behind the scenes was seeing voluminous amounts of violence, hate speech and death threats against my boss, and I thought to myself, ‘Why would anyone want to serve?’” he said.

During his time in the state legislature starting in 2017, Rabb “fell in love with public service, despite the vitriol.” Now, the democratic socialist describes coming to Congress as “surreal,” as he succeeds retiring Rep. Dwight Evans in a deep-blue district based in West Philadelphia.

Rabb is one of more than a dozen incoming members who have worked on the Hill before, ranging from interns to chiefs of staff and everything in between.

Unlike some in the 100-plus-strong freshman class, they already know their way around the hallways. And Rabb has some advice for his new colleagues: “Treat your staff well. Take care of your staff; they’ll take care of you.”

Here are some of the former staffers who will join the House in January.

A couple years ago, Killin was working as chief of staff to former second gentleman Doug Emhoff. But she started out on the Hill.

“It is helpful to know, as I joke, where the bathrooms are, but I still feel like I have a lot to learn,” said the Army veteran, who unseated Republican Rep. Jeff Crank in a Colorado Springs-area district.

She served as the top staffer for three House Democrats: Donna Shalala of Florida, Carolyn Maloney of New York and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington.

“I’ve actually opened up two freshman offices, so it’s helpful to have done that before,” Killin said.

White will be just the third person in modern times to hold the job of nonvoting D.C. delegate. He replaces retiring Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton — also his former boss.

Before his time on the D.C. Council, he worked as her legislative counsel, watching her navigate a role with limited power in her perennial fight for statehood.

“I need to make sure I’m developing a national profile for this seat,” he said, vowing to continue the quest for full representation even as President Donald Trump seeks to exert more control over the District.

One of just a few Republican women in the freshman class, Gruters said she “never in a million years” imagined coming to Congress herself, despite her years as a staffer.

She will replace retiring Rep. Vern Buchanan in Florida’s 16th District, after once serving as his operations director. She also worked as district director for Rep. Greg Steube, R-Fla.

“I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” said Gruters, whose husband leads the Republican National Committee.

Rogers added another title to his résumé last week: freshman class president.

His fellow incoming Republicans tapped him for the role. Not so long ago, he was working for the Senate Judiciary Committee, fresh off a stint at the white-shoe law firm White & Case.

In 2025 he served as general counsel for Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., and plans to keep pushing for a bill he helped draft that aims to crack down on foreign surrogacy contracts. “We are currently selling American children to China, our No. 1 adversary,” Rogers said, describing it as “deplorable.”

Rogers will succeed retiring GOP Rep. Neal Dunn in the Florida Panhandle.

García’s run for her boss’s seat drew controversy from the start. When Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García, D-Ill., waited to publicly announce his retirement until after the filing deadline in Illinois had already passed, critics blasted him for effectively boxing out other candidates and clearing the way for his chief of staff.

He faced a rare formal disapproval vote in the House over the move. But García has insisted she is more than a hand-picked successor, saying on her campaign website that she has “delivered solutions rooted in lived experience.”

The son of Ghanaian immigrants, Boafo is a state delegate who has lobbied on the Hill for tech company Oracle.

He also worked as campaign manager for Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, earning an endorsement from the retiring longtime Democrat and campaign cash from groups aligned with him.

Boafo prevailed in a crowded primary, even as Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi threw her weight behind a different candidate, former Capitol Police officer Harry Dunn.

Sell worked under then-House Agriculture Chair Larry Combest during the 2000 crop insurance overhaul and the fight over the 2002 farm bill. He later joined his former boss in launching an agricultural lobbying firm, Combest, Sell and Associates.

Once a precocious child magician who wrote his own book of tricks, Lasher also got an early start in politics.

“I feel supremely fortunate to have wandered into Jerry Nadler’s political orbit as a teenager 30 years ago, and then to have worked in his congressional office a decade later,” Lasher wrote in an opinion piece for City & State New York.

Backed by the retiring Nadler, the self-described “nerd” beat out a couple of big names in the primary, including a Kennedy family heir. Another former boss endorsed him, too: Gov. Kathy Hochul. Before serving as a New York state assemblyman, Lasher worked as her policy director.

Villegas ousted GOP Rep. David Valadao in a closely watched race in the San Joaquin Valley.

A decade ago, he was an intern for Rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif. And the progressive also interned for former California state Rep. Rudy Salas, who made unsuccessful bids to unseat Valadao in 2022 and 2024.

A San Diego City councilmember, Von Wilpert flipped the seat held by Republican Rep. Darrell Issa, who decided not to run for reelection under a map redrawn by Democrats.

When she worked for the National Labor Relations Board in 2016, she was detailed to the House Education and Labor Committee, working under ranking member Robert C. Scott, D-Va.

Jackie Wang and Nick Eskow contributed to this report.

#6040. Traveler Says American Pilots Should Have Just “Had A Cup Of Coffee” Instead Of Following Federal Law

There’s no denying that traveling by air can be stressful, and that it’s extremely frustrating when things go wrong. Furthermore, not everyone is a frequent traveler, and understands the ins and outs of how the airline industry functions.

So that brings us to a complaint from last night from an American Airlines passenger. The complaint is so incredibly off base in the first place. But what’s even worse is that when this person is confronted with reality, he just doubles down and keeps going. This person deserves to be roasted, and if you ask me, should be banned from the airline.

Late last night, a social media user posted a picture of two airline pilots on X, with the following caption:

I won’t be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn’t drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir

I won't be seeing my family this Thanksgiving because a couple pilots couldn't drink a cup of coffee and get us home. They clocked out in two hours, but we had 3 hr flight. Thanks @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/q1I8pjsM3w

I can totally appreciate how frustrating it is when a flight is canceled, but this is actually very simple — federal regulations dictate the maximum number of hours that pilots can fly, and that’s for good reason. The airline industry operates with the goal of putting safety above all else, and pilot fatigue has been a contributing factor to many accidents over the years.

I totally get it, you want to be home for Thanksgiving, and it sucks things went wrong, but those are the facts. This is federal law, and on top of that, we should want pilots to be well rested, rather than just saying “keep working, just have another cup of coffee.”

I’d like to point out what makes this even worse — this was a flight out of Miami last night, and the airport had shut down due to a ground stop, because a FedEx MD-11 ran off the runway. That was an absolute pain for all passengers out of the airport, and I can assure you that American also wasn’t happy about that happening, and the impact it had on its operations.

All would be forgiven if this traveler either just didn’t say anything further, or acknowledged “ah, I wasn’t aware of that.” Instead, he has had dozens and dozens of posts, just going on and on and on.

He posted about how American claimed the cancelation was the airport’s fault, but insisted “it’s actually these pilots fault,” and suggested “pilots will lie to save money for their company.”

@AmericanAir will cancel your flight the day before Thanksgiving and say it's the airports fault. It's actually these pilots fault. pic.twitter.com/v4t8KPSojR

@AmericanAir pilots will lie to save money for their company @AmericanAir pic.twitter.com/7VmOKILwCL

He then attacked American’s rebooking lines at Miami Airport. Look, I’ll be the first to call out American when they fall short (and they often do!), but if you really can’t figure out why rebooking lines “wrap around the corner” on one of the busiest travel days of the year when there was an accident that shut down an airport, then you really aren’t trying very hard to understand things.

@AmericanAir why do your rebooking lines always wrap around the corner? How bad are your operations? pic.twitter.com/Id8AaTiom1

He also has an issue with bathrooms at Miami Airport, which I get, but goodness, he’s repetitive.

Why do you have the most disgusting bathrooms @iflymia

Why are your bathroom never clean@iflymia

Why are your bathrooms such a health hazard @iflymia

You should hire people to clean your bathrooms@iflymia

He then suggested that he’ll fly Delta or United next time, because they can get you where you’re supposed to go. Yeah, sure bro, they’ll get you out of Miami Airport when it’s closed due to an accident.

Next time I'll fly @united or @Delta because they can actually get you where you are supposed to be when you are supposed to be there…and paid for…unlike the incompetent airline @AmericanAir. I bet your life is full of incompetence

He’s also asking Secretary Duffy to investigate American, because “they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America.” We know the Trump administration loves to investigate corruption, I’m sure they’ll get right on that!

Can you investigate @AmericanAir they are the most unethical and corrupt company in America

Honestly, I think American is perfectly justified in banning this guy. He’s violating the company’s policy on photographing employees, and this kind of behavior doesn’t need to be tolerated.

It sucks when things go wrong while flying, especially for travel around the holidays. But there’s a fine line between a reasonable complaint, and one that’s completely uncalled for. Posting pictures of random pilots and suggesting they’re the reason you can’t see your family for Thanksgiving is not acceptable.

What’s even worse is when people explain that crew rest requirements are federally mandated, but you just remain in denial over that, and double down. American, please do everyone else a favor and ban this guy.

If I were the pilots I'd go after him, posting their pictures multiple times while spreading libelous statements. Does the Pilot's union do anything here? Internet anonymity that harms known people doesn't benefit anyone and only emboldens jerks like this guy

And an early merry Christmas and happy Hanukkah to you all. And for all residing in The States, I hope everyone wishes for an American style "EU/UK 261".

Why would you take this moron’s posts and broadcast it through your platform? Seems like something one should just ignore - which is exactly what I did after reading the first bit of the post.

#6039. Meet One Of The Oldest Boeing 747-400s Still Flying: Built In 1989 & Still Crossing The Pacific

Brandon's passion for aviation started at a young age. He became involved in the flight simulator and VATSIM communities, which sparked his interest in aviation and eventually led him to earn his private pilot license. Outside of work, he continues to build flight hours, explore new airports, and stay involved in the aviation community.

Kalitta Air’s N740CK left Boeing’s factory in 1989, the year the 747-400 entered service, and it still crosses the Pacific almost every day as a freighter. Between November 16 and 22, 2026, it made 17 flights through nine airports in Asia and North America: Chicago, Anchorage, Shanghai, Seoul, New York, Tokyo, Xiamen, Los Angeles, and Kuala Lumpur. Almost every crossing stopped in Anchorage.

That week also shows how a jumbo jet of its age is still being used. The aircraft began its career as a Malaysia Airlines combi before being converted to carry cargo only. Kalitta flies a sister ship built the same year, and several older generations of 747s were flying the same week, but N740CK remains one of the oldest 747-400s still in the air.

Data from the Simple Flying Flight Tracker for November 16 to 22 shows N740CK flying 17 times. Sixteen flights appear in schedule records, and the tracker’s ADS-B receivers picked up one more: a Seoul to Kuala Lumpur leg on November 22 under the callsign CKS442, which appears in no schedule record. Measured in UTC, the aircraft took off at least twice every day of the week.

The routing shows how cargo networks move a single aircraft around the Pacific. N740CK started in Chicago, flew to Shanghai via Anchorage, then went on to Seoul and back across the Pacific to New York before returning to Chicago. It next flew nonstop to Tokyo, returned to Chicago through Anchorage, and then repeated the pattern with Xiamen. From Xiamen it went to Seoul, back to Los Angeles through Anchorage, then to Seoul again, before ending the week in Kuala Lumpur.

The 16 scheduled legs covered about 49,000 miles (78,860 km). The longest was the Chicago to Tokyo flight on November 18, which covered 6,260 miles (10,074 km) in 12 hours and 44 minutes. The shortest was the 511-mile (822 km) hop from Shanghai to Seoul.

Anchorage dominated N740CK’s week. Twelve of its 17 flights either started or ended at Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport (ANC), and the aircraft passed through it six times in seven days. Six of its seven Pacific crossings stopped there. The only exception was the November 18 flight from Chicago to Tokyo, which flew 6,260 miles (10,074 km) nonstop.

Location is the main reason. The airport describes itself as the midway point between New York and Tokyo, within 9.5 hours' flight time of “90% of the industrialised world”. A stop there splits a transpacific trip into two shorter legs, and that changes what a freighter can carry. As Flightradar24 explains, aircraft that stop in Anchorage carry far less fuel than a non-stop, and as a result can haul a lot more cargo. That trade matters on a 747, since FreightWaves puts the maximum payload of a factory-built 747-400 freighter at 249,000 pounds (113,000 kg). Every pound of fuel that a nonstop flight needs comes out of that limit.

Anchorage has also built its business around cargo. The Anchorage Daily News reported that the airport became the largest cargo hub in the US last year, based on Airports Council International rankings. Its location is not the only draw. The state of Alaska promotes liberal cargo transfer rules that let a carrier connect any homeland city the carrier serves to any US city the carrier serves by transferring cargo in Alaska among two or more of the same carrier’s aircraft. For an operator like Kalitta, that turns Anchorage into both a refueling point and a place to reshuffle freight between aircraft heading to different cities in Asia and North America.

Exploring the design of the Boeing 747-400F.

N740CK is a Boeing 747-4H6(BCF), serial number 24405 and line number 745. The US Federal Aviation Administration registry lists its build year as 1989. The “BCF” stands for Boeing Converted Freighter, so the aircraft did not start out carrying only cargo. It was originally delivered to Malaysia Airlines as 9M-MHM, a Boeing 747-4H6M, the combi version that carried both passengers and freight on the main deck. One photo from its Malaysia Airlines years shows it wearing “Visit Malaysia Year 1990” promotional titles. That history adds weight to where the tracker found the aircraft at the end of the week, in Kuala Lumpur.

After leaving Malaysia Airlines, the jet was converted to a full freighter and joined Kalitta. FAA records cited by Flycraft show that its airworthiness date is October 15, 2003, and its FAA certificate was issued March 20, 2008, with the aircraft registered to KALITTA AIR LLC (Ypsilanti, MI). It flies under the name Doug Kalitta Sr. I and has carried Kalitta Air / DHL International titles.

Its build year places it at the start of the 747-400 program. The FAA certified the variant on January 9, 1989, and Northwest Airlines put it into service on February 9 that year. Boeing went on to deliver 694 747-400s between 1989 and 2009. N740CK is not the only survivor from 1989 at Kalitta. Its sister ship N741CK is also a 1989 build, and the tracker recorded it making 12 scheduled flights this week, plus one more seen only on ADS-B between Diego Garcia and Zhengzhou. Because the registry lists only the build year, the tracker data cannot show which of the two is older.

Kalitta remains one of the largest 747-400 operators. The Air Line Pilots Association lists its fleet at 22 Boeing 747-400s and six 777s, with more 777s to come, and FreightWaves has named DHL Express and the US military among its key customers. The 747’s nose door and large main deck have kept the type in demand for outsized and high-volume freight long after passenger airlines retired it.

That role is gradually shrinking. Kalitta has introduced seven Israel Aerospace Industries-converted 777-300ERSF freighters, and ch-aviation has reported the airline’s plan to gradually replace its legacy fleet of 747 freighters with new 777s. The economics favor the twin. IAI says its converted 777 has 14% more volume than a 747-400 converted freighter and is 21% more fuel-efficient. Converted aircraft like N740CK also face rising maintenance costs as they age, and every additional year in service requires more inspection and repair work.

No new 747-400s are coming to replace older ones either. The final 747-400, the last of 694, was delivered in December 2009, so every example still flying is at least 16 years old. Neither of the newest airliner programs from China and Russia offers an alternative in this class: COMAC’s C919, of which China’s three largest airlines received 15 in 2025, and the Yakovlev MC-21, which launch customer Aeroflot does not expect to enter commercial service until the end of 2026, are both narrowbody passenger jets with nothing approaching the capacity of a 747 freighter. For heavy transpacific cargo, operators are choosing between aging 747s and Boeing’s own widebody twins.

The iconic passenger aircraft has been given a second lease of life.

N740CK’s distinction applies only to the 747-400. The same week’s tracker data shows several civil 747s from earlier generations still flying, not counting the US Air Force’s VC-25A and E-4B. They include five 747-200s, registered ER-BAQ, ER-BAR, ER-BAT, EX-47002 and EX-47004, and a 747-300, EW-465TQ. The tracker also recorded one 747SP, Pratt & Whitney Canada’s C-GTFF.

Most of these older jumbos are registered in former Soviet states, with ER prefixes for Moldova, EX for Kyrgyzstan, and EW for Belarus. They also flew regularly during the week. The tracker recorded ER-BAR every day from November 16 to 22, under four different callsigns, and recorded EX-47002 throughout the week even though it transmitted no callsign. Build years for these aircraft are not in the data, because the registry information the tracker draws on covers only US-registered aircraft, so the article cannot rank them by age.

The gap between these aircraft and N740CK is more than a few years on the calendar. The 747-200 and 747-300 rely on a flight engineer, while the 747-400 introduced a glass cockpit and a two-pilot crew, along with winglets and a longer wingspan. That change helped the -400 outlast its predecessors in mainstream fleets, and it explains why most remaining 747-200s and 747-300s fly with smaller operators while 747-400s like N740CK still work for carriers with global networks. Freight is now the main job for all of them, as passenger 747 service has largely ended.

#6037. Kimpton Social Password Winter 2026-2027: “This Calls For Something”

Kimpton has a pretty cool “social password” concept, whereby you can receive extra perks for sharing a phrase at check-in. Kimpton generally has this promotion a couple of times per year — we last saw this in summer, and there’s now a new password for winter.

I’d like to talk about what the new password is, share my experience using it, and also pose a question to Kimpton regulars about the least cringeworthy way to go about saying it.

Kimpton is one of the cooler IHG hotel groups, and there are a variety of things that set Kimpton apart from other IHG brands. One of those things is the social password. The idea is that seasonally, Kimpton provides a phrase through social media that you’re supposed to say when you check-in, and if you do that, you’ll receive something extra.

The new Kimpton password is “this calls for something,” and it’s valid for stays between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027. So just say that when you check-in at a Kimpton property during the promotion period, and you’ll receive a surprise.

For those curious about what happens when you say the Kimpton password, I stayed at the Kimpton EPIC Miami some time back, which was my first Kimpton stay in quite a while (and I haven’t stayed at one since either). It was a good value as well, as I was able to use a free night award earned with the New IHG One Rewards Premier Credit Card (learn more).

I was curious what the benefit would be for using the password. So I shared the password with the front desk agent. At the conclusion of the check-in experience, he brought out a game show-style wheel. I might have spun too hard, as it must have gone around for about 30 seconds. Go figure I landed on the tile that just had me spin again.

Then I spun again, and the prize was free parking. I had a car and was staying for two nights, and parking costs $44 per night. So using the Kimpton password saved me nearly $100 — score!!

Based on looking at the wheel, it seems that some of the other prizes include a free welcome drink, free breakfast, free snacks, and a free movie. There were also a few empty squares, where I guess you don’t win anything. And I’m not sure what the alarm clock, car tipping over, or postcard of Miami get you. Regardless, I’d say those are some awesome prizes, and I got a great reward.

It’s cute how the Kimpton EPIC Miami makes a game of this. I know there’s a lot of inconsistency when it comes to this benefit across Kimpton properties. Some hotels provide meaningful perks (an upgrade, free, parking, etc.), like I got here, while other hotels provide a 19 cent branded koozie.

It’s great that this has stuck around, given that it has presumably become increasingly popular. Years ago not everyone was on social media, so it was a good way to encourage people to follow Kimpton on X, Facebook, Instagram, etc. With the way the internet has evolved, times have changed a bit.

I’m sure I’m not the only one who finds the concept of saying a password at check-in to be kind of weird. So I think it’s fun to compare notes about how people share the password at the front desk. I find it awkward to just blurt out the password out of nowhere.

So when I used this for my stay, I said “I guess I’m supposed to say [social password] as the social password?” That did the trick, but I’d be curious to hear how other Kimpton regulars go about this!

Between November 27, 2026, and February 28, 2027, Kimpton’s social password is “this calls for something.” Just state that phrase when you check-in at a Kimpton, and you should get some sort of a surprise. The gift will vary by property, so there’s no reason not to take advantage of this if staying at a Kimpton.

The last time I used the password I got to spin a wheel at check-in, and then I ended up getting free parking, which was a value of $44 per night.

If you’ve used the Kimpton password, what was your experience like?

#6036. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

Rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

Zinke’s wife, son, and sister currently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

In a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke said.

None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

“While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” said Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Issue One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

“I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” said Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

“Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

It marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s company, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

“We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he said, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

“If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

#6035. WestJet Cancels All Flights To 3 Countries: See Full List Now

WestJet is the second-largest airline in Canada. The carrier flies to more than 30 countries and has been restructuring its network this year. While it has added several new routes, it has also pulled out of a number of markets.

We took a look at the airline's schedule data from aviation analytics provider Cirium, which is currently available through October 2027, and found that WestJet has canceled all flights to three countries: Cuba, Denmark, and Colombia. Interestingly, the latter two were relatively recent additions to the Calgary-based airline's international network.

Cuba has been part of WestJet's network since 2009, when the airline launched three weekly flights between Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ) and Varadero's Juan Gualberto Gómez International Airport (VRA). Since then, the carrier has gradually expanded its presence in the country. It served seven destinations in Cuba this year, as detailed in the table below.

However, Cuba has been facing a shortage of Jet A-1 aviation fuel since the beginning of this year. The country's air navigation authority has repeatedly renewed notices regarding the unavailability of aviation fuel across all ten major international airports. The latest extension runs through at least December 1, 2026.

WestJet initially explored ways to continue its operations without relying on local fuel supplies, such as carrying enough fuel for round-trip journeys or making technical refueling stops outside Cuba. However, it eventually decided to suspend its services to the country indefinitely and has since removed all scheduled flights to its seven Cuban destinations.

Toronto; Montreal; Ottawa; Quebec; Winnipeg;

Calgary; Halifax; Edmonton; Windsor; Vancouver;

The cuts elsewhere are for very different reasons, and we have reached out to WestJet for comment. The Calgary-based airline only entered the Danish market this year. In May, it launched four weekly flights between Halifax Stanfield International Airport (YHZ) and Copenhagen Airport (CPH) using its Boeing 737 MAX 8. The last flights between the two cities operated in September.

When the route was launched, it was expected to benefit from WestJet's codeshare agreement with Scandinavian Airlines (SAS). As is often the case when a new nonstop service is introduced, the route stimulated demand, and passenger traffic between Halifax and Copenhagen rose by an estimated 455% between May and July compared to the same period last year.

However, booking data for May–July 2026 suggests that very few passengers connected to other flights in Copenhagen. Instead, more than 60% of passengers began or ended their journeys in Copenhagen and connected in Halifax, which may have put pressure on yields. As for Colombia, the carrier offered one weekly flight between Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and San Andrés' Gustavo Rojas Pinilla International Airport (ADZ).

It inherited the route from Sunwing Airlines, which WestJet acquired in 2023. The leisure airline launched the winter seasonal service in December 2022. Following the integration of Sunwing's flying operations, the service operated under the WestJet banner during the 2025–2026 winter season but has been removed from this winter's schedule.

Three are long-haul, while the rest are within the Caribbean, Mexico and the US. Find them all here!

This comes as the Calgary-based airline prepares to launch several new routes to sun destinations over the coming weeks. Today, it is launching a weekly service between Winnipeg James Armstrong Richardson International Airport (YWG) and Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ) in the Dominican Republic.

Four more routes will follow in December, all of which will be served on a once-weekly basis. On December 14, the carrier will launch flights from Winnipeg to Philip S. W. Goldson International Airport (BZE) in Belize City, as well as from Regina International Airport (YQR) to Los Cabos International Airport (SJD) in Mexico.

Three days later, it will introduce flights between Calgary International Airport (YYC) and Mérida International Airport (MID). The last of the four routes will launch on December 20, connecting Ottawa Macdonald-Cartier International Airport (YOW) to Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport (LIR) in Liberia, Costa Rica.

#6034. Buy American AAdvantage Miles For 50% Off (1.88 Cents Each): Worth It?

American Airlines is currently offering a rare elevated promotion on purchasing AAdvantage miles. Through December 2, 2026, AAdvantage members can purchase miles with up to a 50% discount, which is potentially an opportunity to buy miles for 1.88 cents each.

While that’s not a price at which I’d proactively pick up miles, there are definitely some situations where that could represent a good value, if you have an immediate use in mind, especially for first and business class travel.

Note that offers like this are extremely rare — while American offers a 40% off promotion on buying miles consistently, the 50% off promotion seems to come around just once or twice per year.

Link: Buy American Airlines AAdvantage miles with a discount

Between 12:01AM CT on November 27 and 11:59PM CT on December 2, 2026, American AAdvantage is offering up to a 50% discount (or 100% bonus, if you prefer) on buying miles. The offer is tiered, and you get a bigger discount the more miles you buy, as follows:

As you can see, you need to buy a lot of miles to get the best price!

Ordinarily American sells AAdvantage miles for 3.5 cents each pre-tax, or 3.76 cents after factoring in the 7.5% federal excise tax. That’s before any discounts or bonuses. In this case if you max out the promotion and buy 500,000 AAdvantage miles, you’d pay a total of $9,406.25, which comes out to 1.88 cents per mile (that factors in the 7.5% tax).

Keep in mind that American Airlines mileage purchases are non-refundable, and buying AAdvantage miles doesn’t count toward your Loyalty Points total (other than any amount you may spend on an eligible credit card). Purchased miles typically post nearly instantly, but in some cases, it can take up to four hours for them to post.

The 50% discount is the best price we’ve seen from American AAdvantage in recent years, and again, it only comes around once or twice per year. With the standard 40% off promotion on buying miles, you’d ordinarily pay 2.26 cents per mile.

The American AAdvantage program ordinarily allows members to buy at most 300,000 miles per account per calendar year, before factoring in any bonuses. However, during this promotion, that cap has been increased to 500,000 miles. AAdvantage accounts less than 30 days old aren’t eligible to buy American Airlines miles. Miles can only be purchased in 1,000-point increments.

The process of buying American Airlines miles is easy — the easiest way is to simply follow this link. Alternatively, you can go to aa.com, click on “AAdvantage” at the top of the page, and then click on “Buy, gift or transfer miles.”

From there, you’ll be prompted to log into your AAdvantage account, and then that’s where you can select how many miles you’d like to buy. When you buy American Airlines miles, they’ll typically post to your account instantly.

Yes, you absolutely can buy American Airlines miles, you just have to be aware of a few restrictions. For one, your account needs to be at least 30 days old. On top of that, you have to stay within the annual cap.

It’s possible to buy miles for yourself or others, but you’ll need to be sure you use the right account to make the purchase.

Here’s every promotion on purchased AAdvantage miles we’ve tracked since November 2025, with the cost per mile for each, so you can see how the current deal stacks up.

Is this a good deal? At 1.88 cents per mile, the current promotion is 50% below the standard price. That matches the best deal we’ve tracked. It’s 0.38 cents above our 1.5-cent valuation of AAdvantage miles.

#6033. Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the new year, making the most of their coming majority.

That means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

Arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, said the pressure will be on from day one.

“Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan said.

Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

The work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

Some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the new Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, said Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

“Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres said.

“There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he said.

In addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the new Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

“For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a big difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

Standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

“But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”

Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

“The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren said.

Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

“There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”

“I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

“We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet announced — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

In prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

“I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin said.

#6032. Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Review: Is The Admirals Club Perk Worth It?

The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (formerly known as the Citi AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard) is American Airlines’ most premium co-branded credit card, as part of the Citi partnership. While the Citi AA Executive Card has a steep annual fee, it offers strong perks, ranging from an Admirals Club membership, to the ability to supercharge your AAdvantage elite status, to credits that can help offset the annual fee.

If you ask me, it’s one of the best value premium airline credit cards out there, and it’s also the airline credit card with the strongest lounge access perks. While products like the American Express Platinum Card® (learn more) and Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) might typically be the first that come to mind when people consider premium cards, this one could make a lot more sense if you’re a frequent American flyer.

In this post, I’d like to take an in-depth look at the Citi AA Executive Card, with my Citi AAdvantage Executive Card review. I think this is especially important in light of the card’s recent refresh, where we saw the annual fee increase, but also saw new perks added.

Link: Learn more about the Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard®

Let me start by briefly summarizing the key details of the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card:

This is the ideal card if you value American Admirals Club lounge access, if you’re going for elite status with American AAdvantage, or if you can just make the credits on the card work. If you’re just an occasional American flyer, there are probably more affordable options that will be easier to justify in the long term. However, with the card’s big welcome bonus, there’s a huge incentive to give this card a try.

One of the reasons that you’ll want to consider applying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the excellent welcome bonus it has. Of course that has to be balanced with the annual fee, and you also have to take into account the eligibility requirements, so let’s go through those details for the Citi AA Executive Card.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card currently has a welcome bonus of 80,000 AAdvantage bonus miles after spending $8,000 within the first three months.

Personally, I value American AAdvantage miles at ~1.5 cents each, so to me, those miles are worth about $1,200. That’s an excellent bonus, especially for a card that also offers a lot of value in the long run. There are so many great uses of AAdvantage miles, including for travel on partner airlines.

For what it’s worth, I value Delta SkyMiles at 1.1 cents each, and United MileagePlus miles at 1.3 cents each, so these are the most valuable miles among the “big three” carriers, based on my math.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card bonus miles aren’t available to those who have received a new cardmember bonus for this card in the past 48 months (however, you are eligible if you’ve had a different American Airlines credit card, including if you’ve received a bonus on a different product).

Then there are the typical rules for Citi credit card applications, including that you can apply for at most one card with Citi every eight days, and at most two cards every 65 days.

There’s not a consistent credit score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines eligibility.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card has a $695 annual fee. There’s also a lot of value to adding authorized users (as I’ll discuss below). You can expect to pay a total of $175 for up to three authorized users (so potentially under $60 each), and then each authorized user after that costs $175.

Keep in mind that if you’re a Citigold customer, you can receive a $145 annual rebate on your annual fee, which is a nice perk.

When it comes to spending money on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, here’s the rewards structure:

In terms of the reward for spending, there are potentially better cards for purchasing airline tickets, and also better cards for everyday spending. However, keep in mind that the most compelling reason to spend money on the card is in order to earn elite status with American Airlines. American Airlines uses its Loyalty Points system for status qualification, and credit card spending can help you earn status.

American’s elite requirements are currently as follows, and you earn one Loyalty Point for every dollar spent on an American Airlines credit card:

Spending on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card could earn you elite status, which I know will interest many. That’s the primary reason you’ll want to consider this card for spending.

I do want to specifically point out one thing that throws people off — you earn one Loyalty Point per dollar spent on the card, unrelated to how many miles you earn for spending. In other words, if you’re making an American Airlines purchase, you’d earn 4x AAdvantage redeemable miles, but only 1x Loyalty Points on the purchase as such.

In addition to earning one Loyalty Point for every dollar spent on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can also earn up to 40,000 Loyalty Points every year just for being a cardmember:

In other words, if you have this card, you’d only otherwise need to earn 170,000 Loyalty Points for Executive Platinum status, since this card would get you a boost of 30,000 Loyalty Points at that level. Those Loyalty Points can be earned in a variety of ways, ranging from flying, to online shopping, to credit card spending, to booking vacation packages. Either way, this Loyalty Points boost would be quite the advantage in terms of qualifying for Loyalty Point Rewards, and even upgrade priority.

The AAdvantage elite qualifying year goes from the beginning of March until the end of February of the following year. You don’t need to have the card at the beginning of the year to take advantage of this, so even if you open the card during the membership year, you could still earn 40,000 bonus Loyalty Points for that year (in other words, the credits can be retroactive).

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this can be a good option for purchases abroad.

While you’ll want to consult the full cardmember agreement and guide to benefits, the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers useful travel protection, including trip cancellation coverage, trip interruption coverage, trip delay protection, lost baggage protection, rental car coverage, and more.

So this is a good card to potentially use for travel purchases, since you have to put them on your card to take advantage of those benefits.

One of the main reasons you may want to get the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the lounge access perks that the card offers. Having the Citi AA Executive Card is the best way to access Admirals Clubs. Let’s discuss how that works.

The primary cardmember on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card receives a full Admirals Club membership, including guesting privileges. That in and of itself is a reason this card makes sense.

While Admirals Clubs aren’t anything to get too excited about, they are improving nicely, in terms of design, and also in terms of the quality of food and beverages. I also appreciate the expansion of the Provisions by Admirals Club concept, whereby the airline offers Admirals Club members grab & go facility, where they can get some drinks or snacks to go before their flight.

Ordinarily, if you were to buy a comparable Admirals Club membership with guesting privileges, you’d pay a minimum of $1,200 per year.

By getting an Admirals Club membership with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you’re saving $505-705 right off the bat.

Note that while you can redeem miles for an Admirals Club membership, it’s a terrible value, as you’re getting only a cent per mile.

What you get with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is a full Admirals Club membership, so you don’t even have to bring your credit card, as your membership will be linked to your AAdvantage number:

Admirals Club members don’t get access to Flagship Lounges, as that access is determined based on the ticket you purchased rather than any membership.

Many people may be considering applying for the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card shortly before taking an American Airlines trip. How soon after being approved for the card does your Admirals Club membership kick in?

Since the primary cardmember gets a full Admirals Club membership, it’s linked to their AAdvantage account. Many may be surprised to learn that this membership could very well kick in before you even receive your credit card in the mail, and you don’t even need your card to enter a lounge.

Fortunately, there’s an easy way to tell if your Admirals Club membership has been activated. To figure it out, pretend that you’re signing up for an Admirals Club membership. Go to this page, enter your AAdvantage number, last name, and password.

If your account has already been updated to reflect the Admirals Club membership, you’ll see that the next page shows “1-Year Citi AADV Exec CC Membership.”

If it hasn’t been updated, you’ll see that it gives you the option of choosing what kind of membership you want to purchase.

Note that this only works for the primary cardmember. Since the authorized users don’t get a full Admirals Club membership, they wouldn’t show up as being eligible online. Authorized users need to present the physical Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, since there’s no membership linked to their AAdvantage account.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card also offers Admirals Club access for authorized users. As I explained above, you can add up to three authorized users for a total of $175, which potentially comes out to under $60 per authorized user. I’d say that’s a real sweet spot, since securing lounge access for friends and family for under $60 each is an amazing value.

Note that authorized users receive Admirals Club access and not a membership, so there are the restrictions:

For the purposes of accessing Admirals Clubs this is more or less the same as an outright membership.

Adding authorized users to the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is super easy, and can be done directly on Citi’s website. Follow this link to access the part of the Citi website where you add authorized users, and then log into your account.

On the next page, you’ll be able to manage authorized users, including adding and removing them.

You’ll just need their name to add them, and you have the choice of whether or not you want to give them permission to access your online account.

Make sure you trust all your authorized users, since any charges they incur will be your responsibility.

The primary reason to get the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is because of the great welcome bonus, ability to earn status with spending, ability to receive 40,000 Loyalty Points annually just for being a cardmember, and Admirals Club benefit.

However, the Citi AA Executive Card offers some other perks that could add a lot of value for card members. These perks range from priority check-in at business class counters, to early boarding, to inflight or Admirals Club credits, to savings with American Airlines Vacations, Lyft, Avis, Budget, Global Entry, or TSA PreCheck, to elite status with Avis and Omni.

Below is what you need to know about all the other perks of the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card.

Those with the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card receive a first checked bag free on domestic American Airlines itineraries not just for themselves, but also for up to eight companions traveling on the same reservation. There’s no need to actually pay for the ticket with your Citi AAdvantage Executive Card — you just have to make sure it’s linked to your AAdvantage account (this benefit applies for the primary cardmember only).

American ordinarily charges $45-50 for the first checked bag, so that’s a $90-100 value per person roundtrip (and if you had eight companions all checking a bag, that would be a value of $810-900).

One thing that sometimes throws off cardmembers is that this benefit doesn’t work for international flights, and it doesn’t work for a second bag, if your fare includes one bag. So just understand this is exclusively a first checked bag benefit on domestic flights.

For being the primary cardmember on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card you receive several valuable airport benefits, including priority check-in, priority airport screening, and early boarding. These are all features that can save you time and money.

There’s no need to show your card, as these perks should automatically be reflected with your ticket when you have your credit card linked to your AAdvantage account (which is automatic when you’re the primary cardmember).

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $500 in statement credits per calendar year toward American Airlines Vacations purchases. American Airlines Vacations is the carrier’s vacation package portal. This credit is semi-annual, meaning you can take advantage of a $250 credit every six months (once in January through June, and once in July through December).

This applies for a booking of two or more travel components, like a flight, car reservation, or hotel booking. Many people find American Airlines Vacations to be a great deal, and a good way to earn bonus Loyalty Points.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $200 in InKind credits every year. This comes in the form of a $100 semi-annual credit, with one being available January 1 through June 30, and the other being available July 1 through December 31. This can be used across multiple meals, and tips aren’t covered by the credit. Either the primary cardmember or authorized users can use the perk, though authorized users don’t get extra credits.

InKind is my favorite dining rewards app, and to me, this is basically good as cash. I dine at InKind restaurants constantly, as there are some really high quality restaurants on the list, so I value this new card perk immensely. If you’re new to InKind, make sure you also register through a refer-a-friend link, so you can get an extra credit.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers up to $180 in Lyft credits every year. This comes in the form of a $15 Lyft credit each month after taking three eligible rides. The Lyft credit expires 30 days after it’s issued. Either the primary cardmember or authorized users can use the perk, though authorized users don’t get extra credits. Admittedly this requires quite a bit of effort to use, so not everyone will get value from that.

Just for having the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can receive up to $120 back on eligible Avis or Budget rentals every calendar year. Just charge an eligible pre-paid rental to your card each year, and you’ll receive a statement credit up to the $120 limit. This can be used toward a single rental or multiple rentals made directly with Avis or Budget. If you rent with Avis and Budget with any frequency, this could be worth face value.

Just for having the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card, you can receive up to $100 in statement credits every calendar year toward spending onboard American flights, or in Admirals Clubs. So you can use this credit to purchase everything from premium drinks or snacks on flights, to premium alcoholic drinks in Admirals Clubs.

Just charge the eligible purchase to your card, and you’ll be reimbursed automatically, with no registration required.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck credit once every four years, which is worth up to $120. Simply charge the purchase to your card and it will automatically be reimbursed. You don’t have to be the one signing up — you can always pay for a friend or family member who is signing up instead.

Personally, I always recommend applying for Global Entry, because Global Entry automatically comes with TSA PreCheck, while the inverse isn’t true.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card now offers some perks with Omni Hotels & Resorts. For those not familiar, Omni operates around 50 properties in the United States and Canada, so there’s value in getting extra perks at these hotels. Specifically:

To take advantage of this, you’ll want to enroll before your stay, book your stay direct with Omni, and pay with the card. If you stay at Omni properties with any frequencies, this is quite a nice value-add, if you ask me.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card offers complimentary Avis President’s Club status, with enrollment available through August 31, 2028.

Avis President’s Club status offers a variety of perks, including car upgrades, expedited service, complimentary additional drivers, and more. If you rent from Avis, you should definitely be able to get some value from this.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is a World Legend Mastercard, meaning that it comes with quite a few benefits you may not be familiar with. In addition to the concierge service, there are also savings and other perks with a variety of businesses, ranging from DoorDash to HelloFresh.

Let me once again state that this card used to be known as the Citi AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard, before recently being rebranded as a World Legend Mastercard.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is a lucrative card that I personally have and also recommend, but only if you’re a frequent flyer with American. If you fly American with any frequency then an Admirals Club membership is valuable, and this is the best way to get an Admirals Club membership. There can even be value in adding up to three authorized users, which will cost a total of $175, as they’d get Admirals Club access as well.

In addition to lounge access, the Citi AA Executive Card offers up to 40,000 Loyalty Points per year (even without spending money on the card), which can make a big difference for anyone chasing status with American. Furthermore, the card potentially offers hundreds of dollars in credits per year, which can help offset the annual fee.

However, this isn’t a card that I’d use for my everyday spending unless I specifically valued the added Loyalty Points from spending. Otherwise, there are much more rewarding cards for everyday spending, and I’d just hold onto this card for the very strong perks, including lounge access, and the bonus Loyalty Points without a spending requirement.

For my mental accounting purposes, I take the $695 annual fee, and then subtract the $200 InKind credit, which I consider to basically be worth face value. That really takes the “out of pocket” on the card to $495 per year for me, which is an amazing deal for the Admirals Club membership and bonus Loyalty Points.

While the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is American’s most premium credit card, it’s also worth being aware of the Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (learn more), which has a $350 annual fee. There are lots of reasons to consider that card, including an excellent welcome bonus. Among other things:

I think there’s potentially merit to having both cards, especially if you value earning the Loyalty Points bonuses. Otherwise I’d say the Citi AAdvantage Globe Card is easier to justify if you’re an occasional American flyer, while I think the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card is easier to justify if you value an Admirals Club membership.

The Citi AAdvantage Executive Card isn’t for everyone. If you’re not a frequent flyer on American then you shouldn’t consider this card. However, if you are a frequent flyer on American then this card is totally for you.

While Admirals Clubs aren’t anything to get too excited about, there’s still huge value in the complimentary snacks and drinks, free Wi-Fi and quiet places to sit, and access to an agent in the event your flight has irregular operations.

Even beyond the Admirals Club membership, the card offers other useful perks, like the ability to earn Loyalty Points, priority services with American, and the ability to receive credits with American Airlines Vacations, InKind, Avis, Budget, Lyft, and more.

I’ve had the Citi AA Executive Card for years, and love it. If you don’t yet have the card, this is a good time to apply, given the offer that’s available.

If you want to learn more about the Citi Executive AAdvantage Card or want to apply, follow this link.

Whether or not one values an Admirals Club visit at $75 for a day pass (or $70 at an Alaska lounge), that's the going rate. So, if a person has 10 or more visits per year and considers no other card benefits, the card is worth the annual fee. Then, throw in the value of guest entry. After that, other card benefits are gravy.

Thanks for this good summary. And thanks too to Peter for his useful comment. One comparative benefit of this card is that certain other ones, such as the Amex Platinum and Capitol One Venture X, now charge for taking in a guest to their affiliated lounges. In contrast, this card does not. I haven't fully explored the new Inkind benefit yet, but its app has worked pretty easily the two times I've used it. Plus Inkind offers other perks, such as (if I understand it correctly) 20 percent off a (pre-tip) restaurant bill and currently $50 off a $150 bill at a particular local restaurant I frequent anyway. I'm finding the lounge access a valuable perk not just generally, but because the nicest lounge in SFO Terminal One, which I usually use, is Alaska's. I used that lounge for both AA and Alaska flights, since they're both in T1. I guess an additional value for the card for me is that, even though its only one point per dollar for most transactions, I still like putting some spending on it since I value and used AA miles so much. While I aim to get another, less expensive Citi card for that purpose, my luck with Citi was pretty bad until I got this card. Apparently in Citi's view, according to the rejection notices, I have too much available credit compared to my spending levels.

This card is a no brainer for many and a no way for others. No brainer for me. If you live in a major metro area, the $200 inKind is as good as cash. It's not just sit down restaurants - my local coffee and pizza place are on inKind. Even if you value the $200 at $130 (can sometimes get discounted $100 inKind gift cards at costco for $64.99) it's still easy money. $120 Avis is easy to use, just can't stack with AA Cars. $100 F&B is an upgrade from 25% off F&B - will actually use that now. $250x2 off AA Vacations... look, it's not the most exciting credit out there, and I'd value it at $0 with any use of it being a bonus. I view it as max $200 off because with AA Vacations you basically have to pay $50/pp for the PDP cancellation protection, otherwise it's like buying basic economy. And it's really only useful for solo travel because otherwise you are sharing the miles/LP with the entire booking party. If you can use it, great, just have to run the math on whether it's actually saving you money. I think if AA does not extend the MaximizeMiles promotion on it (currently expires 12/31, they extended it from 9/30...), it makes the math much harder. For me the sweet spot is AA Hotels / AA Cars. AA Hotels though - you can really get an incredible amount of miles/LP if you have any AA card and any AA status. Plus 12x on spend on the card - it's really fantastic. Like with anything else, you just have to run the math. If you're a hotel free agent like I am - it works out really well to use AA Hotels, although the new Rove set-up is intriguing as well. Hard to put a value on up to 40k LP, but if you value AA status, that has significant value. Obviously if you have citigold and it's $145 cheaper - even better. So you have to value AA status, AA Hotels/Cars and Admirals Club access to make this card worth it. I do, so it's an easy win for me. If you don't value any of those things... probably not the card for you.

#6030. American Airlines Threatens To Call Police On First Class Passenger Over Economy Downgrade

An American Airlines passenger says she was told to leave her first class seat on a flight from New York JFK to Chicago, so another traveler could have it, with an employee asking whether police would need to be called when she objected. She posted a video of the exchange to Instagram and wants an apology and compensation, saying the only offer at the airport was a $300 travel credit. She also asks whether American singled her out because of her race, gender, age, or cat, an allegation the sources reviewed do not show American answering.

The flight appears to be American 3162 on Friday, November 27, a Boeing 737 that left JFK at 3:09 PM and reached Chicago O’Hare (ORD) 33 minutes early. The woman, who describes herself as Chinese and in her 20s, says she paid for first class because she was traveling with her cat, and that a broken seat in the cabin left another passenger needing hers. She says the only other passenger she saw singled out was an Indian man.

In the clip, which begins mid-argument, she asks who made the decision and an employee answers, “The system decided.” Before agreeing, she insists on a refund, and the employee asks whether the passengers will cooperate. A pilot then tells her a refund will come through customer service, and when she asks what proof she has, he says he does not know and that she must move or leave the aircraft. She says she was also warned that the whole flight could be canceled if she stayed put, and she tells staff more than once that she can move. Gary Leff of View from the Wing identified the flight from a seat-pocket safety card marked 737 and the post’s 7:46 PM timestamp, which preceded boarding on American’s only other 737 to Chicago that day.

American’s downgrade list ranks passengers by how they obtained the seat, starting with employees and space-available guests, then upgraded passengers, then award redemptions, and finally paying first class customers, with higher fare classes and elite status offering more protection. Leff argues the computer does not consider race, so the ordinary list explains the outcome, though he says the video still shows poor handling. He adds that the cat could plausibly matter, since American lists pet travel as a reason the app may block check-in, which might have cost her priority, though that is unconfirmed.

Its conditions of carriage say American will not involuntarily remove a boarded passenger to give a seat to another passenger, yet federal rules still allow moving someone to coach on the same aircraft. A downgraded passenger is owed the fare difference automatically, a travel credit may come on top, and no denied boarding payment applies. In July, American told the Transportation Department it would replace its flat 40% refund with a formula that subtracts the average coach fare on the flight from the premium fare, which Leff says can differ from the coach fare a buyer passed up.

Midday AA flight over Wichita saw flight attendants separate two passengers after a reported inappropriate touch.

The episode follows similar disputes, including a Phoenix to Des Moines flight, explained by American in October, where a mother and son in working seats were selected after other seats failed and also alleged discrimination. Leff says staff could have apologized, explained the downgrade process, and offered compensation to the cabin for a voluntary move, as American did in the Phoenix case. Comedian Jim Breuer said in February that he was moved from first class to row 18 on a Honolulu to Phoenix flight to seat a commuting pilot, with Simple Flying reporting that he received a $500 voucher.

In April, another passenger alleged a downgrade to row 13 after an aircraft downsize, though the post gave no route or aircraft details. American has acknowledged a wider problem with cabin conditions, with chief customer officer Heather Garboden telling employees in April that the airline has too many broken seats, and an August report saying American planned to add more than 60 maintenance technicians at six airports under an initiative called OneCabin.
