People often ask me about my favorite hotels or my most memorable travel experiences. But because I travel so frequently (and have been doing so for decades), it’s difficult to pick those all-time favorites. I’ll settle for recapping some of my top travel experiences and hotel stays this year.

More so than ever, I’m focusing on experiencing nature — for me, this is really the way to see the world and create lasting memories. Yes, I can fly in all the first-class cabins, but seeing the world's natural wonders and wildlife has been far more life-changing for me.

This year, I also focused on family travel with my kids and parents. My children will be school-age before I know it, so I want to take advantage of not being tied to school holidays to travel and enjoy shoulder-season and offseason escapes when fewer people are traveling.

These were my top hotel stays and travel experiences of 2026.

I’m actually writing this as I return from an epic Norwegian adventure. I was just in Norway with my two sons and my parents, exploring the country in the blustery weather. I started off with a few days in Tromsø, taking my kids to the aquarium (they loved the seals!) and the library. Then, with my family by my side, I saw the northern lights. I’ve seen them before, but admiring them with my children was extra special.

Then we headed out on boat excursions to realize my dream of swimming with orcas, opting to book with Tromsø Pure because they focus on safety and on finding quieter spots away from other boats for a better experience.

At first, we spotted pods of humpbacks, and I was able to swim with them, which was one of the most out-of-body, exhilarating experiences I’ve ever had. There was even a brief moment when I thought I was about to be kicked and/or swallowed by a whale, which was terrifyingly thrilling (don’t worry — I’m still here).

Even though a few of the days had rough seas and low visibility, I was able to swim with orcas later on during the trip, and I’ll never forget it.

After taking nearly a dozen safaris over the years, I was ready for something different. I’ve done the bigger camps and seen the Big 5, so I wanted to try a more niche wildlife experience.

I stayed at Tswalu’s Loapi Lodge in a two-bedroom villa, complete with a plunge pool and my own private chef. I much prefer a lodge to a tented camp, as hearing lions outside your tent at night and having no running water can be a lot to handle, and I’m done roughing it.

Unlike many safari destinations, Tswalu is unique because there aren’t any elephants, but you can see meerkat colonies and observe them relatively up close. I also spotted many black and white rhinos and cheetahs.

I highly recommend Tswalu to experienced safari-goers, but if it’s your first time, I’d suggest going to Cheetah Plains in Sabi Sands or Royal Malewane in Kruger National Park. You’ll get to see the Big 5 and have the perfect introduction to a safari (and you might get addicted to safaris, like I am!).

Many people skip the Caribbean in summer, but honestly, European summer heat can feel even more brutal, with beaches packed umbrella-to-umbrella in places like Spain, Italy and Portugal. This year, I canceled my summer trip to Portugal after a massive heat wave alert and went to Grand Cayman with my kids instead.

Yes, it was warm, but it didn’t feel any hotter than Europe would have (or even a humid Midwest or East Coast summer), and the beach was uncrowded and uncomplicated — no stairs or rugged terrain, like I’ve had to traverse in Portugal. Plus, no jet lag!

My stay at Palm Heights was peaceful, and even though it's a boutique hotel, it felt very family-friendly. I loved that my suite overlooked the white sands of Seven Mile Beach, and the spa was absolutely gorgeous. I highly recommend it for families, couples, or any type of traveler.

In my opinion, the Ritz Paris represents true luxury. I used Chase Points Boost to book it, getting more than 2 cents per point.

The hotel is unapologetically over-the-top, with gorgeous rooms and lavish decor, but what I really love are the service and amenities. The hotel has a program that lets you check in early in the morning after landing from a transatlantic flight, and consumer-friendly options like this are what make it feel truly luxurious. After all, true luxury goes beyond a beautiful room or view — hotels should solve problems, reduce friction, and make traveling easier.

Did you have any special hotel stays or travel experiences this year? Feel free to drop me a comment below and share yours, and be sure to check out our full list for Where to Go in 2027.

#6028. Latino Democrats celebrate midterm gains, with warning for party

California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, here at a 2020 news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center, is the chair of BOLD PAC. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Latino voters moved sharply away from Republicans this year, and a record number of Latino Democratic candidates were elected.

But California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez has a warning for her fellow Democrats.

“Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” said Sánchez, who leads the campaign arm of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Failure to address rising costs and push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration agenda could once again scramble the political calculus and spark another realignment in two years, said House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar of California.

“While Latinos shifted towards Democrats and … gave us this mandate as a party, Democrats must continue to earn their trust, not just every two years, but every single day,’’ he said.

Leaders of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus joined newly elected Latino members on Tuesday for a news conference to celebrate the recent wins and the role the group played in securing the House majority for Democrats. The caucus will boast 55 members in the next Congress, its largest roster ever, according to Sánchez.

BOLD PAC, the caucus’ campaign arm, invested heavily in Latino candidates this year, including in primaries.

California Rep. Salud Carbajal noted that BOLD PAC raised more than $18.5 million this cycle, which helped candidates leverage outside money.

Working-class majority-Latino districts in South Texas, Arizona and California were among the areas that provided Democrats with their biggest wins. Democrats capitalized on voter dissatisfaction over rising costs, the very issue that helped Trump and the GOP make significant gains among Hispanic voters just two years earlier.

But the wins weren’t limited to districts with sizable Latino populations.

Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who flipped a swing seat in Nebraska, credited BOLD PAC for playing a key role in her win.

“Yes, there are Latinos in Omaha, and those Latinos actually helped decide this race,’’ she said. “BOLD believed in me as a candidate, but they also believed in our community.”

Rep.-elect Bobby Pulido, who came to politics after a successful career as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano singer, flipped a redrawn South Texas border district that Trump would have carried by 18 points in 2024.

“A lot of people feel like they don't belong to either party. But there's one thing about Latinos is we belong to each other,’’ Pulido said. “It's very hard to be a Latino right now in this country. … I expect to see us united, more united than ever, because it's a tough time right now.”

Several of the winning candidates deployed novel strategies to reach voters. Pulido famously began performing at quinceañeras after his Republican opponent dismissed him as a performer.

Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, who flipped a battleground district north of Denver, attended World Cup and Broncos watch parties. “If people don't hear our message, then it doesn't matter,’’ he said.

The candidates “met those voters where they were,’’ Sánchez said. “They went into those communities and interacted in a very real and meaningful way. That's something I think that strategists or consultants don't always get. It's not just about pumping out lots of television commercials.”

Amid those successes for Latino Democrats, Florida, home to one of the largest Latino electorates in the country, was a different story. Republicans held all three majority-Latino districts in the Sunshine State, though former news anchor Eliott Rodriguez, the son of Cuban immigrants, came within half a percentage point of unseating GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar in a district that backed Trump by 15 points in 2024.

BOLD PAC did have a victory to celebrate in Florida, with Rep. Darren Soto, the deputy chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, narrowly prevailing in a district that Republicans redrew as one that no longer had a Latino majority.

“The redistricting wars ended up failing because of the investment by BOLD PAC,’’ Soto said.

#6027. Ryanair Now Withholds Free Seats Until Just Before Departure, Blames Customer Feedback

Ryanair has quietly updated its policy for how it assigns seats to those people who don’t pay the seat assignment fee, as reported by The Irish Times. While I wouldn’t consider this to be anything unreasonable, what I’m amused by is the carrier’s justification. The airline claims that it’s doing this due to customer feedback, rather than to generate more revenue.

Ryanair is known for being an unapologetic ultra low cost carrier. The airline has low base fares, and then charges fees for just about everything. Among other things, the airline charges to assign seats in advance, and those who don’t pay for specific seat assignments are just randomly assigned seats (and often in a rather punitive way).

However, the way the airline is randomly allocating seats has quietly changed as of late October 2026, coinciding with the start of the winter schedule. Historically, the airline has automatically assigned seats to passengers without seat assignments around 24 hours before departure.

Some passengers seemed to “game” this, and would essentially “gamble.” What they’d do is wait until 24 hours out to see what seat they were assigned for free. Then if they weren’t happy with their automatic seat assignment, they could still pay to assign a better seat.

Under the new policy, the airline still issues a boarding pass up to 24 hours out, but without a seat assignment. Then the boarding pass automatically shows the seat assignment within four hours of departure.

The logic here seems pretty clear — some people do care somewhat about where they sit, but want to avoid fees if they can. By withholding seat assignments until hours before departure, passengers are presumably more likely to pay for seat assignments in advance, to avoid that uncertainty.

Ryanair has confirmed this seat assignment policy change in a statement, sharing that “the timing of the allocation of free random seats is determined at all times by the airline.” Right, nobody disputes that the airline has the right to do this.

So, what’s the logic for this policy change? According to the airline, it’s “to allow those passengers who wish to select their preferred seat more time to do so. We had a number of complaints this summer that passengers could not book their preferred seat on the day of travel as it had been already randomly allocated as a free seat up to 24 hours prior to departure.”

The Ryanair representative went on to say that “passengers who choose a free of charge random seat clearly don’t mind where they sit, and their digital boarding pass is automatically updated between three to four hours prior to departure, which is well before they arrive at either their departure airport or their boarding gate.”

Ryanair is of course within its rights to have this policy, but I think the logic is pretty obvious, and it’s to generate more revenue. After all, 24 hours out people would see what they were randomly assigned at online check-in, and would still have a lot of choices if they wanted to pay for seats, since most people don’t check-in online exactly at the 24-hour mark.

But within a few hours of departure, virtually everyone has checked in online, and not many seats will be left. So I imagine the goal is to condition more customers to pay for seat assignments in advance. I love the claim that customers complained that their preferred seats on the day of travel were randomly allocated to others for free:

Ryanair has a new policy for automatic seat allocations. In the past, the airline would automatically assign seats to passengers 24 hours out, giving them quite the window to “gamble” on the free seat assignment, and then pay for a different seat assignment if they weren’t happy with the free one.

The airline has now started only assigning free seats at most four hours out. The airline claims that this is due to customer feedback, so that passengers have more time to assign their choice of paid seats. However, I imagine that’s not quite accurate, and this is instead about conditioning people to pay for seat assignments, rather than “gambling” on the free allocations.

What do you make of this Ryanair seating policy change?

#6026. Allegiant Air Launches 21 New Routes: See Full List Now

With barely more than a month left until 2026 draws to a close, airlines around the world are looking ahead to 2027 and everything that the new year is set to have in store. For US-based ultra-low-cost carrier Allegiant Air, next year is shaping up to be one of considerable growth on the network front, with scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company, showing that it will start 21 new routes next year.

These figures are based on what is known as of late November, and more new additions will likely follow. In any case, the 21 routes in question are emblematic of Allegiant's wider strategy, as they primarily consist of leisure links, with secondary airports playing an important role. Furthermore, every single one of them is domestic.

Minneapolis/St. Paul International Airport (MSP) is one of three airports from which Allegiant plans four new routes in 2027. Three will start in April, with their destinations being Phoenix/Mesa, Sarasota, and Destin/Fort Walton Beach. They will be followed in May by the addition of Asheville in North Carolina. All four will be served by Airbus narrowbody twinjets, namely the A319 and A320.

Elsewhere, Gulf Shores' four additions will all come in May: Indianapolis, Little Rock, Shreveport, and Wichita. Airbus jets dominate, although Boeing 737s will serve some Shreveport flights. Contrastingly, three of Orlando Sanford's four new Allegiant routes (Boston, Grand Forks, and Providence) start in February. Washington Dulles is the exception, beginning in May.

Staying in the Sunshine State, Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL) is also set to see an Allegiant expansion in 2027, with two new routes starting. This facility has established itself as a competitive alternative for Miami-bound flyers in recent years. In February 2027, Allegiant will begin flying from here to Portsmouth and Providence using the 737 MAX 8-200.

Moving north, but staying on the subject of Florida, both new routes Allegiant Air is set to begin operating from Bishop International Airport (FNT) in Flint, Michigan, will also serve destinations in Florida. The destinations are Orlando International Airport (MCO) and Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW), with the Airbus A320 as the aircraft of choice. Their frequencies will peak at four flights a week in March.

Florida is also the common thread when it comes to Allegiant Air's two new routes that are set to start from Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) in 2027. In February of next year, the airline plans to operate two A320 rotations apiece from Boston to Punta Gorda and St. Petersburg, with two more 737 rotations in April. These limited schedules show the highly seasonal nature of such routes.

Allegiant is moving beyond bare-bones flying with a new premium cabin, bigger seats and complimentary drinks for passengers.

That leaves three more new Allegiant Air routes, all linking northeastern destinations with airports in Florida. From Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) in Pennsylvania, the carrier is set to operate 39 A320 rotations to Destin/Fort Walton Beach from May to August, peaking at three flights a week. Allegiant Air already serves another Florida destination from Philly, namely St. Petersburg.

Elsewhere, Allegiant flyers at Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG) can look forward to a new A320-operated link to Orlando. These twice-weekly flights will run from February to August. Finally, Allegiant will operate a limited schedule from Providence to Sarasota, with two A320 rotations apiece in February and April. Once again, these will cover short-term spikes in seasonal demand.

#6025. Book A Southwest Airlines Ticket, Get Promotional Companion Pass

Southwest Airlines has just introduced an incredibly generous promotion, which we see several times per year. With this, you can earn a promotional Companion Pass after booking a single roundtrip ticket, and that could be a great deal.

With a new promotion from Southwest, you can earn a promotional Companion Pass by booking a single roundtrip ticket (or two one-ways). Here are the details of how this works:

This is an extremely generous offer. We usually see an offer like this a few times per year, so it’s nice to see it return. It seems that even with all the other changes at Southwest, this promotion is at least one thing that’s remaining consistent.

For those of you not familiar with Companion Pass, it’s one of the best deals in travel. Those with Companion Pass can have a companion fly with them for just the cost of taxes, regardless of whether paying cash or redeeming points. Essentially think of it as a two-for-one travel pass, which is otherwise pretty unheard of.

Under the current rules, Southwest Companion Pass ordinarily requires 100 flights or 135,000 qualifying points in a calendar year, so this promotion offers quite the shortcut (though also with a limited travel window). We are seeing changes to Companion Pass in 2027, as Companion Pass will become a perk of top tier Platinum elite status, rather than something that’s separately qualified for.

Southwest Airlines has introduced a generous promotion that can earn you Companion Pass. Those who register and then book a roundtrip ticket between November 27 and November 29, 2026, for travel by January 5, 2027, can earn a promotional Companion Pass valid for several weeks early next year.

Obviously this promotion isn’t for everyone, but if you have any travel to potentially plan over the promotion period, then this offer is seriously worth considering. It’s awesome how often Southwest offers this promotion.

Southwest Airlines’ Companion Pass, which allows you to bring a friend nearly for free (you just have to pay the taxes and fees) on unlimited flights, is one of the most valuable assets in the world of points and miles.

It normally takes a whole lot of flying to unlock this pass — and one of the popular shortcuts that allows you to earn this pass with points from Southwest credit card bonuses is ending soon, which will only make it even harder to earn.

But if you'd rather spend your Black Friday weekend booking flights than buying discounted sweatpants, there is some good news. There's a new limited-time opportunity to earn a promotional Southwest Companion Pass if you book one round-trip or two one-way eligible Southwest flights by Sunday, Nov. 29, 2026, and travel on those flights by Jan. 5, 2027.

Your promotional Companion Pass would then be valid for unlimited use between Jan. 8, 2027, and March 3, 2027.

First, register for the promotion with your Southwest Rapid Rewards number. Then, book one qualifying round-trip flight or two one-way flights using your Rapid Rewards number by 11:59 p.m. CST on Sunday, Nov. 29. Flights must be completed sometime from Nov. 27 to Jan. 5, 2027.

Successfully complete the above steps, and you'll earn a promotional Companion Pass valid for use between Jan. 8 and March 3, 2027.

All fare classes, including the carrier’s Basic option, are eligible for this promotion. And it doesn’t matter how you pay for your flight, as there's no specific spending requirement. Rapid Rewards point redemptions and Cash + Points bookings qualify too, as long as you book through Southwest channels, such as the carrier’s website or mobile app.

If you have existing flights on Southwest, they won't automatically count for this promotion. However, if you can cancel those reservations, register and rebook before the promotion ends on Sunday, that should work (provided you complete your travel within the qualifying travel window). Be sure to check for any fare differences before canceling.

Southwest’s Companion Pass is almost legendary in the world of points and miles. It lets you bring a companion along on unlimited flights, whether you book with cash or points, for almost free. As long as there’s an open seat on the plane, your companion can fly with you for just the cost of taxes and fees (which start at $5.60).

You must designate a companion in your Rapid Rewards account. However, you’re allowed to change your designated companion up to three times per year, and this rule applies to promotional passes as well.

If you'd like to earn a Companion Pass for longer than just eight weeks or so this promotional pass is valid, there is still time to earn a Companion Pass for all of 2027 using the welcome bonuses from the Southwest credit cards as outlined here. You have to act quickly, though, since those rules are changing soon.

Related: Best Southwest Airlines credit cards

The Southwest Companion Pass can be extremely valuable for those who like to travel with a companion. Earning one is about to become a lot harder, so this is a great promotion for those who can register, book eligible travel by Sunday and travel between now and Jan. 5, 2027.

#6021. Mobile Passport Control: Free App That Speeds Up US Immigration

Frequent travelers to the United States are probably familiar with Global Entry, which allows enrolled members to get expedited immigration at US airports. However, applying for Global Entry is a bit of a process, and there’s a cost to participate.

If you don’t want Global Entry (or aren’t eligible), your next best option is Mobile Passport Control. This is sort of a hidden program that doesn’t get talked about enough, given that it can significantly cut down your wait times at US immigration. In this post, I’d like to talk about how this works, as I’ve used it a couple of times now (when traveling internationally with our younger son, who doesn’t yet have Global Entry).

Mobile Passport Control (MPC) is a free app that allows travelers to submit their travel document, photo, and customs declaration information, before they arrive at the immigration checkpoint at a US airport.

Travelers just have to download the app, which is available for Apple and Android. The idea is that the app streamlines the traveler’s entry process to the United States by reducing passport control inspection times and overall wait times.

Those who use MPC can access a separate immigration screening checkpoint. Really that’s the biggest advantage — because not many people use this program (as of now), the wait times are generally much shorter than the standard wait times.

There are some important things to be aware of, as you’d expect:

In the interest of being thorough, here are the current airports participating in Mobile Passport Control:

The Mobile Passport Control app couldn’t be much easier to use. I’d recommend downloading the app prior to boarding your flight to the United States, and completing the basic requirements. Then you have to submit your customs declaration after you land in the United States (within four hours of when you intend to clear immigration).

Once you download the app, there are several pages explaining how the app works, plus you have to agree to a disclaimer statement.

After that you can go through steps required for a particular entry to the country. Note that you can use one app to submit your application for multiple people in the same family. Furthermore, you can save the passport details in the app for multiple trips, eliminating the need to submit all of this information each time (though you do need to make a customs declaration each time).

To start the process, you’ll have to state which CBP port you’ll be arriving at, and they all show on a dropdown menu.

At that point you’ll have to select the travelers who will be entering the country. If you’ve already saved people to your profile, they’ll show on that page. Otherwise you can start from scratch, which just requires scanning the document, and then all the information will be auto-populated.

You’ll then need to capture traveler photos. This doesn’t need to be a passport-quality photo — you just have to follow some very basic guidelines, like removing hats and sunglasses, and making sure only one person’s face is visible.

The above can all be saved to your profile. However, what you do need to complete with each trip is answering six standard CBP declaration questions.

You’ll only want to submit this when you arrive at your point of entry in the United States. The app asks you to submit this once you’ve arrived at the airport, though in reality you have up to four hours to go through immigration from the time that your application is submitted.

Once you submit your document, you’ll be given a receipt with a QR code, which you’ll need to scan when you see an immigration officer.

Once you land at your US point of entry and arrive in the immigration hall, look for the Mobile Passport Control signage. This will bring you to an area separate from the standard US immigration line.

You still need to queue to see an immigration officer, and when you get to the officer, you’ll see a scanning device where you should scan your QR code. The benefit is that this line is usually much shorter, and also that you generally won’t be asked as many questions (since you’ve already answered some questions via the app).

Both times I’ve gone through the MPC lane, the wait was less than five minutes, while the general immigration line looked much longer. The main benefit of MPC isn’t even the time savings from getting some of the work done in advance through the app, but rather just having access to a shorter line.

Mobile Passport Control isn’t as good as Global Entry, plain and simple. With Global Entry there’s almost never a wait, you just have to look at the camera, an officer acknowledges you, and then you’re usually sent on your way. The Mobile Passport Control experience isn’t as seamless. However, it’s the next best thing.

There’s no enrollment cost, using the app takes maybe a few minutes to set up, and then with each trip it just takes a minute or so to answer the declaration questions. Getting access to a special immigration line for that is awesome, as it could potentially save you a significant amount of time.

Of course like many things in life, I imagine that as this app becomes more popular and well known, it will also become less useful. After all, when everyone gets access to a special lane, no one gets access to a special lane. 😉

Mobile Passport Control is an awesome free app that can save you time at US immigration. The app is easy to use, and allows you to submit your documents and customs declaration prior to speaking to an immigration officer. Most valuable of all, those with MPC get access to a special lane at immigration, which is typically much shorter than the standard one.

While I’d still recommend Global Entry, those who don’t have it should use MPC if they’re eligible.

Have you ever used Mobile Passport Control before? If so, what was your experience like?

#6020. Here's How 10-Abreast Seating Feels On The Airbus A380's Main Deck

The Airbus A380 offers an interesting experience for passengers. On one hand, it's the largest commercial airliner ever built, which means that the cabin is wider and the ceilings are higher than on other aircraft types. At the same time, economy passengers on the main deck are seated in a 10-abreast layout on the A380, a configuration that is usually disliked.

It was initially used on the Boeing 747, but today it's most common on the Boeing 777, where passengers usually criticize the layout for the narrow seat width. Economy is not, of course, the only cabin that airlines install on the main deck of the A380. Many carriers install premium economy on the main deck, while some airlines also install a first class cabin at the front of the main deck.

Meanwhile, carriers may install first class, business class, premium economy, and sometimes even economy on the upper deck. The experience on the upper deck can actually be quite different from on the main deck due to the different cabin dimensions.

The A380 is enormous. While even a 777 is a large aircraft, the Boeing twinjet's interior cabin width measures 19 feet three inches (5.86 meters). The upcoming 777X's interior cabin maxes out at 19 feet seven inches (5.97 meters), while the main deck on the 747 is about 20 feet (6.1 meters) wide. Meanwhile, the main deck of the A380 is about 21 feet seven inches (6.58 meters) wide.

It is a significantly larger cabin than what the 747 and 777 offer, yet it fits the same number of economy seats per row. This means that, per row, everything is wider. The seats can be wider on the A380, as well as the aisles. This gives aisle seat passengers better comfort, since passengers and crew are less likely to bump into said customers, while aisle egress is easier.

The armrests could technically be made wider as well, although there's little variability in real-world economy armrests. Meanwhile, seats on the A380's main deck are among the widest in economy because of the cabin's width. Generally, airlines install seats that are at least 18 inches (45.7 centimeters) wide on the A380, but some carriers go even wider.

18.5 inches (47 centimeters) is a good premium economy seat size on some airlines, yet some carriers offer this in economy on the A380 or even wider (admittedly, with smaller armrests). While it's the same per-seat layout as on most 777s today, the experience inside the seat is markedly different because the aircraft is so huge, making for a much more comfortable ride.

Not only does the A380 have a wide cabin, but the main deck also has one of the tallest ceilings of any commercial airliner. Combined, this makes the cabin much larger overall, giving it a sense of spaciousness that you simply cannot find on another airliner. Visually, the sidewalls of the cabin also don't curve inwards like on so many other aircraft types, further contributing to this perception of space.

This is particularly important for the A380 because of how many passengers are typically present, helping prevent passengers from feeling crammed. The A380's engines were state-of-the-art when the aircraft type debuted in 2007, with better fuel efficiency and lower noise levels than prior models.

Because the aircraft's engines are also located very far from the fuselage, the noise levels inside the cabin are much lower than passengers would otherwise expect. The A380 is routinely considered to be one of, if not the quietest airliners ever built, on par with newer types that use more advanced engines like the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350.

The superjumbo is known to handle turbulence well and generally provides a smooth ride. Although the A380 has a metal fuselage, the interior pressure altitude is more similar to that of the newer A350 and 787 rather than older types like the 777 and 747. With a lower cabin altitude, passengers feel less fatigued, and the impact of jet lag is noticeably reduced. Altogether, while the A380 isn't the newest type in service anymore, it remains one of the most comfortable.

Ryanair is notable for asking Boeing to build a specific MAX 8 variant for high-density seating, while others configure A350s ten-abreast.

While the A380 is noticeably more spacious than other aircraft, the 10-abreast layout in economy still has drawbacks. A significant number of the seats are middle seats, which are generally less desirable. This also makes it harder for window seat passengers to leave their seat during the flight.

In addition, some may dislike the general idea of traveling with hundreds of other passengers on one aircraft, even if the interior is spacious, as this could give some a 'cattle car' feeling. Notably, one of the biggest issues with flying on an A380 today isn't the plane itself, but the interiors that many airlines have installed.

Most A380s were delivered in the late 2000s and early 2010s, but relatively few have been refurbished with modern interiors ever since due to the massive costs associated with retrofitting one of these double-decker giants. This means less ergonomic seats with older technology, which may include smaller, lower-definition screens, and charging options may be limited.

While the interior window panel on the lower deck of the A380 is quite large, the actual cutout for the window is sized similarly to older Airbus widebodies, and it's noticeably smaller than the cabin windows on the newer 787 or A350. This does reflect on the aircraft's age, as it entered service about four years before the 787 and over seven years before the A350. Still, the A380 is overall a comfortable ride for passengers regardless of the airline, even if there are some drawbacks.

Airlines have installed all four cabins on the upper deck of the A380, although it is most commonly used for premium seating. Airlines that do install economy on the upper deck generally only install a low number of economy seats. While the A380's upper deck offers a more unique experience than the main deck, it is smaller.

The upper deck has a usable width of roughly 19 feet (5.8 meters), while the ceiling is lower and the sidewalls curve inwards more than on most aircraft types. The upper deck of the A380 is actually quite wide compared to other widebody types, but the curvature of the sidewalls means that airlines can generally only install eight seats per row in economy, using 18-inch (45.7 centimeters) wide seats.

What Airbus has done with some of the remaining space is install storage bins along the sidewalls, which is, of course, beneficial for upper deck passengers. In addition, the aisles are generally fairly wide, and the upper deck is even quieter than the main deck. Interestingly, modern business class seats on the A380 are not necessarily more spacious than other long-haul jets.

This is because a four-abreast direct aisle access layout is standard on almost all widebodies regardless of the actual cabin width. Since the A380's upper deck is narrower than the cabin on a 777, this means that the seats will be narrower. The bigger issue in business class, however, is again that many airlines have not modernized the interiors of their A380s, resulting in a large discrepancy between what customers now expect versus what they usually get.

Discover the surprising difference in wingspan between two aviation giants.

Singapore Airlines debuted its latest interiors on the A380 in December 2017, and these are actually its newest long-haul cabins currently in service. Emirates had its A380s fitted with largely the same premium seat models from 2008 to 2021, but with technological and visual updates over the years.

The A380s flown by Qatar Airways and Etihad Airways still feature their original interiors from the 2010s, which include direct aisle access business class seats that are no longer cutting-edge, but still above average. ANA's three A380s were delivered in 2019 and 2020, and their interiors remain largely modern today.

Airbus A380 Operators (Per Planespotters.net)

Qantas's examples were all refurbished with new business class seats that offer direct aisle access, while Lufthansa is undergoing the same process. Notably, the German flag carrier is using the Thompson Vantage XL (the same seat as Qantas), rather than its new Allegris interiors. Meanwhile, British Airways, Asiana Airlines, and Korean Air are still flying their A380s with their original interiors.

For British Airways, this means its old Club World 'yin-and-yang' seats, while Asiana uses the Stelia Solstys, an older staggered seat. Korean Air's business class on the A380 is configured six-abreast, not even offering direct aisle access. British Airways, however, will soon refurbish its double-deckers with all-new cabins, including an updated version of its Club Suites in business class, and this will mark the first time that an airline has installed suites with sliding doors in business class on the A380.

#6019. Chase Ink Business Unlimited Bonus: 75K Points Welcome Offer

The Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card is part of the Chase Ink Business card portfolio, and is one of the best no annual fee cards out there. It’s one of the rewarding Chase cards for everyday spending, and a great complement to some of Chase’s more premium cards.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at the Chase Ink Business Unlimited bonus, as it’s one of the best welcome offers you’ll find on any no annual fee card.

Link: Learn more about the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card with 75K bonus points

The Chase Ink Unlimited Card is offering a welcome bonus of 75,000 points after spending $6,000 within the first three months. You’ll see the Ink Unlimited bonus is marketed as offering cash back, rather than points, so it’s described as being worth $750. Indeed, you could redeem the rewards as cash back.

However, if you have the card in conjunction with a card earning Ultimate Rewards points, like the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) or Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more), then rewards can be transferred to Ultimate Rewards airline and hotel partners.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, and that increases the value of the points by 70% right there, as far as I’m concerned. I consider the 75,000 points to be worth $1,275. That’s a great bonus, especially for a no annual fee card.

With the ability to transfer Chase points to partners at a 1:1 ratio, that opens up all kinds of great redemption opportunities, including:

How does the Chase Ink Unlimited 75,000-point offer compare to past publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the card? Below is a chart with the Chase Ink Unlimited welcome offer history in recent years.

As you can see, the Chase Ink Unlimited publicly available welcome offer typically ranges from 75,000 to 100,000 points. The offer of 75,000 points is excellent, but is the standard offer. If you are willing to wait, we might see another offer of 90,000 points, or a return of the best-ever offer of 100,000 points.

However, the offer of 75,000 points is still great, and I’d decide whether to apply now or wait based on how much value you’d get from the card in the coming months. For a no annual fee card, the offer of 75,000 points is still industry leading.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Unlimited Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card or any other Chase for Business card without an annual fee. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the Ink Unlimited bonus isn’t available to you if you’ve had this exact card, or another Chase business card without an annual fee, including the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (learn more). So there is an element of cards being mutually exclusive.

However, the key here is that you “may” not be eligible, and not that you absolutely won’t be eligible. I don’t love that level of vagueness, though the good news is that if you apply for the card and aren’t eligible for the bonus, you should receive a pop-up message informing you of this, before there’s a hard pull. So that at least means the downside of applying is limited.

The good news is that eligibility for the bonus is completely unrelated to whether you have a Chase business card with an annual fee, like the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (learn more) or Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more).

It’s fine to apply for Chase business cards as a sole proprietorship, corporation, etc. If you apply as a sole proprietorship, you can just enter your Social Security Number in the section where you’d otherwise put your EIN.

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Chase Ink Unlimited, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card eligibility.

The Chase Ink Unlimited Card has no annual fee, and there are several reasons to consider picking it up. The way I view it, there are a few points that are most important.

For one, the card has a solid rewards structure, as it offers a minimum of 1.5x points on all spending, making it one of the best Chase cards for everyday spending (the card does have foreign transaction fees, though, so I’d only recommend using it for US purchases). Furthermore, the card offers primary rental car coverage, which can come in handy if you rent cars with any frequency, and is incredibly rare for a no annual fee card.

Also, since the card has no annual fee, there’s really no opportunity cost to holding onto it, and it allows you to create a great portfolio of cards to maximize rewards.

Read my review of the Chase Ink Unlimited Card.

The Chase Ink Unlimited Card is one of the most lucrative no annual fee cards out there, and it’s currently offering a welcome bonus of 75,000 points upon completing minimum spending.

Not only does the card have a great bonus that’s too good to turn down, but it offers rewards that can make it worth holding onto, like 1.5x points on everyday spending, plus rental car coverage. If you’re eligible for this card, I think there’s a lot of merit to picking it up. Taking advantage of this bonus is a no-brainer, if eligible.

#6018. Jeffries puts immigration bill high on Democratic priority list

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., holds a news conference in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is signaling Democrats will move quickly on immigration legislation when the party reclaims the House in January, while acknowledging it still has work to do in shaping its healthcare agenda.

Jeffries, who is expected to secure his spot as the next speaker during a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday, identified immigration and health care as among the top priorities for the incoming majority during a Tuesday news conference.

“One of the things that we need to do is to move the Dream and Promise Act for DACA recipients and TPS recipients,” Jeffries said, referring to a Democratic bill introduced last year. “We should actually move that bill immediately.”

The proposal aims to create a path to citizenship for certain Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals recipients and Temporary Protected Status holders. Similar legislation has been a top priority for Democrats in both chambers for more than a decade, with Democrats unable to advance this bill in the House while Republicans have held the majority.

Jeffries also reiterated his calls to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and redirect funding allocated to the agency through Republicans' budget law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, while expressing a desire for bipartisan cooperation on immigration more broadly.

“We think the border should be safe and strong and secure, and we think our immigration system overall is broken,” Jeffries said. “We need to fix it in a comprehensive way, and certainly, it's our hope that a handful of Republicans will be willing to join us, so we can fix it in a bipartisan way.”

On healthcare, however, Jeffries offered fewer specifics, suggesting Democrats still have decisions to make before taking control of the chamber. Democrats broadly agree on the need to restore subsidies for plans purchased through health insurance markets that expired at the end of 2025. But the question of what additional steps the party should pursue with the goal of expanding coverage and lowering prices is likely to be a major test of Democratic leadership’s ability to find consensus among its robust new majority.

When asked how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that's all part of an ongoing conversation.”

The New York Democrat outlined several broader healthcare priorities, including reversing Medicaid cuts enacted under President Donald Trump, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, all of which Democrats have vowed to do over the last year.

“Out of the gate, what we clearly have to do is fix our broken healthcare system in terms of the damage that's been done by Donald Trump and MAGA extremists over the last two years, and that clearly involves reversing the Medicaid cuts and extending the Affordable Care Act tax credits, and beginning to engage in supporting medical research, particularly things like research for pediatric cancer,” Jeffries added.

Democrats established a healthcare working group earlier this Congress, led by Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. and Terri Sewell, D-Ala., to gather perspectives and develop policy proposals as the party works toward a broader agenda.

Without an announced challenger, Jeffries has expressed confidence that he’ll secure the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who have said they remain “undecided” ahead of Wednesday’s elections. Jeffries, who was introduced as “Speaker Jeffries” on election night, said last week he was “very confident we’ll get there” and confirmed that the caucus will hold a recorded vote in the contest.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to go forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives, many aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America, had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

Jeffries said Tuesday the approach mirrors the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who is best positioned to lead based on “track record, experience and vision.”

This report was corrected to reflect Rep. Nancy Pelosi’s status as a current member.

BermudAir is making moves to be a major player in the booming market between the U.S. and the Caribbean.

The airline announced a plethora of new routes this past week, marking a major expansion across North American markets, including direct flights to Caribbean destinations.

BermudAir will add service from Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY), Nashville International Airport (BNA), Tweed New Haven Airport (HVN) in Connecticut, Burlington International Airport (BTV) in Vermont, Portland International Jetport (PWM) in Maine, San Antonio International Airport (SAT) and Fredericton International Airport (YFC) in New Brunswick, Canada.

Those seven join BermudAir's existing North American airports: Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), Westchester County Airport (HPN) in New York, Boston Logan International Airport (BOS), Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport (BWI), Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU), Orlando Sanford International Airport (SFB), St. Pete–Clearwater International Airport (PIE), Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ), Montréal-Pierre Elliott Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and Halifax Stanfield International Airport (YHZ).

The airline, meanwhile, is adding to its list of direct and nonstop destinations beyond L.F. Wade International Airport (BDA) in Bermuda, with flights to: Ian Fleming International Airport (OCJ) in Ocho Rios, Jamaica; El Salvador International Airport (SAL) in San Salvador, El Salvador; and Ramón Villeda Morales International Airport (SAP) in San Pedro Sula, Honduras.

The new airports join BermudAir's roster of previously announced destinations: Clayton J. Lloyd International Airport (AXA) in Anguilla; Philip S.W. Goldson International Airport (BZE) in Belize; Owen Roberts International Airport (GCM) in Grand Cayman; La Aurora International Airport (GUA) in Guatemala; and Providenciales International Airport (PLS) in Turks and Caicos. The airline also offers flights to and from its Bermuda hub.

"2027 represents an exciting new chapter for BermudAir," Adam Scott, BermudAir's founder and CEO, said in a statement. "We're bringing our distinctive brand of premium leisure travel to more cities and opening up more opportunities for travelers to experience Bermuda, the Caribbean and Central America."

While it is typically difficult for an airline to fly between two countries that are not the airline's home nation, BermudAir notes that it plans to operate the routes as fifth freedom flights originating in Bermuda, Turks and Caicos, Grand Cayman or Anguilla — all British Overseas Territories, which appears to satisfy regulatory statutes.

BermudAir launched in 2023 as a boutique carrier that planned to run flights between Bermuda and North America using small and efficient Embraer jets. It launched its first flights between North America and other destinations as part of its winter 2026-27 schedule.

The airline's expansion has been rapid, and if successful, the new routes would make BermudAir a regional force in the Caribbean leisure market.

#6016. How Many Fifth Freedom Routes Does Emirates Fly Into The United States?

As one of the world's largest airlines, Emirates flies to all corners of the world, connecting millions of passengers every year from its hub at Dubai International Airport (DXB). There is, however, a possibility to travel on the Gulf carrier between two countries outside the United Arab Emirates without routing through Dubai at all.

It is all thanks to fifth-freedom traffic rights, which allow an airline to fly from its home hub to a second country and carry local passengers and cargo onward to a third country, provided the flight starts or ends in the carrier's home state. This article takes a look at how Emirates utilizes these rights, how those links operate across the Atlantic and the Americas, and why such routes are highly integral to Emirates' global route network.

Emirates operates fifth-freedom flights touching the United States between New York (JFK) and Milan Malpensa (MXP), between Newark Liberty (EWR) and Athens (ATH), and between Miami (MIA) and Bogotá (BOG). The airline can sell standalone tickets on those beyond-Dubai segments, so travelers can fly the carrier across the Atlantic or between North and South America without ever setting foot in the United Arab Emirates. Those three links are made possible by two distinct flight structures and widebody aircraft types, the Airbus A380 and Boeing 777 variants.

Two of the routes link the New York metropolitan area to Southern Europe as extensions of Dubai services, while the third uses South Florida as a stopover on the way to Colombia. On the European side, JFK and MXP operate as EK205 and EK206, alongside EWR and ATH operating as EK209 and EK210). These flights are designed to capture both local transatlantic demand and connecting traffic to and from Dubai. By contrast, the MIA–BOG leg (EK213/EK214) operates as an onward tag from Dubai via Miami across a 1,513-mile (2,435-km) Americas sector.

Emirates' US fifth-freedom count has shifted as routes launched, paused, or resumed rather than remaining frozen at two. EWR–ATH debuted in March 2017 alongside established MXP–JFK service, while a 2024 launch brought MIA–BOG into the lineup before 2026 Middle East airspace disruptions forced temporary schedule adjustments ahead of its May 2026 resumption, as detailed in Simple Flying coverage.

Emirates is able to operate these three fifth-freedom routes because of geography, aircraft performance, fleet utilization, and point-to-point passenger demand. Fifth-freedom legs do not get added wherever demand looks promising, and Emirates only turns an intermediate stop into a standalone ticketed route when the economics and limits of the flight line up just right. In practice, that filter explains why JFK–Europe and MIA–BOG exist when other city pairs never make the cut.

Aircraft range, airport elevation, and ground-turn efficiency weigh heavily on how each route is built. Bogotá's El Dorado International Airport sits at 8,360 feet (2,548 meters) above sea level, as per Road Genius, where thinner air and hot-and-high conditions limit takeoff payload over ultra-long distances, making a route through Miami practical on a Boeing 777 across a 1,513-mile (2,435-km) leg. By contrast, Milan Malpensa and Athens serve as European stepping stones on DXB–JFK and DXB–EWR flights, letting Emirates pair long-haul sectors with local transatlantic traffic and not leave widebody jets sitting idle on the ground.

A 777 arriving in Miami (MIA) from Dubai (DXB) can use daytime ground time to fly a quick 1,513-mile (2,435-km) round-trip down to Bogotá (BOG) and back before its return leg east, squeezing extra block hours out of a single airframe. On the JFK–Europe links, by contrast, Emirates balances transatlantic sector lengths (~3,989 miles / 6,413 km between JFK and MXP) and local point-to-point demand against through-flight punctuality, so an intermediate stop strengthens the network as opposed to dragging down schedule reliability.

Emirates is scheduled to operate 16 5th freedom flights in March as it seeks to fill up its high-capacity widebody aircraft.

Emirates' fifth-freedom flights into the United States sit right in the middle of a long-running clash over Open Skies aviation policy and competitive fairness. While Emirates frames fifth-freedom flying as a lawful commercial tool that boosts connectivity and consumer choice, the Big Three US legacy carriers of American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and United Airlines have lobbied hard against Gulf carrier expansion, as reported by NPR. As a result, the US fifth-freedom count has stayed at three core routes, yet to expand into a sweeping US network.

Through the Partnership for Open & Fair Skies, US legacy carriers and labor groups accused Gulf airlines of receiving tens of billions of dollars in state support and distorting competition on transatlantic and international lanes, as per Business Travel News. Emirates and UAE officials pushed back sharply against those claims, arguing that Emirates operates on a commercial footing, pointing to past dividend and profit-sharing payouts, and noting that US carriers themselves benefited from bankruptcy protections, slot protections, and federal assistance over the years.

Meanwhile, Emirates leadership has acknowledged that adding more US fifth-freedom routes is still tempting when market opportunities arise, even as political and bilateral sensitivities make every new proposal closely watched.

In practice, that standoff has turned fifth-freedom approvals into more challenging negotiations, having to watch out for bilateral treaty rights and political pushback in Washington. Even when route economics look attractive on paper, adding a new US fifth-freedom leg invites immediate scrutiny from domestic rivals and unions claiming home-market turf is at stake. As a result, Emirates has tended to focus on sustaining and optimizing its existing three US fifth-freedom links rather than testing every possible city pair at once.

Comparing Emirates' three US fifth-freedom routes (JFK–MXP, EWR–ATH, and MIA–BOG) to nonstop Dubai flights or rival fifth-freedom carriers comes down to trip duration, cabin appeal, and redemption value. For travelers who want to experience Emirates without committing to a 12 to 16.5-hour flight to or from Dubai (DXB), those shorter regional and transatlantic legs offer a direct way into its widebody cabins. At the same time, other foreign carriers operate competing fifth-freedom links from the US, such as Singapore Airlines on JFK–Frankfurt (FRA) or Los Angeles (LAX)–Tokyo Narita (NRT), giving flyers distinct cabin products and loyalty partners to decide on.

Booking through Emirates Skywards or transfer partners can make these three routes attractive on points, though fees and availability vary by program and cabin. Published award guides show Skywards redemptions starting around 17,000 to 17,500 miles one-way in economy, 87,000 miles in business, and 102,000 miles in first on JFK–Europe sectors, while partner programs like Aeroplan can offer lower mileage tiers on certain routes alongside different surcharges. Conversely, nonstop US or European carriers often win on schedule frequency, alliance connections, or lower cash/fee totals when award seats are tight.

Ultimately, the three-route count matters most when a traveler's origin and destination line up with JFK–MXP, EWR–ATH, or MIA–BOG. If you are flying from the US to a different European city or connecting onward beyond the gateway, a domestic or European carrier with denser daily frequencies may beat a single daily fifth-freedom flight on timing and flexibility. Where those three routes shine is giving travelers a clear shortcut to sample Emirates on point-to-point or short-hop trips.

How many can you guess? Find them all here!

The flights originate in or route through Dubai (DXB) at some point, so regional airspace disruptions, seasonal schedule trims, and cabin-retrofit rotations can alter how a route runs or even temporarily pause operations. As seen when 2026 Middle East airspace disruptions affected MIA–BOG before its May 2026 resumption, and as seen in periodic frequency or aircraft adjustments across the network, a static route count only captures a snapshot in time.

Travelers also face practical drawbacks that do not apply on point-to-point domestic flights. Delays or airspace detours thousands of miles away in the Gulf or Europe can end up affecting an inbound jet, while single-daily or reduced-weekly frequencies leave fewer same-day rebooking seats if something goes wrong. Aircraft swaps between A380 frames and 777-300ER or 777-200LR variants can also change seat layouts, first class availability, or cabin refurbishment status between booking and departure.

Even on paper, a route operating once a day or as a tag onto a long-haul rotation leaves far less margin than a multi-frequency domestic corridor. What looks like a straightforward seat map or fixed mileage tier when booking can change entirely as fleet assignments rotate, seasonal demand fluctuates, or regional airspace conditions force timetable adjustments. For a fifth-freedom flight, the schedule published months in advance is less a guarantee of exact hardware or timing than a starting point shaped by everything happening upstream along the route.

Emirates flies three fifth-freedom routes touching the United States, including New York-JFK to Milan Malpensa, Newark Liberty to Athens, and Miami to Bogotá, with each serving a distinct operational purpose. Whether linking New York-area hubs with Southern Europe or linking Miami with Bogotá as an onward leg from Dubai, those routes reflect how Emirates balances fleet utilization, local demand, and competitive realities.

Emirates' ongoing A350-900 deliveries and widebody cabin retrofit program will gradually reshape how the airline allocates aircraft and cabins across its US network. Even as Emirates evaluates selective growth opportunities alongside future fleet additions, those three routes are still the core benchmark for where travelers can book standalone fifth-freedom flights between the United States and another country.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#6015. Royal Air Maroc Business Class Boeing 787 Review: The World’s Worst Flat Bed?

To finish off the return portion of our Orient Express adventure via Africa trip, we flew Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class on the 8hr25min flight from Casablanca (CMN) to Miami (MIA). While the flight operated relatively on schedule, it otherwise had quite some room for improvement.

The version of Royal Air Maroc’s 787 that we flew had what I’d consider to be the world’s worst flat bed business class seat. When you combine that with no Wi-Fi and incredibly lackluster service, it’s hard to praise the airline too much.

To Royal Air Maroc’s credit, the airline is on balance the best northern African carrier, in my opinion. And the flight attendant working our part of the cabin was at least well intentioned. The food was relatively decent as well. It also has to be pointed out that Royal Air Maroc’s 787s have four different types of configurations, and these seats are limited to most of the 787-8s (while the 787-9s have better seats).

So while I have a hard time giving Royal Air Maroc too much credit for our experience, I also view the airline in a better light than carriers like Air Algerie, for example.

Ford and I booked an itinerary on Royal Air Maroc all the way from Malaga to Miami via Casablanca. The reason was because the airline offered the best schedule that would get us home the same day after our Orient Express Sailing Yachts cruise.

Royal Air Maroc often makes only one business class seat available, so I had to get a bit creative to make this work. I ended up booking one ticket using 57,500 American AAdvantage miles plus $85.72 in taxes & fees, while the other ticket was booked with cash, at the cost of $1,620, with the following itinerary:

10/09 AT989 Malaga to Casablanca departing 2:15PM arriving 1:30PM10/09 AT204 Casablanca to Miami departing 3:00PM arriving 7:45PM

Obviously paying cash for a ticket wasn’t ideal, but that still ended up being less out of pocket than flying British Airways business class through London on awards, factoring in the carrier surcharges.

We had a fairly short connection in Casablanca, as we had just arrived in Royal Air Maroc’s 737 business class from Malaga. We first had to clear transit security, which only took a few minutes. While we would’ve had access to Royal Air Maroc’s lounge, we didn’t really have much time, so we headed straight to our departure gate.

Our flight was departing from gate A10, with boarding scheduled for 2:10PM, 50 minutes before departure. As is common for US-bound flights, the departure area was roped off from the rest of the terminal, and there were some boarding pass checks. However, we weren’t subjected to extra screening (I assume that’s just for those with “SSSS” on their boarding pass).

I must admit, Royal Air Maroc’s livery is pretty beautiful, no?

I also have an embarrassing confession to make. Boarding started a few minutes ahead of the published 2:10PM time, and I attempted to board… only to find out that I was accidentally attempting to board the flight to New York. Gate A9 and A10 are right next to one another, the monitor was tiny, etc. In fairness, I wasn’t the only person attempting to board the wrong flight, so it seems like that could maybe be organized a little better. 😉

Anyway, boarding did end up starting right on schedule, with wheelchair passengers being invited to board first, followed by business class passengers and oneworld elite members.

Royal Air Maroc’s Boeing 787-8 business class takes up the entire space between the first and second set of doors. It consists of 18 seats, spread across three rows, in a 2-2-2 configuration. We were in seats 2A and 2C, the window and aisle seat in the second row on the left side.

Royal Air Maroc has the Stelia Equinox 3D seat, which like I said, is the worst flat bed business class in the world, in my opinion. I just don’t understand what the designer of this seat was thinking.

I understand that in theory this is supposed to be a high density layout, but with just 18 seats in that space, it’s hardly efficient — American has 20 reverse herringbone seats in the same space on the same plane (though admittedly on Royal Air Maroc the lavatories are also in front of the second set of doors, so it’s not a fully fair comparison).

What makes these seats so bad? Well, basically everything. The seats completely lack storage, and they have the most bizarre top/bottom configuration when you recline your seat. Fortunately I was traveling with Ford (no one I’d rather be in these top/bottom seats with!), but if next to a stranger, these are just downright bad.

Where do we even begin? For one, these seats have the padding (and look) of an ironing board. So the comfort is definitely lacking.

Ford had never been in these kinds of seats before, and as he sat down and looked forward, he was genuinely confused by how the ottomans were at completely different levels — that’s understandable confusion!

In this configuration, the tray tables fold out from the center side of the seat, and are so poorly designed. They basically refuse to stay in place, and if they move even just a little, they sort of “plop” down, as they go off the edge of the little “holder.”

Then there’s the whole console between seats, where you’ll find a panel with the seat controls, a headphone jack, an entertainment controller, an AC power outlet, and a USB-A outlet (there’s no USB-C or wireless charging).

The seat just completely lacks when it comes to storage and comfort, as there’s not really anywhere practical to place things. For example, if you have your laptop out and then the meal service starts, where are you supposed to place it? There’s nowhere to put it, other than the floor.

Perhaps the one positive thing I can say about this Royal Air Maroc hard product is that there were individual air nozzles, which at least helped with being able to regulate the feeling of being too warm.

I’m not trying to be sarcastic, but I do consider this to be the world’s worst flat bed business class. On the plus side, I guess at least it’s not angled (is that really a thing anymore?), and the version of this seat on Philippine Airlines A330s is worse.

Royal Air Maroc’s 787 business class has 18.5″ seat back entertainment screens, with audio and video on demand. The system was far from cutting edge and the selection wasn’t massive, but it also wasn’t terrible. There was a decent selection of movies, TV shows, music, games, and of course the map feature.

I tried my best to count the number of entertainment options, and I got to around 230 movies, so that’s not a bad selection. However, the options also weren’t terribly modern, for the most part.

Unfortunately there was no Wi-Fi on this plane, which is pretty uncompetitive nowadays. The good news is that Royal Air Maroc plans to introduce Starlink Wi-Fi in 2027, so that’ll be a major upgrade.

When it comes to Royal Air Maroc business class amenities, a pillow and blanket were waiting at my seat upon boarding. The blanket was cozy without being overly luxurious or warm, while the pillow was fine, but a little on the small side.

Later on in the flight I discovered there were also mattress pads in the overhead bin, but go figure that no crew member ever informed any passenger of this (let alone offered to make beds), which is such a missed opportunity. How sad when the airline invests in something like that, but it’s totally wasted, as I didn’t see a single passenger using these.

Headphones were also waiting at each seat, but they were very much on the cheap side, and didn’t have good noise cancelation, and also weren’t very comfortable.

Amenity kits had been placed at the seats before boarding, and were fine. I kind of liked the Royal Air Maroc branding on the kit as such. In terms of contents, there were socks, eyeshades, a dental kit, and a small selection of products from Moroccan skincare brand Nectarome.

During boarding, the crew came around with pre-departure drinks, including the choice of lemon mint juice or water, followed by warm towels.

The menu and drink list for the flight were also distributed.

There were no slippers or pajamas. All-in-all, the amenities were okay. They weren’t terrible, but also weren’t memorable.

Boarding took a rather long time, as the flight was full. The main cabin door closed at 3:10PM, 10 minutes after our scheduled departure time. At that point the safety video was screened, which was interesting to watch.

At 3:15PM we began our pushback, and then at 3:25PM we began our taxi.

We had a brief taxi out to runway 35R, where we had to hold for a few minutes. We were cleared for takeoff at 3:40PM, and rocketed off into the afternoon sky. The views on the climb out were lovely, and the seatbelt sign was turned off around five minutes after takeoff.

Once we leveled off, we had around eight hours remaining to Miami.

In business class on this Royal Air Maroc flight, the main meal was served after takeoff, while a snack was served before landing. In theory the menu talked about how there was dine on demand.

I’m sure that could’ve been requested, but that’s not something the crew ever offered — they just took meal orders before takeoff, and then served everyone the main meal after takeoff. Much like with the mattress pads, it just seems like there’s a gap between what they’re trying to go for, and what they’re actually offering.

You can find the Royal Air Maroc business class menu and drink list below.

The first round of drinks were served around 35 minutes after takeoff, so credit to the airline for the speed at which the first drink was served, plus the overall presentation.

I had a glass of the Moroccan white wine. That was served with a canapé consisting of sweet chili prawn with sesame seeds, smoked salmon rose, and a foie gras mousse bite, along with two packaged snacks (cheese biscuits and roasted salted almonds).

That was a lovely start to the meal, but Ford had less luck. He ordered a Diet Coke, and when he opened the can, it exploded. I understand the concept of cans sometimes having issues, but I’ve never seen anything like this before.

It wasn’t just that an ounce or two immediately sprayed out, but instead, within two seconds, there was no liquid left in the can, and instead, it was all over him and the cabin. I don’t even understand how that could happen. So it took quite a while for us to clean up that mess.

There were three options for starters. I ordered the tuna tataki with mixed lettuce, mango, and wasabi cream, while Ford had the harira and dates (for the record, I would’ve gone for the more Moroccan option as well, but wanted to give Ford his first choice, and get pictures of different things). Both were quite decent, but nothing great.

Eventually our appetizers were cleared, and then our mains were brought out. I had the grilled sea bass with chimichurri sauce, with quinoa, lentils, and mushrooms, while Ford had the beef tajine with prunes, dried apricot, and almonds. Both dishes were fine — the fish surprisingly lacked flavor, and the beef tajine was just okay, not bad, but not as good as you’d hope for the flag carrier of a country.

After the main course, there was the choice of a couple of desserts, fruit, or cheese. Ford and I each ordered one of the desserts (cheesecake and a pastry with amlou), and then split a cheese plate.

All-in-all, the meal wasn’t bad, and wrapped up within two hours of departure. The challenge was more the service. I understand based on the above pictures, everything actually looks pretty decent and organized. But the crew had a complete inability to offer drink refills and remove plates, even when specifically requested. It wasn’t that they weren’t nice, they were just really disorganized and slow with responding to requests.

For example, below is what Ford’s tray looked like when we were having the cheese course. You’d think they could’ve cleared something, but nope, they just kind of looked at it. I’ll talk more about service later, but getting a drink refill was quite the undertaking.

Royal Air Maroc’s 787 business class lavatory situation is a bit confusing. There’s one lavatory at the very front of the cabin, but it seems to be reserved for the crew. At least that’s the impression I had, as that’s what the flight attendants suggested to me.

There were then two lavatories behind business class, but the one on the left (on my aisle) was for economy (so the curtain was hung around it accordingly), while the one on the right (the other aisle) was for business class.

One lavatory for 18 business class passengers isn’t ideal. The issue isn’t the ratio as such, but instead, if one person is using the lavatory for an extended period, you’re kind of just locked out. The bigger issue is that going from the left aisle to the back right requires either going through the economy galley or forward galley, and the crew didn’t seem thrilled by traffic there.

Anyway, the lavatory as such was a standard Dreamliner one, so wasn’t half bad. And while I wouldn’t say it was clean, it also wasn’t filthy.

Once back at my seat, we reclined both of the seats to get some rest. This is where you really realize how absurd these seats are. Imagine you’re sitting in one of these seats next to a stranger, or imagine if you’re in the “top” seat and want to sleep, while the person in the “bottom” seat doesn’t. The person in the “top” seat is basically hanging over you.

Since we were traveling together, this wasn’t a huge deal, but I just can’t believe anyone thought this would be a good seat standard on a long haul flight.

With no Wi-Fi and not a whole lot to do, we tried to get some rest. We fell asleep with around 6hr30min remaining to Miami, while approaching the Azores…

…and we woke up with around two hours remaining.

Honestly, that was some very good rest for me on a plane, since I’m usually a terrible sleeper. And while I’d love to credit the seat, the truth is that just not knowing what to do with yourself really helps with getting some rest. I knew I couldn’t be productive, there wasn’t much on the entertainment system for me to enjoy, etc.

The crew served the pre-landing snack around 90 minutes before landing, and there were two choices. One choice was a salmon sandwich and tandoori chicken sandwich, and the other choice was a beef burger and chicken burger, and we had one of each. That was served with a side of yogurt with almonds, dates, and amlou.

I didn’t find it to be a terribly large meal, but it was sufficient.

In addition to water, I accompanied the meal with a mint tea, which was relatively nicely presented.

Compared to Air Algerie, service on Royal Air Maroc was excellent… but that’s about all I can say. To the crew’s credit, they were relatively charming, and smiled every once in a while. So friendliness wasn’t the issue.

Instead, the problem was just how reactive service was. If there was an empty glass, they’d just look at it, rather than removing it, or offering a refill. And even if you asked for a refill during a meal, it would take 15 minutes for it to happen. As another example, with the pre-landing meal, they never proactively asked anyone if they wanted something to drink — they just poured water, and that was it (though they were happy to fulfill requests). These just seem like basic things that should be fixed.

This felt like assembly line service to the max, in terms of the service flow being about what was convenient for the crew, rather than what passengers wanted.

At around 7:15PM Miami time, the captain was on the PA to announce that we’d soon start descending, and would be landing in around 45 minutes. Our approach ended up stretching on quite a bit, as we flew down the coast of Florida, before flying out over the Everglades, and then turning around.

We ended up touching down in Miami at 8PM, on runway 9. While we got off the runway very close to our arrival gate, we ended up just holding position for around 15 minutes on a taxiway, with no update from the pilots. We finally pulled into our gate at 8:20PM.

We quickly cleared immigration and customs, and were excited to be heading home, wrapping up a fun and memorable trip!

I can’t complain too much about our Royal Air Maroc 787 business class flight. We were close to on time, the crew wasn’t unfriendly, and since I was traveling with Ford, I didn’t mind these seats. The food also wasn’t bad.

However, when compared to other business class experiences, there’s definitely huge room for improvement. These seats are really quite uncompetitive, the lack of Wi-Fi was disappointing, and the service was just lacking. Royal Air Maroc will soon introduce Starlink Wi-Fi and is also introducing upgraded business class seats, and I feel like if they invested a bit in service training, they could really be a very competitive airline.

I’d say that by regional standards, Royal Air Maroc is still the best carrier in northern Africa. But that’s not to say that there isn’t (big) room for improvement.

What do you make of Royal Air Maroc’s 787 business class?
