#6014. Buy British Airways Club Avios For 30% Off (1.61 Cents Per Avios): Worth It?

British Airways Club is currently offering a promotion on purchasing Avios. Through December 7, 2026, British Airways Club members can purchase Avios for up to 30% off, which is potentially an opportunity to acquire them for 1.61 cents each (in USD).

While some people might find this to be worthwhile, I’d only recommend buying Avios with a specific use in mind, especially with all the ways there are to rack up this rewards currency. Also keep in mind how easily Avios can be moved between the various “flavors,” given that several airlines use Avios as their rewards currency.

Link: Buy British Airways Club Avios with a promotion

Between 12AM GMT on November 27 and 11:59PM GMT on December 7, 2026, British Airways Club is offering up to a 30% discount on purchased Avios. With this promotion, you can receive a 30% discount as long as you purchase at least 2,000 Avios in one transaction (pre-bonus).

With British Airways Club, the cost to purchase Avios varies based on how many you buy, even without any promotions — the more Avios you buy, the lower the cost per Avios. Furthermore, the cost varies based on where your account is registered. With this 30% discount offer, you can expect to pay the following to max out this promotion:

At this point, the US promotion is the best version of this offer, thanks to the weakness of the USD, though as you can tell, the difference is minimal. The exact rate you’ll pay is based on where your account is registered, so it’s not like you have a choice in the matter.

Ordinarily British Airways Club lets members purchase up to 100,000 Avios per account per calendar year, before factoring in any bonuses. However, during promotions, that cap is often increased, as is the case now. Currently you can buy up to 200,000 Avios.

Note that while purchased Avios typically post instantly, in some situations it could take up to three business days for them to post. Purchasing Avios doesn’t count toward British Airways Club status.

Note that the purchase of Avios is refundable for 14 days, assuming they haven’t been redeemed. To cancel, use the refund option in your confirmation email, or contact the Avios program through the “Contact Us” link on avios.com.

British Airways Avios purchases are processed by points.com, meaning they don’t count as an airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending. Therefore I’d recommend using a card on which you’re trying to reach minimum spending, or otherwise, a credit card that maximizes your return on everyday spending.

Just to be crystal clear, purchasing Avios wouldn’t qualify as a British Airways airfare purchase for the purposes of credit card spending.

Here’s every promotion on purchased British Airways Club Avios we’ve tracked since July 2025, with the cost per point for each, so you can see how the current deal stacks up.

Is this a good deal? At 1.73 cents per point, the current promotion is 30% below the standard price. That’s 0.25 cents more than the best deal we’ve seen (1.48 cents, last available July 9 to 16, 2026). It’s 0.53 cents above our 1.2-cent valuation of British Airways Club Avios.

Nowadays the overall Avios ecosystem is quite the points currency powerhouse. Avios is the rewards currency used by British Airways Club, Iberia Club, Aer Lingus Aer Club, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, and Finnair Plus, and you can transfer rewards between all the currencies.

Ultimately there are lots of great uses for Avios, though it all depends on what you’re looking for. Avios can be useful for short haul awards on oneworld partner airlines, they can be useful for premium cabin travel on British Airways and Qatar Airways, and they can even be redeemed for travel in JetBlue Mint. There are lots of possibilities.

Everyone will value points currencies differently. Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider British Airways Avios to be worth 1.2 cents each, based on the ways to get outsized value with the distance based award pricing. However, I tend to value points pretty conservatively, and there are many ways to get way more value from British Airways Avios than that.

When it comes to the rewards expiration policy, British Airways Avios expire after 36 months of inactivity. Any earning or redeeming of Avios will reset the expiration of your balance.

When it comes to acquiring Avios, it’s worth pointing out that the various Avios “flavors” have promotions on purchasing Avios, and in some cases, you’ll find better pricing through other programs. In particular, Finnair Plus buy Avios promotions and Qatar Airways Privilege Club buy Avios promotions frequently get you a lower price per point, so are worth keeping an eye on.

While I think there’s a lot of value to be had with Avios, do keep in mind that there are quite a few ways to earn Avios with US credit cards. British Airways Club partners with a few transferable points currencies, including Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, and Chase Ultimate Rewards, and all points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. Also keep in mind for any transfer bonuses, to stretch your points further.

On top of that, there are three Avios earning credit cards issued in the US.

British Airways is offering a 30% discount on purchased Avios, which is an opportunity to acquire Avios for a little over 1.6 cents each. The program only rarely sells Avios with a promotion nowadays, so this offer is worth being aware of.

Personally my preferred way to acquire Avios continues to be to earn them through Amex Membership Rewards, Bilt Rewards, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, etc. However, if you don’t have access to US credit cards, some might consider this to be worthwhile. Just also keep in mind that other Avios currencies are sometimes sold at a lower cost, and can be moved around.

Could MSC Cruises soon be as big with North Americans as it is with Europeans?

That's the goal at the fast-growing Europe-based line, which is in the midst of a major expansion into the North American market.

In an exclusive interview this week aboard the line's newest ship, MSC World Asia, MSC Cruises CEO Gianni Onorato told TPG the brand is aiming for 5 million American passengers a year within a decade — more than double the number it carries now.

It'll get there in part by growing its North American passenger count to 50% of its business, up from around 30% to 35% today, he said — a shift in passenger mix that would make North Americans the biggest segment of its customers.

"The cruise industry has always been, is today, and will be tomorrow represented by 50% North American guests, and I believe that MSC should reflect this share," Onorato said during a one-on-one interview on MSC World Asia as it was being unveiled in France.

The debut of MSC World Asia — at 216,638 gross tons, one of the largest cruise vessels ever built — ties into MSC Cruises' growth strategy for North American customers as it'll sail in North America starting late next year after initial sailings in the Mediterranean.

It'll operate a series of seven- and 14-night winter sailings in the Southern Caribbean out of Martinique, Guadeloupe and Barbados that'll complement the line's growing number of Caribbean itineraries out of Florida and Galveston, Texas.

Related: The 6 types of MSC Cruises ships, explained

It's just the latest big new ship that MSC Cruises has earmarked for North America as part of its North American growth strategy.

The line's 19-month-old MSC World America, a sister ship to MSC World Asia that also is among the biggest cruise vessels ever built, already is sailing out of Florida.

Custom-built for the North American market in a way no other MSC Cruises ship has been before, MSC World America is significantly bigger and more venue-packed than any other ship MSC Cruises has deployed to the region.

A third ship in the same series debuting in late 2027, MSC World Atlantic, also will be devoted to the North American market with sailings out of Port Canaveral, Florida.

All three of the ships are part of the line's new World Class series, which are by far the biggest MSC Cruises vessels ever built. Capable of carrying nearly 6,800 passengers with every berth filled, they are the first to rival the biggest ships from cruise giant Royal Caribbean in size and amenities.

In all, MSC Cruises will have seven vessels sailing out of U.S. ports for all or part of 2027, plus another two vessels sailing from Caribbean ports, for a total of nine ships in North America. That's an enormous increase from just a few years ago. As recently as 2017, MSC Cruises had just one ship sailing year-round from a U.S. port plus a handful more sailing from Caribbean ports.

With the addition of MSC World Asia, MSC Cruises has 24 vessels in all.

The expanded footprint in North America includes MSC Cruises' first sailings to Alaska, which began in May, and its first sailings from Galveston, which began in December.

MSC Cruises also has invested heavily the past few years in North American port infrastructure and a private destination in the region, the Ocean Cay MSC Marine Reserve in the Bahamas.

Onorato told TPG the line eventually could expand its North American cruise offerings to more U.S. ports, though not for a few years.

"This is an opportunity with us, and we will be looking at this," he said. "But not in the very short term. We're not [planning this] for 27, for 28 or for 29 yet. But in the future, why not?"

Onorato noted the line needs to balance its growth in North America with its growth in Europe, where it wants to maintain its dominant position.

"We don't want to reduce the capacity in Europe, because in Europe today we are living a situation of market leadership, which I like a lot, and so I don't want to lose it," he said.

Onorato also noted the company is growing significantly in Asia with an announcement earlier this month that it would deploy a second ship to the region starting in late 2028. It'll offer cruises out of Singapore.

Related: Why MSC World America is the best new cruise ship of the year

Staying strong in Europe, in particular, ties into the company's strategy to grow North American passenger counts as Americans can become a bigger feeder market into the brand's Europe-based ships, Onorato suggested.

"I believe being the leader in Europe ... we are the ideal cruise line for North Americans traveling to Europe, because we have so many different embarkation ports," he said.

Onorato noted that MSC Cruises lets passengers board its ships in 10 different ports around the Mediterranean, far more than any of the North American brands operating in the region, with departures starting every day of the week.

These include departures from such secondary ports as Marseille, France; Genoa, Italy; and Naples, Italy. The latter, he noted, can now be reached via daily nonstop United and Delta flights from the United States.

Related: Why we love MSC World Europa for Europe sailings

"Nobody else is giving you this opportunity," he said.

In all, MSC Cruises is aiming for 10 million passengers a year worldwide within a decade, up from a bit more than 5 million passengers a year today.

The growth will come in part due to a significant expansion in ship capacity.

MSC Cruises has five more of its new World Class ships on order for delivery by 2031. It also has ordered a new class of four slightly smaller vessels to debut between 2030 and 2033.

Toegether, the nine ships will increase the line's capacity by nearly 50%.

#6011. Global Entry Member Had $250K Of Undeclared Cartier Jewelry Seized, And CBP Says It Knew In Advance

Many people will shop for luxury goods when traveling abroad (especially if going to places like Milan or Paris), and love to point out how it’s “such a good value” compared to shopping in the US. That’s perhaps true, if part of that math includes requesting a tax refund in the foreign country, and then not declaring it upon your return to the United States, in violation of customs laws.

A reader asked me an interesting question about this topic, and I didn’t have a good answer, so I think it makes for a good discussion. First let’s talk about the background, and then I’ll pose the specific question a reader asked me.

To keep this example specific to the United States, when you return to the country from abroad, you’re typically asked by a Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer if you have anything to declare.

Travelers have to declare all kinds of things (meat, produce, drugs, etc.), including any purchases above the $800 standard personal exemption, which is the limit of merchandise acquired abroad that can be imported without paying taxes (tangent — it really is time that limit is raised, since it has been the same for over two decades, and there has been quite some inflation in that time!).

In other words, if you made $2,000 worth of personal purchases abroad, you’re supposed to declare that, and you’d have to pay import taxes on $1,200 worth of those purchases.

The idea is that travelers make purchases abroad and pay the local sales tax, but then upon departure, foreigners can request a refund of those sales taxes. This typically has to be done at the airport, assuming the country allows tax free shopping.

The way people often mentally process this is that they’re able to shop “tax free.” That’s even how many stories will market things. What that of course conveniently overlooks is that you’re supposed to then declare these items when you return to the United States, and pay taxes there.

With some frequency, you’ll see people posting online about the huge issues they have with this, and it tends to fall into one of two categories:

You’ll see stories all the time of people having their Global Entry revoked over things like this, along with facing other punishment. And that brings us to the question a reader posed…

Several weeks ago, CBP put out a press release about how it seized more than $250K in undeclared jewelry from a Global Entry member at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). Okay, I’m not surprised stuff like this happens, but here’s the part of the story that is most interesting:

The traveler, a Pennsylvania resident, was referred for a secondary baggage examination after arriving on a flight from Amsterdam. During the inspection, the traveler initially told CBP officers that she had purchased only a few thousand dollars’ worth of souvenirs.

Prior to the traveler’s arrival, CBP officers obtained information indicating the traveler had purchased a Cartier bracelet valued at $183,818 and a Cartier ring valued at $67,811.

CBP officers provided the traveler multiple opportunities to declare the jewelry, but she did not. The traveler declared the items only after officers informed her that they were aware of the purchases. The traveler later admitted she had discarded the jewelry boxes and receipts.

Obviously two jewelry items worth over $250K is a major “haul,” but the part of the story that a reader asked me is the claim that CBP obtained information about this prior to the traveler’s arrival.

Is that actually true, or were they bluffing? Do various customs authorities share details with one another, where one country will say “oh, this person just received a tax refund on a $250K purchase and is now boarding a flight to the US?” I can’t find any credible information online suggesting that information is shared in this way.

Obviously agencies of various countries do coordinate on some important things, but this seems different than having someone on the “most wanted” list board a flight. But what is the alternative explanation? Is the claim here that a private citizen somehow made CBP aware of this?

Was this person somehow bragging on social media about their purchase while abroad, and CBP came across it, and then confronted her? I otherwise have a hard time imagining a tip from a citizen would get “processed” that quickly by CBP, given the timeline we’re talking about.

Many people like to shop while abroad, and view it as a great deal, since they can often claim a tax refund in that country. That conveniently overlooks that the personal tax exemption when entering the United States is $800, so anything above that amount is supposed to be declared, with import taxes having to be paid.

Of course the thing is that many people try to get away with not disclosing their purchases abroad — some people just don’t even think to do so, while others will intentionally throw away boxes and receipts, etc.

CBP recently reported how it seized $250K+ in jewelry at Philadelphia Airport, claiming they were already tipped off to this before the traveler arrived in the US. The traveler just had two small (but very expensive) Cartier pieces, so that raises an interesting question that a reader asked me about.

I assume that when you make a tax free declaration in one country, they’re not immediately turning around and sharing that with another country, but obviously I can’t say that authoritatively. But what other explanation is there? Was someone just stupid and bragging on social media, and somehow CBP came across it, or what?

Can anyone answer this question better than I can? Because now that I’ve been asked it, I’m curious as well!

Why is the picture on the home page showing Dublin Airport??

CBP expects and accepts a certain amount of non-compliance, but there are programs in place to catch (and subsquently make an example of) whales such as this traveler.

I live in Switzerland and it’s very well known that German (EU) authorities immediately and automatically sent information about VAT refunds to residents of Switzerland to the Swiss *customs* authorities, and vice versa. If you claim a VAT refund from Germany but don’t pay VAT at the Swiss border you will automatically get a fine in the mail and possibly a criminal prosecution. When you leave the EU and reclaim VAT you have to indicate where you live. Some Swiss people who bought Rolexes in the Caribbean, Sint Marten, which is part of the Netherlands, and got a VAT refund learned the hard way that customs officials share this data on both sides of the Atlantic. Contrary to what the “retired customs officer” seems to say, a VAT is not “financial information.” As EU law allows EU countries to send and receive such information from Switzerland I see no reason why they shouldn’t also share it with the United States.

#6010. Citi AAdvantage Business Card Review—75,000 Miles And Status Credit For Two People From The Same Spending

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] can turn $125,000 in eligible spending on an employee card into American Airlines Platinum Pro status for two people. That’s without even earning any Loyalty Points from flying, a hotel booking or shopping through American’s portal.

The Citi AAdvantage Business Card is the best airline credit card for spending toward status. I have the card, and I’m keeping it. The limited-time initial bonus is strong, the first year has no annual fee, and the recently announced refresh adds benefits. But the reason to put spending on this card is that two people can get status credit for the same purchases.

The current limited time offer is 75,000 American Airlines AAdvantage bonus miles after $5,000 in purchases within the first five months of account opening. Purchases by the primary cardmember and employees count toward that requirement. There’s no annual fee for the first 12 months. The card’s regular annual fee is currently $99, but it rises to $150 with renewals beginning January 24, 2027. Someone opening the card now will see a $150 annual fee at renewal. Employee cards have no additional annual fee, and there’s no foreign transaction fee. The initial bonus alone can cover a one way Japan Airlines business class award between the U.S. and Japan when partner award space is available. American miles remain especially strong for premium cabin awards on partners. Prices largely remain at the same level they were a decade ago, while numerous other progams have devalued. Citi’s 48 month restriction applies to an initial bonus on this business card, including its former CitiBusiness AAdvantage Platinum Select-named product. Citi also restricts eligibility after converting another Citi account with a recent initial bonus into this product. Having a separate personal American Airlines card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. How The Same Citi AAdvantage Business Card Spending Earns Status For Two People Normally each cardmember earns one Loyalty Point per dollar on their purchases. When an employee uses their card, those Loyalty Points go to the employee. Through December 31, 2028, the primary cardmember also receives one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible employee card spending. That’s an additional credit to a second person’s account. Spending on the primary cardmember’s card still earns that person one Loyalty Point per dollar. When I covered the refresh, American confirmed to me that all Citi AAdvantage Business cardmembers were included after the former Barclays business accounts migrated. This used to be called a targeted promotion because legacy Barclays cardmembers didn’t qualify. Here’s what eligible spending on one employee’s card can accomplish in a single status qualification year, assuming neither person earns Loyalty Points elsewhere: Employee Card Spending Primary Cardmember Employee $40,000 Gold Gold $75,000 Platinum Platinum $125,000 Platinum Pro Platinum Pro $200,000 Executive Platinum Executive Platinum American’s qualification year starts March 1 and runs through the end of February. You can combine the card’s Loyalty Points with qualifying activity from other sources. A business owner with several employee cards receives the additional Loyalty Points across their eligible spending. Each employee gets credit for the purchases on their individual card. Authorized users must be employees or contractors of the business, and need to be enrolled in AAdvantage and AAdvantage Business to receive their Loyalty Points. A spouse who works in the business fits this. The Business Controls The Miles Redeemable miles work differently from status credit. The miles from purchases, including employee purchases, and the initial bonus go into the company’s AAdvantage Business account. The business can then transfer miles to registered travelers’ personal AAdvantage accounts, including the primary cardmember’s. You don’t have to decide which person will ultimately use the miles when you make a purchase. So unlike a consumer card where the miles go into the primary cardmember’s account, these are transferable AAdvantage miles. The Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® also waives American’s small business program’s usual requirements of five active travelers and $5,000 in eligible American Airlines flight spending to access earned miles. That lets you ‘double tip’ with American, earning business program miles and miles from the same travel, and tickets credited to a small business account earn an extra loyalty point per dollar spent too. The AAdvantage Business program awards the company one mile per eligible airfare dollar and registered travelers one additional Loyalty Point per eligible airfare dollar. What You Earn On Purchases The Citi AAdvantage Business Card currently earns: 2 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 2 miles per dollar at gas stations, car rental merchants, telecommunications merchants, and cable and satellite providers. 1 mile per dollar on other purchases. Starting January 24, 2027, the refresh adds 3 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings, plus 2 miles per dollar in one selected category: U.S. shipping providers, office supply stores or U.S. advertising services. The selected business category can be changed quarterly and has no spending cap. Checked Bags, Boarding And The Companion Certificate The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation receive a first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries and Group 5 boarding. You don’t have to buy the ticket with this card to receive those benefits. They follow the primary cardmember’s AAdvantage number on the reservation. An employee traveling separately doesn’t get free checked bags or preferred boarding merely from an employee card. After $30,000 in purchases during a cardmembership year and renewal, the primary cardmember can earn a companion certificate for an eligible domestic Main Cabin roundtrip. The companion pays $99 plus taxes and fees. You buy a qualifying Main Cabin ticket, the companion must have eligible fare inventory available, and you book through American Airlines Meeting Services. Travel is generally within the contiguous 48 states, with additional provisions for residents of Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. The account must remain open for a full billing cycle after its anniversary month to receive the certificate. The card also offers 10% savings on eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. What The January 24 Refresh Adds To The Citi AAdvantage Business Card The Citi AAdvantage Business Card annual fee rises by $51, and the biggest new credit replaces an existing benefit. Up to $100 in inflight credits each calendar year. Eligible food, beverage and paid Wi-Fi purchases replace the current 25% savings on inflight food and beverages and Wi-Fi. This doesn’t cover purchases in Admirals Clubs. Up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years. Useful if you need it, but many readers already have this benefit through another card. 25% off a Melio subscription. This discounts the subscription plan, not the processing fee charged for paying bills with a credit card. Travel protections. The card adds trip delay, trip cancellation and interruption, lost or damaged luggage, and rental car coverage. Spend $100 on qualifying inflight purchases and the old 25% rebate returned $25. The new credit returns $100, an improvement of $75. After the $51 annual fee increase, you’re $24 ahead on those two changes alone. At $400 in qualifying inflight spending, both versions return $100. Above that, the old uncapped 25% rebate was worth more. I don’t know many people who spent $400 inflight on food and beverages with American Airlines. As I detailed when the changes were announced, business card trip delay coverage is up to $500 per covered trip after an eligible delay exceeding six hours, limited to two claims per account in a 12 month period. It isn’t $500 for each traveler. For trip delay and cancellation or interruption coverage, the full covered trip must be paid with the card or an eligible combination of the card and AAdvantage miles, certificates, vouchers, coupons or discounts. When I’d Put Spending On This Card For $100,000 in purchases outside bonus categories, a 2% cash back card would return $2,000. This card produces 100,000 miles. Put that spending on an eligible employee card and it also produces 100,000 Loyalty Points for each of two people. Whether those miles are worth more or less than $2,000 depends on how you use them. The status credit is what can make this a real winning play and it has more value when two people will use the status. If you’re only interested in redeemable miles, other cards can earn more rewards on ordinary spending, including transferable points. Citi’s Strata Premier nad Strata Elite can earn points faster and transfer to American. The business card makes sense for earning status. The Executive Card Can Make This More Valuable The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds: 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. You don’t have to earn the qualifying points by spending on the Executive card. Points from business card spending can trigger the bonuses. Suppose the business primary cardmember and one employee each also hold a separate Executive card as a primary cardmember. Then: $105,000 in eligible purchases on that employee’s business card earns each person 105,000 Loyalty Points. Each person’s Executive card adds 20,000 Loyalty Points from the first two thresholds. Each reaches 125,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum Pro and oneworld Emerald. That requires two separate Executive accounts, each with a $695 annual fee, in addition to the business card. I’ve written about doing this with my wife. I already have the business and Executive cards. Giving her an employee card for the business, and having her hold a separate primary Executive card, could help both of us earn oneworld Emerald from the same business spending. For my family, that has a great use. If we’re flying home from Sydney on an eligible oneworld flight, two Emerald members can each bring a guest into the Qantas first class lounge. We’d have access for all four of us even when we’re flying business class. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® Topics on this pageAAdvantageAmerican AirlinesAlaskaBarclaysCitibankGlobal EntryHawaiiJapanJapan AirlinesOneworldPlatinumPuerto RicoQantasSydneyTransportation Security AdministrationUnited States Virgin IslandsWi-Fi+15 more More From View from the Wing

The current limited time offer is 75,000 American Airlines AAdvantage bonus miles after $5,000 in purchases within the first five months of account opening. Purchases by the primary cardmember and employees count toward that requirement.

There’s no annual fee for the first 12 months. The card’s regular annual fee is currently $99, but it rises to $150 with renewals beginning January 24, 2027. Someone opening the card now will see a $150 annual fee at renewal. Employee cards have no additional annual fee, and there’s no foreign transaction fee.

The initial bonus alone can cover a one way Japan Airlines business class award between the U.S. and Japan when partner award space is available. American miles remain especially strong for premium cabin awards on partners. Prices largely remain at the same level they were a decade ago, while numerous other progams have devalued.

Citi’s 48 month restriction applies to an initial bonus on this business card, including its former CitiBusiness AAdvantage Platinum Select-named product. Citi also restricts eligibility after converting another Citi account with a recent initial bonus into this product. Having a separate personal American Airlines card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you.

Normally each cardmember earns one Loyalty Point per dollar on their purchases. When an employee uses their card, those Loyalty Points go to the employee. Through December 31, 2028, the primary cardmember also receives one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible employee card spending. That’s an additional credit to a second person’s account. Spending on the primary cardmember’s card still earns that person one Loyalty Point per dollar. When I covered the refresh, American confirmed to me that all Citi AAdvantage Business cardmembers were included after the former Barclays business accounts migrated. This used to be called a targeted promotion because legacy Barclays cardmembers didn’t qualify. Here’s what eligible spending on one employee’s card can accomplish in a single status qualification year, assuming neither person earns Loyalty Points elsewhere: Employee Card Spending Primary Cardmember Employee $40,000 Gold Gold $75,000 Platinum Platinum $125,000 Platinum Pro Platinum Pro $200,000 Executive Platinum Executive Platinum American’s qualification year starts March 1 and runs through the end of February. You can combine the card’s Loyalty Points with qualifying activity from other sources. A business owner with several employee cards receives the additional Loyalty Points across their eligible spending. Each employee gets credit for the purchases on their individual card. Authorized users must be employees or contractors of the business, and need to be enrolled in AAdvantage and AAdvantage Business to receive their Loyalty Points. A spouse who works in the business fits this. The Business Controls The Miles Redeemable miles work differently from status credit. The miles from purchases, including employee purchases, and the initial bonus go into the company’s AAdvantage Business account. The business can then transfer miles to registered travelers’ personal AAdvantage accounts, including the primary cardmember’s. You don’t have to decide which person will ultimately use the miles when you make a purchase. So unlike a consumer card where the miles go into the primary cardmember’s account, these are transferable AAdvantage miles. The Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® also waives American’s small business program’s usual requirements of five active travelers and $5,000 in eligible American Airlines flight spending to access earned miles. That lets you ‘double tip’ with American, earning business program miles and miles from the same travel, and tickets credited to a small business account earn an extra loyalty point per dollar spent too. The AAdvantage Business program awards the company one mile per eligible airfare dollar and registered travelers one additional Loyalty Point per eligible airfare dollar. What You Earn On Purchases The Citi AAdvantage Business Card currently earns: 2 miles per dollar on eligible American Airlines purchases. 2 miles per dollar at gas stations, car rental merchants, telecommunications merchants, and cable and satellite providers. 1 mile per dollar on other purchases. Starting January 24, 2027, the refresh adds 3 miles per dollar on eligible AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings, plus 2 miles per dollar in one selected category: U.S. shipping providers, office supply stores or U.S. advertising services. The selected business category can be changed quarterly and has no spending cap. Checked Bags, Boarding And The Companion Certificate The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation receive a first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries and Group 5 boarding. You don’t have to buy the ticket with this card to receive those benefits. They follow the primary cardmember’s AAdvantage number on the reservation. An employee traveling separately doesn’t get free checked bags or preferred boarding merely from an employee card. After $30,000 in purchases during a cardmembership year and renewal, the primary cardmember can earn a companion certificate for an eligible domestic Main Cabin roundtrip. The companion pays $99 plus taxes and fees. You buy a qualifying Main Cabin ticket, the companion must have eligible fare inventory available, and you book through American Airlines Meeting Services. Travel is generally within the contiguous 48 states, with additional provisions for residents of Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. The account must remain open for a full billing cycle after its anniversary month to receive the certificate. The card also offers 10% savings on eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. What The January 24 Refresh Adds To The Citi AAdvantage Business Card The Citi AAdvantage Business Card annual fee rises by $51, and the biggest new credit replaces an existing benefit. Up to $100 in inflight credits each calendar year. Eligible food, beverage and paid Wi-Fi purchases replace the current 25% savings on inflight food and beverages and Wi-Fi. This doesn’t cover purchases in Admirals Clubs. Up to $120 for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck every four years. Useful if you need it, but many readers already have this benefit through another card. 25% off a Melio subscription. This discounts the subscription plan, not the processing fee charged for paying bills with a credit card. Travel protections. The card adds trip delay, trip cancellation and interruption, lost or damaged luggage, and rental car coverage. Spend $100 on qualifying inflight purchases and the old 25% rebate returned $25. The new credit returns $100, an improvement of $75. After the $51 annual fee increase, you’re $24 ahead on those two changes alone. At $400 in qualifying inflight spending, both versions return $100. Above that, the old uncapped 25% rebate was worth more. I don’t know many people who spent $400 inflight on food and beverages with American Airlines. As I detailed when the changes were announced, business card trip delay coverage is up to $500 per covered trip after an eligible delay exceeding six hours, limited to two claims per account in a 12 month period. It isn’t $500 for each traveler. For trip delay and cancellation or interruption coverage, the full covered trip must be paid with the card or an eligible combination of the card and AAdvantage miles, certificates, vouchers, coupons or discounts. When I’d Put Spending On This Card For $100,000 in purchases outside bonus categories, a 2% cash back card would return $2,000. This card produces 100,000 miles. Put that spending on an eligible employee card and it also produces 100,000 Loyalty Points for each of two people. Whether those miles are worth more or less than $2,000 depends on how you use them. The status credit is what can make this a real winning play and it has more value when two people will use the status. If you’re only interested in redeemable miles, other cards can earn more rewards on ordinary spending, including transferable points. Citi’s Strata Premier nad Strata Elite can earn points faster and transfer to American. The business card makes sense for earning status. For trip delay and cancellation or interruption coverage, the full covered trip must be paid with the card or an eligible combination of the card and AAdvantage miles, certificates, vouchers, coupons or discounts. When I’d Put Spending On This Card For $100,000 in purchases outside bonus categories, a 2% cash back card would return $2,000. This card produces 100,000 miles. Put that spending on an eligible employee card and it also produces 100,000 Loyalty Points for each of two people. Whether those miles are worth more or less than $2,000 depends on how you use them. The status credit is what can make this a real winning play and it has more value when two people will use the status. If you’re only interested in redeemable miles, other cards can earn more rewards on ordinary spending, including transferable points. Citi’s Strata Premier nad Strata Elite can earn points faster and transfer to American. The business card makes sense for earning status. The Executive Card Can Make This More Valuable The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] awards 10,000 additional Loyalty Points at each of four thresholds: 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. You don’t have to earn the qualifying points by spending on the Executive card. Points from business card spending can trigger the bonuses. Suppose the business primary cardmember and one employee each also hold a separate Executive card as a primary cardmember. Then: $105,000 in eligible purchases on that employee’s business card earns each person 105,000 Loyalty Points. Each person’s Executive card adds 20,000 Loyalty Points from the first two thresholds. Each reaches 125,000 Loyalty Points, enough for Platinum Pro and oneworld Emerald. That requires two separate Executive accounts, each with a $695 annual fee, in addition to the business card. I’ve written about doing this with my wife. I already have the business and Executive cards. Giving her an employee card for the business, and having her hold a separate primary Executive card, could help both of us earn oneworld Emerald from the same business spending. For my family, that has a great use. If we’re flying home from Sydney on an eligible oneworld flight, two Emerald members can each bring a guest into the Qantas first class lounge. We’d have access for all four of us even when we’re flying business class. #6009. Chase Ink Business Cash Bonus: 75K Points Welcome Offer

The Ink Business Cash® Credit Card is part of the Chase Ink Business card portfolio, and is one of the best no annual fee business cards out there. It’s one of the Chase business cards with the most lucrative spending multipliers, and given the card’s lack of an annual fee, it’s a useful part of a larger Chase card strategy.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at the Chase Ink Business Cash bonus, as it’s one of the best welcome offers you’ll find on any no annual fee card.

Link: Learn more about the Ink Business Cash® Credit Card with 75K bonus points

The Chase Ink Cash Card currently has a welcome bonus of 75,000 points after spending $6,000 within the first three months. You’ll see that the bonus is marketed as offering cash back, rather than points, so it’s described as a $750 bonus. Indeed, you could redeem the rewards as cash back.

However, if you have the card in conjunction with a card earning Ultimate Rewards points, like the Chase Sapphire Reserve® Card (learn more) or Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more), then rewards can be transferred to Ultimate Rewards airline and hotel partners.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Ultimate Rewards points to be worth 1.7 cents each, and that increases the value of the points by 70% right there, as far as I’m concerned. I consider the 75,000 points to be worth $1,275. That’s a great bonus, especially for a no annual fee card.

With the ability to transfer Chase points to partners at a 1:1 ratio, that opens up all kinds of great redemption opportunities, including:

How does the Chase Ink Cash 75,000-point offer compare to past publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the card? Below is a chart with the Chase Ink Cash welcome offer history in recent years.

As you can see, the Chase Ink Cash publicly available welcome offer typically ranges from 75,000 to 100,000 points. The offer of 75,000 points is excellent, but is the standard offer. If you are willing to wait, we might see another offer of 90,000 points, or a return of the best-ever offer of 100,000 points.

However, the offer of 75,000 points is still great, and I’d decide whether to apply now or wait based on how much value you’d get from the card in the coming months. For a no annual fee card, the offer of 75,000 points is still industry leading.

When it comes to getting approved for the Chase Ink Cash Card and earning the welcome bonus, what rules should you be aware of? Well, there are the card specific policies, and then also the more generic Chase policies. When you pull up the application, you’ll see the following terms:

The new cardmember bonus may not be available to you if you have ever had this card or any other Chase for Business card without an annual fee. We may also consider factors pertinent to your business in determining your bonus eligibility.

As you can see, officially the welcome bonus isn’t available to you if you’ve had this exact card, or another Chase business card without an annual fee, including the Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (learn more). So there is an element of cards being mutually exclusive.

However, the key here is that you “may” not be eligible, and not that you absolutely won’t be eligible. I don’t love that level of vagueness, though the good news is that if you apply for the card and aren’t eligible for the bonus, you should receive a pop-up message informing you of this, before there’s a hard pull. So that at least means the downside of applying is limited.

The good news is that eligibility for the bonus is completely unrelated to whether you have a Chase business card with an annual fee, like the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (learn more) or Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (learn more).

It’s fine to apply for Chase business cards as a sole proprietorship, corporation, etc. If you apply as a sole proprietorship, you can just enter your Social Security Number in the section where you’d otherwise put your EIN.

Beyond that, there are some general Chase rules to be aware of:

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to get approved for the Chase Ink Cash, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that impacts card eligibility.

The Chase Ink Cash Card has no annual fee, and there are several reasons to consider picking it up. The way I view it, there are a few points that are most important.

For one, the Ink Business Cash has a phenomenal rewards structure, which can earn you lots of points:

The Ink Business Cash offers 1x points on other spending. Do be aware that the card has foreign transaction fees, so I’d only recommend using it for purchases within the United States, charged in USD.

Furthermore, the Ink Business Cash offers primary rental car coverage, which can come in handy if you rent cars with any frequency, and is incredibly rare for a no annual fee card. Also, since the card has no annual fee, there’s really no opportunity cost to holding onto it, and it allows you to create a great portfolio of cards to maximize rewards.

Read my review of the Chase Ink Cash Card.

The Chase Ink Cash Card is one of the most lucrative no annual fee cards out there. The card has a welcome bonus of 75K points upon completing minimum spending, which is excellent for a no annual fee card.

Not only does the card have a good bonus, but it offers rewards that can make it worth holding onto, like 5x points in select categories, plus rental car coverage.

Do you have the Chase Ink Cash Card, and if so, what has your experience been?

#6008. Hyatt Regency LAX Caps Stays At 21 Days—The Legal Risk That Makes Hotels Turn Away Paying Guests

Hyatt Regency LAX won’t let you stay more than 21 consecutive days. Booking separate reservations won’t get around it. The hotel even counts back-to-back stays. They seem to be worried about a guest becoming a tenant under the law. A customer who wants to keep paying can become someone the hotel needs to turn away. The published policy says: The hotel does not accept reservations that result in a guest staying more than 21 consecutive days, whether through one reservation or multiple back-to-back reservations. Meanwhile, its frequently asked questions advertises “Extended Stay Regency Suites” and tells guests to contact the property about extended stays or special arrangements. Apparently there’s extended, and then there’s too extended. Why A Hotel Might Want You Gone Before A Month I’d put 90% odds at avoiding residential tenancy exposure being the main explanation for this policy. Once someone qualifies as a tenant, ending their stay can require notices and a court eviction instead of ordinary hotel checkout procedures. Depending on the jurisdiction and property, rent regulation and restrictions on the grounds for eviction can enter the picture, too. The hotel may have to spend money establishing that an exception applies before it can get its room back. In the city of Los Angeles, the rent stabilization ordinance brings hotel accommodations occupied as someone’s primary residence for more than 30 days into its definition of a rental unit. Building age and other exemptions matter, too, though. California also has a separate exclusion for qualifying hotels that retain access and control and offer a specified set of services, including housekeeping, mail and room services. The relevant Los Angeles threshold is 30 days. A 21 day limit looks like a conservative buffer, leaving room to deal with a delayed departure before getting close to it. Although a hotel might want to preserve rooms for shorter, more profitable bookings, or limit payment risk. Other Hotels Have Limits, Including Right Next To California In Vegas Hyatt Regency LAX isn’t alone. Here are published limits at some other properties: Hotel Published Stay Limit Hyatt Regency Valencia 28 days Hyatt Regency Westlake 28 days Best Western Los Angeles Worldport, Wilmington 28 days The LINE Los Angeles 29 days, contact the hotel for stays over 21 Wynn Las Vegas / Encore Terms state a 14 day maximum for all reservations Oasis at Gold Spike, Las Vegas 14 consecutive nights The LINE Austin 29 days, contact the hotel for stays over 21 The LINE Washington, D.C. 28 days, contact the hotel for stays over 21 The legal differences at play: Nevada has a 30 day trigger. Its residential landlord-tenant statute excludes hotel or motel occupancy of less than 30 consecutive days, unless the occupant clearly shows an intent to remain for a longer continuous period. Texas looks at the relationship between property and guest. As Texas Legal Aid explains, length of stay, payment arrangements, contract terms, housekeeping and control of the room all help distinguish a guest from a tenant. The state’s 30 day hotel tax exemption also applies. Florida gives the written agreement more weight. Its current definition treats hotel and motel occupancy as transient unless a written rental or lease agreement expressly says the unit is the guest’s sole residence. Transient hotel occupancy is excluded from the residential tenancy chapter. New York has more than one route to protection. State law includes a nontransient hotel resident in possession for at least 30 consecutive days within its tenant definition for eviction proceedings. But in a New York City hotel covered by rent stabilization, a guest can acquire permanent tenant status much sooner simply by requesting a qualifying lease. Sometimes A Stay Limit Doesn’t Solve The Problem A hotel can’t necessarily make tenancy law disappear by putting a checkout date in its terms. California prohibits a residential hotel from requiring an occupant to move, or check out and re-register, before 30 days when a purpose is keeping them legally transient. That rule applies to residential hotels, not automatically to every hotel. Los Angeles also counts forced room changes and checkouts intended to avoid its rent-stabilization rules. New York City’s rules for covered hotels go further. An occupant who’s never had a lease can request one at any point during occupancy. The request makes them a permanent tenant, and the owner must provide a lease of at least six months within 15 days. The rules also prohibit refusing to continue a tenancy solely to prevent permanent-tenant status. In that setting, a claim can arise after the first night. I understand preventing an apartment landlord from evading the law by calling the building a hotel. But making it difficult for an actual hotel and a willing customer to agree on a temporary stay has costs, too. Someone working on a project, waiting for a home repair, or staying near a hospital may want six weeks of housekeeping and a front desk. They don’t necessarily want an apartment lease. If accommodating that person creates a costly risk of being unable to recover the room, the hotel has an incentive to refuse the booking. The New Yorker Guest Tried To Take The Whole Building The Wyndham New Yorker case I’ve covered took these risks to their absurd extreme. Mickey Barreto booked one night in 2018 for $149 plus tax, requested a lease, and wouldn’t leave. After the hotel removed him, he went to housing court and obtained an order restoring possession of his room. And the hotel subsequently lost a contested eviction case and its appeal. To establish the exemption it claimed from rent stabilization, the property needed to prove that the room rented for more than $350 a month or $88 a week on May 31, 1968. In 2020, an appellate court upheld the eviction case’s dismissal because the hotel hadn’t supplied sufficient evidence. A 1966 hotel directory and a 1969 accountant’s report didn’t establish the necessary room rate on the statutory date. Imagine trying to get your hotel room back in 2020 and losing because you can’t adequately document what it cost in 1968. While the room dispute was going on, Barreto treated his possession order as a basis to claim the entire building. His theory was that the property hadn’t been subdivided, so rights to his room somehow gave him the hotel. He filed documents purporting to transfer ownership to himself and his nonprofit, Mickey Barreto Missions. According to Manhattan prosecutors, he demanded rent from a tenant, demanded control of the hotel’s bank accounts, told the real owner to leave, and approached Wyndham about transferring the franchise. He even went to its lenders to try to borrow against the property. The city recorded fraudulent documents. The courts protected possession of a room. A 2019 judgment declared the deed void and confirmed the real owner’s title. He nevertheless made further false filings in 2023. Tenancy law didn’t authorize stealing a skyscraper. But the hotel was already fighting over a one night guest’s right to remain when it had to start defending its title, its accounts and its dealings with tenants and lenders, too. Barreto was finally evicted in 2024. In February 2026, nearly eight years after checking in, he pleaded guilty to fraud. His sentence was six months already served and five years of probation. The relevant Los Angeles threshold is 30 days. A 21 day limit looks like a conservative buffer, leaving room to deal with a delayed departure before getting close to it. Although a hotel might want to preserve rooms for shorter, more profitable bookings, or limit payment risk.

Hyatt Regency LAX isn’t alone. Here are published limits at some other properties: Hotel Published Stay Limit Hyatt Regency Valencia 28 days Hyatt Regency Westlake 28 days Best Western Los Angeles Worldport, Wilmington 28 days The LINE Los Angeles 29 days, contact the hotel for stays over 21 Wynn Las Vegas / Encore Terms state a 14 day maximum for all reservations Oasis at Gold Spike, Las Vegas 14 consecutive nights The LINE Austin 29 days, contact the hotel for stays over 21 The LINE Washington, D.C. 28 days, contact the hotel for stays over 21 The legal differences at play: Nevada has a 30 day trigger. Its residential landlord-tenant statute excludes hotel or motel occupancy of less than 30 consecutive days, unless the occupant clearly shows an intent to remain for a longer continuous period. Texas looks at the relationship between property and guest. As Texas Legal Aid explains, length of stay, payment arrangements, contract terms, housekeeping and control of the room all help distinguish a guest from a tenant. The state’s 30 day hotel tax exemption also applies. Florida gives the written agreement more weight. Its current definition treats hotel and motel occupancy as transient unless a written rental or lease agreement expressly says the unit is the guest’s sole residence. Transient hotel occupancy is excluded from the residential tenancy chapter. New York has more than one route to protection. State law includes a nontransient hotel resident in possession for at least 30 consecutive days within its tenant definition for eviction proceedings. But in a New York City hotel covered by rent stabilization, a guest can acquire permanent tenant status much sooner simply by requesting a qualifying lease. Sometimes A Stay Limit Doesn’t Solve The Problem A hotel can’t necessarily make tenancy law disappear by putting a checkout date in its terms. California prohibits a residential hotel from requiring an occupant to move, or check out and re-register, before 30 days when a purpose is keeping them legally transient. That rule applies to residential hotels, not automatically to every hotel. Los Angeles also counts forced room changes and checkouts intended to avoid its rent-stabilization rules. New York City’s rules for covered hotels go further. An occupant who’s never had a lease can request one at any point during occupancy. The request makes them a permanent tenant, and the owner must provide a lease of at least six months within 15 days. The rules also prohibit refusing to continue a tenancy solely to prevent permanent-tenant status. In that setting, a claim can arise after the first night. I understand preventing an apartment landlord from evading the law by calling the building a hotel. But making it difficult for an actual hotel and a willing customer to agree on a temporary stay has costs, too. Someone working on a project, waiting for a home repair, or staying near a hospital may want six weeks of housekeeping and a front desk. They don’t necessarily want an apartment lease. If accommodating that person creates a costly risk of being unable to recover the room, the hotel has an incentive to refuse the booking. The New Yorker Guest Tried To Take The Whole Building The Wyndham New Yorker case I’ve covered took these risks to their absurd extreme. Mickey Barreto booked one night in 2018 for $149 plus tax, requested a lease, and wouldn’t leave. After the hotel removed him, he went to housing court and obtained an order restoring possession of his room. And the hotel subsequently lost a contested eviction case and its appeal. To establish the exemption it claimed from rent stabilization, the property needed to prove that the room rented for more than $350 a month or $88 a week on May 31, 1968. In 2020, an appellate court upheld the eviction case’s dismissal because the hotel hadn’t supplied sufficient evidence. A 1966 hotel directory and a 1969 accountant’s report didn’t establish the necessary room rate on the statutory date. Imagine trying to get your hotel room back in 2020 and losing because you can’t adequately document what it cost in 1968. While the room dispute was going on, Barreto treated his possession order as a basis to claim the entire building. His theory was that the property hadn’t been subdivided, so rights to his room somehow gave him the hotel. He filed documents purporting to transfer ownership to himself and his nonprofit, Mickey Barreto Missions. According to Manhattan prosecutors, he demanded rent from a tenant, demanded control of the hotel’s bank accounts, told the real owner to leave, and approached Wyndham about transferring the franchise. He even went to its lenders to try to borrow against the property. The city recorded fraudulent documents. The courts protected possession of a room. A 2019 judgment declared the deed void and confirmed the real owner’s title. He nevertheless made further false filings in 2023. Tenancy law didn’t authorize stealing a skyscraper. But the hotel was already fighting over a one night guest’s right to remain when it had to start defending its title, its accounts and its dealings with tenants and lenders, too. Barreto was finally evicted in 2024. In February 2026, nearly eight years after checking in, he pleaded guilty to fraud. His sentence was six months already served and five years of probation. During my working life I often spent more than 21 days at a time in a particular hotel. Having to move hotels from time to time would’ve been a PITA.

Mickey Barreto could own that hotel given the new rent laws being enacted in NYC

I once lived in a hotel for 334 days on a consulting contract. I never thought about trying to claim tenant rights because I’m an honorable person.

Same on long projects. Near LAX the easy workaround is alternating with El Segundo, the Rosecrans Ave hotels are 10 min away and much quieter than Century Blvd. Two moves in six weeks beats arguing with the front desk

@FNT Delta Diamond: I don’t think claiming tenancy is dishonorable on its own. Long-term hotel residency has a long history (e.g. there were long-time residents at The Plaza, including one person who ended up with a rent controlled suite for 35 years).

Mickey Barreto went a step further – he hit the jackpot (he got into a deadlock where he was able to live rent free because the hotel was intransigent in the face of a court order) and couldn’t stop pushing.

AirBnB hosts have been snagged by the “residential tenancy” issue. One had a “guest” who was scheduled for 21 days; then asked for an extension and stayed past 30 days. Then the “tenant” refused to leave! The owner went thru Hell with court costs, attorney fees, and lost rental revenue to get rid of the “tenant”.

I get asked a lot about credit cards and how to maximize points and miles. One of the simplest strategies I always recommend is to never settle for earning just 1 point or mile per dollar on your purchases.

That strategy is especially valuable when you're running a business and want to maximize expenses.

I have plenty of credit cards that earn bonus rewards in specific spending categories, but not every business expense fits neatly into one of them.

This is why the Capital One Venture X Business is a regular part of my card rotation. It earns at least 2 miles per dollar on every purchase, helping me turn everyday business expenses into valuable travel rewards.

And because Capital One miles are transferable to airline and hotel partners, I can put all those miles earned through business spending toward my next big trip.

Here's why the Venture X Business continues to earn its place in my wallet.

Learn more: Capital One Venture X Business

When you're running a business, you have enough decisions to make without having to think about which credit card to pull out for every expense. That's what I appreciate about the Venture X Business: Its straightforward earning structure makes it easy to rack up miles without keeping track of bonus categories.

Think about how much your business spends on things like equipment, professional services, insurance and other expenses that may not fall into traditional credit card bonus categories.

Depending on your business, those purchases alone could add up to thousands of dollars each month.

And those miles can add up surprisingly quickly.

For example, if your business spends $10,000 a month on purchases earning 2 miles per dollar, that's 240,000 Capital One miles in a year — before factoring in any welcome or anniversary bonuses.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, that's $4,440 in potential travel value from expenses your business was already going to incur.

Right now, the Venture X Business also has a huge welcome offer.

New cardholders can earn up to 300,000 bonus miles and a $1,000 travel credit. Here's how it breaks down:

Don't get me wrong, that's a hefty spending requirement. But if your business spends that kind of money, or you have big expenses coming up, consider for a moment the enormous value you can get from that bonus.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, the full offer is worth up to $6,550, including the $1,000 travel credit.

The $395 annual fee is also easier to justify thanks to a $300 annual Capital One Business Travel credit and 10,000 anniversary bonus miles (worth $185, per TPG's valuations). Throw in unlimited access to Capital One Lounges, and I have no trouble getting my money's worth.

Related: Brian Kelly’s wallet: Why the United Club Card still earns a spot

My favorite use of Capital One miles is transferring to one of the issuer's 15-plus airline and hotel partners. By moving miles to these loyalty programs, often at a 1:1 ratio, you can book flights and hotel stays using their rewards currencies, often getting more value than you would by redeeming miles directly through Capital One.

I have often been able to get at least 2 cents in value per mile when I leverage my miles with airline partners, particularly for international business-class flights.

Anyone who knows me knows how much I love flying Air France, particularly its La Première first-class experience. I recently traveled to Paris to see Céline Dion, and France is a destination I never get tired of visiting.

While only Flying Blue Platinum and Ultimate elite members can redeem miles directly for La Première award tickets, you don't need elite status to score a great redemption in Air France business class.

And one of my favorite ways to stretch my miles even further is by taking advantage of a transfer bonus.

For example, Capital One is currently offering a 20% transfer bonus to Air France-KLM Flying Blue through Nov. 30.

I found business-class awards to Europe for as little as 45,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, meaning you could book one of these flights by transferring just 38,000 Capital One miles with the bonus (subject to award availability and applicable taxes and fees).

That same flight would cost more than $2,000 in cash. Even after accounting for award taxes and fees, you'd get about 4 cents in value per Capital One mile, more than double TPG's valuation.

Of course, you don't have to transfer your miles to get value from the card. Capital One also lets you redeem miles to cover eligible travel purchases at 1 cent apiece, which is a straightforward option if you don't want to deal with award availability.

Related: Capital One vs. Chase: Which is better for business travel?

The Venture X Business isn't for everyone, but I think it's a great option for business owners who have significant expenses and want to earn valuable, transferable miles.

However, if most of your business spending falls into categories like advertising, shipping or office supplies, you may get more value from a card that earns higher rewards in those categories.

Related: The best business cards of the month

I have a wallet full of credit cards, but the Venture X Business is one I keep coming back to. Earning at least 2 miles per dollar on business expenses is a no-brainer for me, especially when I can transfer those miles to airline and hotel partners to get even more value.

Between the $300 annual travel credit, 10,000 anniversary miles and lounge access, I get more than enough value to justify the $395 annual fee.

And if your business meets the spending requirements, the current welcome offer is one I'd seriously consider.

For more details, check out our full review of the Capital One Venture X Business.

#6006. Senators still see NDAA as chance for online safety legislation

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

The Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”

“I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” said Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”

The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

Hawley said that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

“They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley said. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very company that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”

A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

“We require age checks for chat, place users under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson said. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a company’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”

Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She said Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

She also said that Hawley’s new arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

“Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles said. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”

The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

#6005. Korean Air Called Out For Discriminatory, Homophobic Mileage Policies, Doubles Down

I understand that same-sex rights differ greatly around the world, but Korean Air certainly has one of the more discriminatory policies as it impacts its frequent flyer program. Fortunately it looks like the airline might finally have to evolve a bit on this front, as reported by Korea JoongAng Daily.

Korean Air’s SkyPass frequent flyer program has limits on who members can redeem their miles for, and who they can pool miles with. As a general rule of thumb, miles can only be used for or pooled with direct family members, per the below chart.

South Korea doesn’t recognize same-sex marriage or civil unions, so how does that impact Korean Air’s policy for mileage pooling? Well, up until now, the carrier has recognized same-sex relationships only under the following circumstances:

Meanwhile members who are Korean and who were married abroad but who reside in Korea haven’t been recognized as family for the purposes of mileage redemptions and pooling.

So that brings us to the fact that the National Human Rights Commission of Korea (an agency within the government’s executive branch) has ruled that this policy is discriminatory, and doesn’t reflect the diversity of modern families. The commission recommended that Korean Air revise its mileage program to recognize de facto family relationships.

The decision was based on two legal provisions — this includes Article 11 (1) of the Constitution, which guarantees equality and prohibits discrimination, and Article 2 (3) of the National Human Rights Commission of Korea Act, with the latter identifying 19 grounds for discrimination, including sexual orientation.

This whole thing ended up coming to light after a same-sex Korean couple got married in Hawaii last year, and obtained a marriage certificate there. So the couple submitted their marriage certificate and notarized documents, attesting their marriage. However, the airline rejected this request:

“If you submit a marriage certificate issued overseas, you must also provide proof of citizenship or permanent residency in that country, as well as proof that you actually reside there.”

The National Human Rights Commission of Korea of course had a different take, writing the following:

“Korean Air allows foreign same-sex couples and Korean same-sex couples who married and reside overseas to register for its family mileage program. However, it does not extend the same benefit to Korean same-sex couples who married overseas but reside in Korea. This excludes same-sex couples who can demonstrate a genuine marital relationship solely because they live in Korea. It is difficult to find reasonable grounds for such discriminatory treatment.”

Even after this ruling, Korean Air has doubled down on its policy, claiming that it’s not discriminating based on sex:

“The key criterion for registering a spouse is whether the applicant falls under the legal jurisdiction of the country that issued the marriage certificate. The decision is not based on sex.”

This topic isn’t at all about how you feel about “traditional” marriage, or what your personal beliefs are. The point is that the concept behind family mileage pooling and redemptions is to prevent people from bartering miles, and instead, only being able to redeem miles for those who are close to them.

Does Korean Air really think that people are getting married abroad just so they can game the carrier’s system for mileage redemptions? Korean Air’s defense is basically “oh, we’re just following the law” and nothing more, but that’s a really lame excuse. They could also, you know, use their brains and apply common sense.

Logically, do Korean Air executives really think there should be a difference in policy between a Korean couple that got married abroad based on whether or not they reside in that foreign country?

Korean Air is a global airline serving diverse customers, and I think that has to come with a higher level of acceptance than just doing the absolute minimum the law requires. For that matter, Delta owns an equity stake in Korean Air. Will Delta stand up for same-sex couples, and compel Korean Air to pull their heads out of their you-know-what?

I can appreciate how maybe Korean Air hadn’t put a lot of thought into this policy in the past. But if the company is so stubborn and close-minded that it simply doubles down on its policy after being called out by the government agency, I find that to be incredibly disappointing. As the complainant accurately points out:

“I don’t think this is simply a question of whether we can pool our miles. Heterosexual newlyweds can see marriage as a way to improve their quality of life because they can receive benefits such as priority access to new housing and lower interest rates on loans. But we face numerous obstacles to building wealth together simply because we are of the same gender. Some people ask why we can’t just live as legally unmarried individuals. But we see each other as spouses, and having to deal with these inconveniences feels like very real discrimination to us.”

A Korean government watchdog has ruled that Korean Air is discriminating against same-sex couples with its mileage policy. The airline lets families pool miles, but same-sex couples can only pool miles if they reside abroad. Meanwhile Korean couples who were married abroad but reside in Korea can’t pool miles.

Korean Air insists it’s simply following the letter of the law, but that’s a really disappointing (and illogical) policy for a global airline to take. Here’s to hoping the airline evolves on this a bit, especially with the government agency in a not terribly progressive country (on this front) calling the airline out…
