#6004. Fake Amex Black Cards For $1,000—People Are Buying Status, But They May Be Committing A Crime

A man apparently made a fortune selling fake American Express Black Cards for about $1,000 apiece. The cards used buyers’ real account numbers, so when they paid for items the charges went onto their own bills. They were buying the appearance of being a Centurion cardmember. That’s the story told in this viral clip from Inside True Crime. His claim that customers could simply flash the cards to get into airport lounges is a lot harder to square with reality. View this post on Instagram

That’s the story told in this viral clip from Inside True Crime. His claim that customers could simply flash the cards to get into airport lounges is a lot harder to square with reality.

A post shared by Matthew Cox | Inside True Crime (@insidetruecrime)

Cox says the man put customers’ existing American Express numbers onto cards that looked like Centurion cards. They could pay for things, impress a date, and supposedly get waved into exclusive spaces. He says the business went on for years.

The comments split between people asking what the crime was, people asking where to order one, and frequent travelers pointing out that lounge access isn’t granted based on the look of the card – they run it through their system.

I’ve covered this sort of thing for years. Back in 2015, I wrote about a company that would turn an existing credit card into a custom metal card. Prices started at $99, with custom designs at $149 and gold plating at $249. That service couldn’t handle payment chips at the time. The payment system charges the account identified by the card’s credentials. Changing the material or artwork doesn’t change the rewards, spending power, or benefits attached to that account. And American Express itself has experimented with the physical form. In 2021, I covered artist-designed Centurion cards and a Prada wearable. Those were options Amex provided to real Centurion members. The Airport Lounge Claim Isn’t Plausible The reel makes a weird claim. It says the black card “doesn’t work,” then says it can pay for things. In the longer discussion, he means it doesn’t acquire the spending power he associates with a real Black Card. More importantly, Centurion Lounge access belongs to eligible cardmembers. A Gold account dressed up as Centurion is still a Gold account when its eligibility is checked. It hasn’t acquired lounge access, Centurion access priority, or any other benefit. Paying Your Own Bill Doesn’t Make It Legal The comments ask “what’s the crime?” Using someone else’s account to steal money is different from paying your own restaurant bill with a customized card. But there are several separate issues here. The maker copying Amex branding. Selling a replica with American Express branding raises trademark infringement issues. The concern is whether it falsely appears to be an Amex-issued or approved product. Depending on the marks and conduct, criminal trademark counterfeiting can also apply. The customer paying normally. An altered card isn’t automatically federal credit card fraud. The federal access-device statute includes altered and counterfeit cards, but requires intent to defraud. Merely wanting a date to think you’re rich isn’t enough. The customer claiming benefits they haven’t earned. Passing off the card as proof of Centurion membership to obtain restricted lounge services, a waived fee, or another benefit creates a different problem. It’s not obvious this would even work. And paying the bar tab doesn’t pay for the separate service obtained through deception. Using the fake credential to support false claims in a credit transaction would be a separate problem. Several state laws could be implicated. Texas has separate credit card, forgery, and counterfeit card rules. And Amex’s October 2023 U.S. merchant regulations instructed merchants not to accept a card that appeared physically altered. Getting a transaction approved doesn’t prove the replacement card was authorized, even if the merchant doesn’t know. Banks spend money on cards that look and feel good. Paying $1,000 to pretend you have a different one is an expensive way to impress someone who’s watching you pay. That’s more than the $895 first year’s annual fee on an actual Platinum Card, which comes with actual Centurion Lounge access. The card just wouldn’t be black. #6003. Olivia Ferney (Travelwithlivii), The Viral Billionaire Travel Agent: Does Her Story Add Up?

Olivia Ferney has gone viral on social media over the past 18 months or so, and is unarguably the world’s most famous travel advisor at this point. She has over 1.3 million followers on Instagram, and she has gone viral for sharing the endless, insane requests she receives from her alleged billionaire clients. She has gotten so much attention that she was named to the Time100 Creators list in 2026.

Odds are that if you’re into luxury travel, you’ve come across her social media, and she claims to be “one of the most awarded luxury travel agents in the world.” There’s only one problem — in the actual luxury travel world, very few people I’ve spoken to have interacted with her, with several hoteliers at the world’s top properties sharing that they’ve never knowingly received a booking from her or her team.

The logical question is whether her content is actually based on real interactions, as she claims, or if there’s something else going on here? Let me just say upfront that my intent here isn’t to hear down an honest, hardworking entrepreneur, as I’m all for people succeeding and finding a unique niche. However, I also think the public collectively often doesn’t do enough research about people who go viral based on certain claims, including things like pointing out the obvious areas where stories don’t add up.

26-year-old Olivia Ferney has the travelwithlivii Instagram account, where she has racked up over 1.3 million followers for her incredibly entertaining videos. She claims to be a luxury travel advisor who primarily works with billionaires, and posts endless videos of her reportedly talking to clients.

A post shared by Olivia Ferney (@travelwithlivii)

Or the client who was getting divorced, and put her new breast implants on her ex-husband’s credit card, but then was panicking when she found out that her breasts could explode because of the high altitude at which planes fly, so she needed a private jet.

A post shared by Olivia Ferney (@travelwithlivii)

Or a client’s daughter who asked that Ferney call her billionaire dad and demand she buy her a $900K yacht for her friend’s birthday.

A post shared by Olivia Ferney (@travelwithlivii)

Or when a client’s son gambled away a $324K watch, so she had to replace it before the dad found out, by simply walking into a jewelry store, interrupting someone, and then walking off with it less than a minute later, without any sign of payment.

A post shared by Olivia Ferney (@travelwithlivii)

This is just a tiny sampling of the dozens and dozens of absolutely insane requests she claims to receive. In a New York Times article, Ferney claimed that all of the videos are either real (with the client’s permission) or based on real interactions she has had with clients. Not only that, but she claimed that “the calls I post are less than 10 percent of what we get,” and a majority remain private, because she is “very highly NDA’d.”

In a recent podcast interview, Ferney explained her alleged business model:

So pardon my confusion here, but you’re collecting $5 million in fees, you’re just turning down $20 million (or more) in commissions for giggles, you’re making money on corporate bookings, you’re making money as an influencer with 1.3 million followers, and you’re “only” clearing a million bucks this year?

A post shared by Financial Tea Podcast (@financialteapodcast)

Here’s the other thing I find funny. She claims that she has such a high retainer fee because that way she works with billionaires rather than millionaires, and she insists that billionaires are easier to work with. She also claims that this allows her to be “very selective” with the people she works with, saying “my job would be miserable if I was being yelled at all day.”

Yet of her 50 clients, she has dozens of the most insane requests anyone has ever heard, and she claims that’s less than 10% of the requests she receives? Please make it make sense! I’ve easily counted 50 insane stories she has posted to social media, so that would mean that in just over a year, she has received 500+ of those requests. And those clients are easy?!?

A post shared by Olivia Ferney (@travelwithlivii)

I guess one logical question would be whether it even matters if what Ferney says is based on reality or not.

If you ask me, I think the reason that Ferney has gone so viral is because she insists that these interactions are real, so therefore it’s viewed as a way for the public to get a glimpse into the life of billionaires. The belief here is “wow, this is an industry leader, how cool to get an insight into their life.” If this were instead a case of someone just making up the most absurd stories they could come up with, it wouldn’t have nearly the appeal.

It’s worth noting that in interviews, Ferney has talked about how she has a background in digital marketing, and then she met her now fiancé, who is a travel advisor. I mean, she has certainly done an incredible job promoting that business (being a digital marketer!), and it does seem like the group booking portion of it is legitimate.

So why am I even covering this, and why does it matter? Well, I think shockingly we see a lack of mainstream media fact checking or requiring verification of claims. Ferney claims she’s one of the world’s most awarded travel agents. Could she share which awards she has won?

The major luxury hotel groups do rank advisors based on revenue and volume, and of the people I’ve spoken with, no one has ever seen her at any of the industry top producer events, or on any list of top producers. If you are doing $250 million per year in revenue, you would literally be the top producer for everything.

Let me also be very clear about something. My husband is a travel advisor, but he stays out of the drama, and hates when I get involved in this (sorry!). He has no part in any of this — quite to the contrary, I know quite a few travel advisors, and they’re the ones who have been getting me intel on all of this. Among other things, I’ve received verification from contacts at some of the world’s most prestigious properties that they’ve never seen a booking from her, let alone have her as one of their top bookers.

Obviously the barrier to being a luxury travel advisor is low, but the actual circle of very high volume agents is also very small, and they all know one another. The only context in which any of these people that I’ve spoken to seem to known Ferney is through her videos, which leave those people perplexed. Again, I’ll let everyone draw their own conclusions, but if you ask me, nothing here is making a whole lot of sense…

Olivia Ferney has done an absolutely incredible job building up a viral online presence as a travel advisor, by posting videos of her alleged billionaire clients making insane requests. She claims to limit herself and her team to working with 50 clients per year, charging them each a $100K retainer, with them each spending a minimum of $4-5 million per year, all while she reportedly just turns down commission for no reason?

She claims she chooses to work with billionaires because they’re easy to work with, but also posts dozens and dozens and dozens of videos of the insane requests she gets from those billionaires, while claiming that covers less than 10% of the actual insane requests she receives.

Of course her online presence is incredibly intriguing, and if true, I’d understand the attention. What’s fascinating is how widely known she is publicly, while seemingly being unknown in the industry, aside from many travel advisors and hoteliers rolling their eyes at her claims.

Everyone can draw their own conclusions here, but I do think once in a while a little objectivity is needed…

I call b.s. I can't imagine any wealthy individual putting up with what is essentially a contract employee airing out their laundry like this. Clickbaitosaurus

Her videos pop up on my feed all the time, definitely seems odd she doesn’t pull any commission…just completely ignored revenue. I’m guessing she just doesn’t put an IATA number in? I have noticed she really only plugs the same few hotels frequently, all I really associate her with is Faena NYC / Miami.

I remember seeing a couple of her reels a while back during doomscrolling sessions. They were entertaining for the absolute stupidity of the clients, but I didn't think they were very realistic. Of course I'll never play in those circles, so what do I know? Thankfully the algorithm moved on from those types of reels. If they truly are real stores, then all I can say is (as the old saying goes), money can't buy class.

#6002. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s new ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

But it quickly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

“I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”

Still, Cruz said the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization plan so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz said that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

For his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

“I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not big on government running things.”

Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

“This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he said. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”

He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy said, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

“I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy said. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”

Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he said that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create issues in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”

The decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

When considering which rewards credit card deserves your next application, its welcome offer should be a top factor.

Many bonuses are worth hundreds of dollars (or even more than $1,000) in the form of cash back or travel rewards. However, these offers sometimes carry steep spending requirements, requiring you to spend anywhere from $4,000 to $10,000 within the first few months of having the card.

It doesn't have to be that way. Here, we dive into high-value card bonuses that are easier to earn. Each of the offers we've listed here comes with a minimum spending requirement of $2,000 or less.

While this isn't an exhaustive list, these are 10 of the best cards you can add to your wallet with an easy-to-earn welcome bonus.

If flexibility is what you want, the  may appeal to you.

Welcome bonus: Earn a $200 online cash rewards bonus after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first 90 days of account opening.

Why we chose it: The Bank of America Customized Cash Rewards credit card lets you customize your rewards structure, allowing flexibility in your cash-back rewards strategy.

Being a member of the BofA Rewards™ program means you’ll earn even more cash back on every purchase.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Customized Cash Rewards.

The Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card is an all-around winner when it comes to earning cash-back rewards in popular bonus categories.

Welcome bonus: Earn a $200 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Why we chose it: It's easy to stack up cash-back rewards with the Capital One Savor. It earns bonus rewards across popular categories like dining, entertainment, grocery stores (excluding superstores like Walmart® and Target®) and select streaming services.

Plus, the card is a solid one to bring abroad, as it charges no foreign transaction fees.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Savor.

Learn more: Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card

The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card — Miles Boost is a solid option for travelers looking to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

Welcome offer: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, which peg Capital One miles at 1.85 cents apiece, this offer is worth $740.

Why we chose it: The Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card — Miles Boost offers an accessible way to earn transferable miles without paying an annual fee.

With just $1,000 in spending required to earn 40,000 bonus miles, this offer could be a solid match for those looking to get started with points and miles. Plus, cardholders have access to Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel transfer partners.

Keep in mind that this version of the VentureOne doesn't offer an introductory 0% APR period, unlike the standard Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card*, which has a smaller welcome bonus and lower spending requirement.

*0% introductory APR for 15 months on purchases and balance transfers, followed by a variable APR of 18.74%-28.74%.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card and our guide to the two VentureOne offers.

Learn more: Capital One VentureOne Rewards Credit Card - Miles Boost

One of the best no-annual-fee cards on the market is the  (see rates and fees).

Welcome bonus: Earn a $200 bonus after spending $500 on purchases within the first three months from account opening.

Why we chose it: The Chase Freedom Unlimited is a great card for nonbonus spending since it earns at least 1.5% cash back on all purchases.

If you also have a card that earns Chase Ultimate Rewards points, you can pair them with the Freedom Unlimited to convert your cash back into valuable, transferable Ultimate Rewards points. You can then transfer them to airline and hotel partners for potentially even more value.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

The (see rates and fees) makes it easy to earn solid cash-back rewards on every purchase.

Welcome bonus: Earn $200 cash back after spending $1,500 on purchases in the first six months of account opening.

Why we chose it: The best perk of the Citi Double Cash is its simple rewards structure. Cardholders earn 2% cash back on all purchases (1% when you make a purchase and another 1% when you pay it off).

Plus, the card is a fantastic choice if you want to fit it into a larger Citi-oriented strategy. That's because cash back is earned in the form of Citi ThankYou Rewards points, and you can unlock higher-value redemption options if you hold certain ThankYou Rewards cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Double Cash.

The (see rates and fees) provides a valuable bonus and great earning rates, especially when you consider it charges no annual fee.

Welcome bonus: Earn 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening.

Based on TPG's November 2026 valuations, this welcome offer is worth $390.

Why we chose it: The Citi Strata earns ThankYou Rewards points at a high rate across multiple categories. Plus, you can make your rewards flexible thanks to its bonus category on quarterly self-select categories.

As with the , you can receive more value from your rewards if you pair this card with certain ThankYou Rewards-earning cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Citi Strata.

The  comes with solid perks and earning rates for those who occasionally stay with Hilton.

Welcome bonus: Earn 70,000 bonus points and a free night reward after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership. Offer ends Jan. 13, 2027.

TPG's November 2026 valuations value this offer at $280, not including the value of the free night reward.

Why we chose it: The Hilton Honors Amex is an entry-level card in the Hilton Honors hotel program. You'll earn bonus Hilton points in multiple bonus categories and receive complimentary Hilton Silver elite status.

These are decent perks for a card with no annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Honors Amex.

Many cobranded hotel cards come with exorbitant annual fees, but the (see rates and fees) is an exception.

Welcome bonus: Earn 80,000 bonus points after spending $2,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. This offer is worth $480, per TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Why we chose it: If you want a no-annual-fee hotel credit card, there is a lot to like about the IHG One Rewards Credit Card.

One of its best perks is the fourth-award-night-free benefit when you redeem IHG One Rewards points. With this benefit, you'll pay no points for every fourth night on an award stay of four nights or longer. Starting in 2027, cardholders will need to spend $5,000 on purchases in a calendar year to unlock this benefit.

To learn more, read our full review of the IHG One Rewards Credit Card.

For those who fly United Airlines occasionally, the (see rates and fees) is worth considering.

Welcome bonus: Earn up to 50,000 bonus miles: Earn 40,000 bonus miles after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, earn 10,000 bonus miles after adding an authorized user in the first three months from account opening.

This offer is worth up to $600 (including the miles from adding an authorized user), according to TPG's November 2026 valuations.

Why we chose it: United's entry-level cobranded credit card offers a simple way to earn United MileagePlus miles across several bonus categories. Plus, the card provides a discount on United inflight purchases and United Club premium drink purchases.

It’s a solid option for beginners looking to earn United miles without paying an annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Gateway.

If you bank with Wells Fargo, the (see rates and fees) provides simple cash rewards earnings for you to enjoy.

Welcome bonus: Earn a $100 cash rewards bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Why we chose it: You can earn unlimited 2% cash rewards on purchases, making it a great choice for those seeking a straightforward earning structure.

The card also provides cellular telephone protection and zero liability protection, which are notable perks for a no-annual-fee card.

To learn more, read our full review of the Wells Fargo Active Cash.

Welcome bonuses are a great way to get your account balances off to a good start. Even the easiest bonuses to hit are typically worth at least a few hundred dollars. Still, note that each issuer has its own set of rules regarding when you’re able to earn a bonus.

Even though these cards have minimum spending requirements on the lower side, spend mindfully to ensure you unlock the full value of the welcome offer. A valuable introductory bonus can give your rewards strategy a supercharged boost.

#5999. Rove’s Travel Tuesday Deals Offer Up To 13x Miles—Plus 10,000 Bonus Miles On A $1,000 Hotel Booking

Rove‘s Travel Tuesday promotion will offer up to 13 miles per dollar through its shopping portal, including 11 miles per dollar at SpotHero, ResortPass and Samsonite, plus up to 10,000 bonus miles on a first hotel booking. The offers run December 1, 2026 only, ending at 11:59 p.m. Eastern. The hotel bonus is worth trying to take advantage of on an independent property, where you aren’t giving up hotel chain points and elite benefits. Rove is free to join, and you don’t need a particular credit card. New members can get 1,500 miles instantly using this link, with no purchase required. (My referral link, better than the standard referral offer.) Up To 13 Miles Per Dollar At 30 Travel Merchants The highest rate is 13 miles per dollar at Airport Parking Reservations. SpotHero rises from 3 to 11 miles per dollar, and ResortPass jumps from 2 to 11. Using 1.5 cents per Rove mile as a comparison – which I can usually get on loyalty-eligible hotel redemptions, even apart from points transfers – 11 miles per dollar is a 16.5% return and 13 miles per dollar is 19.5% adn that’s on top of credit card rewards for the spending. #5998. Senate Dems dismiss talk of earlier leadership election; Schumer confident

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., leaves the Senate Democrats’ lunch meeting in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Senate Democrats moved Tuesday to squelch talk of an accelerated timeline for the vote for a new majority leader, signaling they intend to keep the contest on Dec. 1.

That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

But supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

“I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”

“And fortunately, I think that will fail.”

Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

“No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., said Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”

“Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”

Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”

Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the new people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

“They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she said.

Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday said at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”

“We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he said. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

But there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

“I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”

Several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve said many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

That included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”

Kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

“Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”

“The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”

Sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but said, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

“I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for new leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

“They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

“We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”

“That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”

Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”

Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

“I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”

#5997. Chicago Used A Strip Of Land Less Than 33 Feet Wide To Claim O’Hare Airport—And Collect Its Taxes [Roundup]

News and notes from around the interweb: O’Hare is part of Chicago as part of a tax scheme. Back in the 1950s, Chicago wanted O’Hare inside its borders so the city could collect the massive tax revenue from the airport. Because suburbs like Norridge and Harwood Heights stood in the way, Chicago could not just annex the airport directly. In 1956, Mayor Richard J. Daley got around this rule by annexing a thin strip of land along Higgins Road. At its skinniest points, that original path was less than 33 feet wide.

While Chicago is still – today – a big card spend market, I wonder how much this will matter over the long term. United and American are fighting over it – and it probably still makes sense to fight over – but for how much longer? Chicago’s metro economy grew just 5% from 2018 to 2023 versus 12–14% for its big-city peers, leaving the city with a slow-growing tax base, an $882 million budget gap and debt and pension payments that consume about 40% of its operating budget. High business taxes, rising fees and unpredictable permitting discourage investment, while restrictive zoning and costly building rules push up rents and make it harder to attract residents. Indians spitting on food? That’s considered highly sanitized compared to most of their methods of food preparation.

Great analysis on Chicago, and I’m agreed with all of it in terms of the city itself. That said, O’Hare is around 32 % connecting traffic (neither originating nor terminating in Chicago), and even that understates it: The location of Chicago is such that many fly to it and drive a rental to one of the many adjacent cities (which is what I do every month). All in, I wouldn’t be surprised if only 50 % of ORD traffic is originating or terminating in Chicago, which makes the local credit card spend issue moot.

You’re definitely right that ORD pulls from a wide regional catchment area across southern Wisconsin, northern Illinois, and northwest Indiana, where plenty of travelers drive in or grab a rental car for better frequencies and fares. That said, your starting baseline actually understates ORD’s connecting traffic—airport-wide, O’Hare runs closer to 38%–40% connecting (and roughly 45%–52% connecting for AA specifically, given how much regional spoke feed it relies on). Even with that higher starting point, knocking true local O&D all the way down to 50% is a big stretch: that would imply roughly 1 in every 6 “local” ORD passengers—over 8 million people a year—is renting a car and leaving the metro area. With a metro population of nearly 10 million, a massive corporate base, and huge convention traffic, the overwhelming majority of ORD’s O&D volume is genuinely bound for Chicagoland, and the drive-in travelers from nearby markets still live in the region and carry co-branded cards anyway. More importantly, that doesn’t make local credit card spend moot—if anything, it’s the exact opposite. Co-branded card economics depend on total local market volume and household/corporate spend, not the connecting percentage. Even if you took your 50% figure at face value, 50% O&D on ~85 million annual passengers is still 42+ million local O&D passengers a year, making Chicago one of the top three or four O&D markets in the country. Connecting traffic doesn’t cancel out local card spend; it enables it by supporting the broad nonstop network that convinces local residents and businesses to put their everyday spend on an airline’s card—while also giving flyers in smaller Midwestern spoke cities a reason to carry that same card for one-stop access through ORD. Ironically, if that logic held up, DFW would fail the test far worse than O’Hare. Airport-wide, DFW runs roughly 60% connecting and 40% O&D—and for AA specifically, it’s closer to 62%–69% connecting (31%–38% O&D), largely because Southwest siphons off a big chunk of North Texas’s local domestic traffic. That puts DFW much closer to connection-heavy hubs like ATL (~62%–65% connecting) and CLT (~70%–75% connecting) than to balanced mega-O&D hubs like ORD and DEN (~36%–42% connecting). Nobody would argue DFW’s ~60%+ connecting share makes North Texas credit card spend moot, because DFW is AA’s single biggest loyalty profit engine. ORD actually has a much healthier O&D balance than DFW, ATL, or CLT; American’s real challenge in Chicago isn’t a lack of local O&D or card spend, it’s simply having to split that massive pie with United rather than enjoying an 80%+ fortress share.

The original article was how Daley ran things. The Chicago Way. The legacy continues. The dominant issue under subsequent regimes has not been whether Chicago is ready for reform but “where’s mine”?

#5996. Politics, money and Thanksgiving dinner: Just two words can help avoid argument

Dr. Joel Brown, a communication expert, shares how replacing one common phrase and asking a simple question can help defuse disagreements and keep holiday gatherings civil.

As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense.

Dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, says swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil.

"‘But’ shows disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation."

Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he said. Rather, it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions."

FOOD PRICES ARE RISING BEFORE THANKSGIVING. AN ECONOMIST SHARES WAYS TO SAVE

Dr. Joel Brown says the holiday dinner table can quickly become a source of tension when family members disagree, but choosing the right words can make all the difference in preventing heated exchanges. (iStock)

If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that."

The question, he says, can help you understand how someone arrived at their view instead of turning the exchange into a debate.

He also cautions against opening with "I disagree," which can put people "in an oppositional place" before they have fully heard one another. Rather than trading facts and figures to win an argument, he said, people may make more headway by sharing personal stories and listening to the experiences behind someone else’s opinion.

"If you’re going into these exchanges as looking to win an argument, maybe change your approach," Brown said. "Maybe instead of trying to win that argument, you try to understand the other person’s perspective."

BLACK FRIDAY DEALS ARE EVERYWHERE. HERE’S HOW TO SPOT REAL SAVINGS

Holiday gatherings can bring family and friends together, but differing opinions and heated conversations can sometimes lead to tension. (iStock)

Brown said it helps to decide in advance what you want from the interaction, whether that’s getting through the meal, building a relationship or persuading someone. That goal can shape how you respond.

Political topics aren't the only ones that can get tense when families come together.

For personal questions about marriage, children or other life choices, Brown recommends setting expectations before the gathering. Talk with family or friends about what would help everyone feel comfortable, and be clear about what you do and do not want to discuss.

Additionally, if a conversation becomes stressful, take a breath, sip water or step away from the table. Brown said people should know their own triggers and remember they are not responsible for managing every interaction.

Making small changes to the way people communicate may help keep holiday celebrations peaceful, enjoyable and focused on togetherness. (iStock)

He encourages approaching disagreements with empathy, which he described as listening to another person’s story without taking on their position.

Family members may not see eye to eye, he said, but the holiday can still be a chance to learn from one another.

"Look at these as learning opportunities," Brown said.

#5995. United Airlines Added 3 Flights Just For A Macy’s Parade Band — They Were Going To Take The Bus From New York To Texas

On Thanksgiving morning, a United Airlines customer service leader heard that a high school marching band was going to take the bus from New York all the way back to Texas. By Friday, his colleagues had lined up three planes and the crews to fly 450 people home to Houston. The Pride of Pearland Band and Color Guard had been planning this trip for more than a year. It was their first invitation to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. They’d already rehearsed on the street in Manhattan. Then, during the second act of a Broadway matinee of Wicked on Wednesday, band director Ryan Demkovich got the news. With heavy rain and high winds coming, the 100th parade would be the first one ever postponed. It would take place Saturday, but the school’s trip was supposed to end Friday. Try extending a reservation for a high school band at the Marriott Marquis in Times Square over Thanksgiving weekend – the hotel was booked. The band found rooms near the Meadowlands in New Jersey. And you’re not going to find nearly enough seats out of New York at the end of Thanksgiving weekend. They couldn’t get space until Monday and Tuesday, so the district announced they’d charter buses after the parade and get home Sunday. Former Pearland mayor Kevin Cole says it took just over three hours to raise $350,000 toward the extra hotel nights, meals and transportation. Gringo’s Mexican Kitchen pledged $100,000, CenterPoint Energy $50,000 and Houston furniture salesman Jim “Mattress Mack” McIngvale $40,000. Demkovich said people were handing the kids cash on the streets of New York. By Thanksgiving morning they knew they could stay and march, but it was going to be a grueling trip. Watch Pearland’s Thanksgiving morning performance on Fox Square. The bus ride was still ahead of them. United’s Joshua Freed says the idea to do something about that came from a customer service leader “who would be mad if I named him.” His team started making calls on Thanksgiving. The operations center, reservations and crew scheduling got involved. United confirmed two extra flights from Newark and one from LaGuardia. Joshua Freed on finding planes and crews for nearly 450 people. I’ve written about American Airlines sending a plane for a Montana high school band after a storm stranded them at Dallas Fort Worth. American did that for 67 kids and ten adults. Across town, Alaska Airlines added a Saturday evening flight from New York JFK to Seattle for more than 200 Hawaii band members and supporters connecting home. And for everyone asking why Macy’s didn’t chip in, the Hawaiʻi band said Friday night that the Macy’s Foundation gave $50,000 to each parade band on top of the $10,000 Macy’s offered each band when it issued the invitations. Back in Texas, Cole is inviting folks to welcome the kids back at Pearland High School. The three groups are expected at the school between 9:30 and 11 p.m. Saturday. #5994. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

Former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola said in a statement after the race was called.

The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

She entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The New York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

Peltola has said she had no connection to the scheme.

Prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

The Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

"56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot."

In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

The race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

She wants an apology and compensation. At the airport, she says, all American offered for the downgrade was a $300 travel credit.

The video starts mid-argument. At first a passenger says, “I do not accept.” The employee asks whether they’re going to cooperate and tells someone else, “Yeah, they are not moving.” The woman wants her refund. The employee asks whether they’re going to have to call the police. The woman says for a second time that she can move.

A pilot tells her she’ll get a refund through customer service. “How? What proof do I have?” she asks. He answers “I don’t know” then tells her, “Right now we need you to move or get off the airplane.”

This looks like American Airlines flight 3162 on Friday, November 27. A blue safety card in the seat pocket says “737.” The passenger wrote that this happened “today,” and the post was created at 7:46 p.m. New York time. The morning flights on the route used an Airbus and a regional jet. American’s other 737 to Chicago that day was scheduled for 8:30 p.m., and the video was already online before its boarding time. The flight, operated by aircraft N987NN, left gate 36 at 3:09 p.m. and arrived at Chicago O’Hare gate K12 33 minutes early at 4:23 p.m.

American Airlines, like other airlines, has a standard procedure for downgrading passengers in a case like this. American explained its process in October, in a remarkably similar complaint. On flight 1336 from Phoenix to Des Moines, everyone was seated when the captain reported the oxygen system at 2D and 2F was inoperative. American selected a mother and son sitting across the cabin in perfectly good seats, 1A and 1C. That family also alleged ethnic discrimination. The airline’s system generates a downgrade list based on elite status, fare class and time of check-in. The computer doesn’t use the passenger’s race or ethnicity. Here’s the order I’ve reported, starting with the people most likely to lose a seat. Employees and guests traveling space available (with exceptions for employees the airline has to transport). Passengers who upgraded, starting with complimentary upgrades, followed by systemwide upgrades, then mileage or cash upgrades. Passengers who redeemed miles for a first or business class award. Passengers who bought premium cabin tickets, with higher fare classes getting more protection. Status matters within those groups. The ordinary downgrade list explains what happened. But I think that the video still gives plenty of reason to criticize how the event unfolded, even though race wasn’t invovled. Oddly enough, the cat is the one part of her theory with a plausible connection to the formula. American lists traveling with a pet as a reason its app may not let you check in. If she had to check in at the airport while everyone else could check in the day before, that could have cost her priority. We don’t know whether that mattered here. A first class seat American had marked out of service on another flight. Can American Downgrade You After You’ve Boarded? What Do They Owe You? American can change seat assignments and its contract of carriage provides for downgrades. Here’s the protection in American’s conditions of carriage. “We will not involuntarily remove a revenue passenger who has already boarded to give a seat to another passenger.” Federal rules protect a confirmed, paying passenger against being put off the plane once they’ve checked in on time and the gate agent has accepted their boarding pass. There are exceptions for safety, security, health and disruptive or unlawful behavior. Moving somebody to coach on the same plane is allowed. Then: Take the flight in coach. American owes the difference between the first class fare and the fare for the cabin flown on that segment, automatically, back to the original form of payment. A $300 credit toward future travel is something American can offer on top. Decline the downgrade. She can ask for the next flight with first class available. If she chooses to give up the trip and declines rebooking or a voucher in lieu of money, she’s entitled to a refund of the unused ticket value. There’s no bump payment for flying in coach. The denied boarding rules don’t award the multiples of the fare people associate with getting bumped. American didn’t have to auction off a downgrade if everyone could still fly. How much money? American used to refund a flat 40% of the fare for the affected segment. That was an unfair calculation that could have left the airline making money by selling seats they didn’t have. In July it told the Transportation Department it would change the calculation. It would take the portion of her premium fare allocated to JFK–Chicago and subtract the average fare paid by customers who bought and flew coach on that flight and segment. That can still be quite different from the coach fare she passed up when buying first class. She had good reason to want proof before moving. When one passenger’s American Airlines seat broke, American maintained she’d flown in business class. She’d saved the paper boarding pass for 20C and ultimately got a $226 refund and a $300 travel credit. American Airlines JFK Customer Service One Instagram commenter summed up the way the conversation went in two words. “it’s JFK.” Another suggested, “Allow for questions, let people finish a sentence. Listen.” The employee could have offered, “I’m sorry.” They could have explained that they lost seats in first class, that without enough first class seats for passengers they had a process for downgrading customers, and what those factors are. They could have offered downgrade compensation to the cabin to see if another passenger would have moved voluntarily. In the Phoenix case, American actually did that. We’ve been here before, at JFK. Brazilian actress Ingrid Guimarães said American took her working premium economy seat on a flight to Rio because somebody else’s business class seat broke. She said staff blamed her for the delay and threatened to ban her. She, too, reported a $300 credit. Then there’s the Executive Platinum passenger upgraded to 6A from JFK to Los Angeles. Another customer’s seat wouldn’t recline. He says he was told to take coach or get off. He pushed back and kept his seat. How Long Should American Keep Flying With A Broken First Class Seat? I once wrote about a reader flying Nice to Philadelphia with a six-year-old and a broken tray table at 13K. The flight attendant asked whether they wanted to delay the whole plane to fix it? It’s one thing when an issue is discovered at the last minute. If the aircraft can fly safely with a seat blocked, holding the flight can strand people who would’ve made their connections. On the next segment, though, American knows what it’s got. It can block the seat before boarding, tell the customer while they still have choices, and schedule the repair where the plane, a technician and the part will be in the same place. Here’s the first class seat photographed on American flight 563 from Orlando to Philadelphia in April 2024. Other passengers reported seeing this same seat on this same plane like this for weeks. I’ve covered broken headrests, armrests and tray tables. Here’s more American Airlines broken first class seats I’ve written about. American’s chief customer officer Heather Garboden told employees in April, “we have too many broken seats.” In August, JonNYC reported that American planned to launch OneCabin the following month, adding more than 60 maintenance technicians and dedicated teams at Charlotte, Dallas–Fort Worth, Los Angeles, Miami, Philadelphia and Phoenix – putting numbers to an initiative I covered earlier in the year. @All: How many people reading this blog would have accepted the contract of duress imposed on the young woman in this instance?

This woman was more than reasonable. The american representative was rude and should be disciplined. I dont think she was a flight attendant based on the radio and ID badge. None the less they could have been nicer about it. Asked for volunteers and if there is a system, they should have compensated her well. NOT acceptable.

She has a cat–in first class (which means she made reservations to have a cat in cabin). And they told her to downgrade to coach? what was the reason? Some exec wanted her seat? A whiney Million Miler??

@Gary: I disagree with your statement that the FA should have said, “I’m sorry”. We are inundated today with meaningless, perfunctory pseudo-apologies where the corporate entity does nothing and doesn’t care.

AA should have figured it out before boarding. Alternatively, the other passenger, who obviously boarded after her, should have been the one downgraded.

AA obviously learned nothing from UA and Dr. Dao.

American is in the wrong here. Bad customer service too. If the seat was broken, then the passenger assigned to it simply had to be put on the next flight, with compensation, or some other customer care applied in the form of cash and miles. The woman who bought a first class seat for herself and her cat should never have been moved.

American’s pivot to premium seems to be working well.

It seems that involuntary downgrades have no “scruples” attached. If the passenger bought a first class ticket and was involuntarily downgraded, the passenger should be allowed a FULL REFUND of that ticket and then “charged” the price of the downgrade based on the price at the time the original fare was booked. I’m not totally convinced about the “pecking order” for downgrades but I guess that the airline has to “reward” the most loyal flyers first. I totally agree that when this type of event occurs, LISTEN and keep your mouth shut until the issue is explained. THEN ask for options and politely negotiate from the maximum down. The fact that a deadheading pilot can bump a paying passenger is ludicrous too but one can thank the unions for protecting the union members before protecting the person that “pays the salary”. For the passenger though, remember that failure to adhere to crew instructions won’t get you anywhere. Complying with the captain’s orders is mandatory…period…the end and the airline and the law will defer to the captain.

Hi Gary, I think this is a very sensitive issue, and it’s actually something I’ve encountered before. First of all, this isn’t just about the downgrade itself—it’s about American Airlines’ business conduct and integrity. When a customer buys a First Class ticket (whatever a ticket with AA), that is a binding contract. While a broken seat is understandable, failing to provide the cabin the passenger paid for means AA is breaking the contract. Because of that, the gate agent or supervisor in charge should have started with a sincere apology and politely discussed options with her. Since the airline breach the contract, they should be offering substantial compensation—such as triple the ticket price—rather than just a $300 credit. Instead, forcing a downgrade and threatening to call the police shows complete corporate arrogance.

Gary Leff writes that American Airlines may bump passengers already seated in first class to coach for people it deems more worthy. As he puts it, “the people most likely to lose a seat [are] employees and guests traveling space available (with exceptions for employees the airline has to transport).” So if you’ve paid and are seated in a first-class seat and an American Airlines C-suite executive suddenly decides to fly home for the holidays, does the airline consider that executive an employee it simply has to transport—or just someone whose title comes with unusually powerful holiday travel benefits like ruthless priority and preemption of any first-class seat?

Agree. A full refund, and free ride with an apology would be the way most companies would have handled this situation.

Even flying AA or from JFK for free is a proposition that almost always ends up feeling like one lost.

This is a textbook example of when an airline should buy their way out of their problem by offering suitable compensation to anyone willing to downgrade. Keep going up and eventually someone will accept.

At least United has somewhat learned from the Dr. Dao situation. Once a passenger is seated, United’s own policies state that they cannot be moved. This was the policy before Dr. Dao was brutalized, and it remains the policy today as far as I know. American should take a clue from it. Once you are seated, your bags stowed, etc., then that’s it. They shouldn’t be able to force you to move. They can ask, even dangle some incentives like miles or a lounge pass to entice you to move, but threatening the police and by implication arrest? That’s insane.

There’s a reason that I don’t fly American, and haven’t for over twenty years. Well, there are several reasons, but this is one of them. American decided long ago that its chief competitors weren’t United or Delta. No, they were competing with Spirit and Frontier, and they treat their passengers accordingly. United has made strides attempting to treat passengers better. They aren’t perfect – far from it – but better. American? Sorry, no, Just no.

“She wants to know whether American picked her because of her race, gender, age, or cat” If only there were a black person up there. They would have been pulled first. Asians are next.

There is a legal issue here about American selling broken seats

Turkish Airlines' Miles&Smiles program is known for being a hidden gem of a loyalty program that offers an award chart with some attractive redemption rates for economy and business-class travel.

Although rates increased significantly in 2024, useful options remain, including domestic partner awards within the U.S. Miles&Smiles is also a direct transfer partner of four U.S.-accessible rewards currencies.

Here's everything to know about Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles, including how to book a one-way business-class ticket between North America and Istanbul for just 65,000 miles.

The Miles&Smiles program has three elite membership tiers (aside from its basic membership, Classic):

Status generally lasts until the end of the month two years after it begins. Status miles only count toward qualification; regular miles can be redeemed for awards.

Renewal thresholds are lower. Classic Plus requires 17,000 status miles or 30 flights in the first year, or 35,000 miles or 60 flights over two years. Outside of Turkey, Elite requires 25,000 miles in year No. 1 or 37,500 miles over two years; Elite Plus requires 40,000 or 60,000 miles in the first or second year, respectively.

There are plenty of ways to boost your Miles&Smiles balance.

The Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles Premier Visa Signature® Credit Card has a $99 annual fee. New cardholders can earn up to 40,000 bonus miles: 25,000 after spending $2,000 on eligible purchases in the first 90 days of account opening and 15,000 additional bonus miles after spending another $6,000 (for $8,000 total) in the first 12 months. The second bonus posts after the first anniversary if the account remains open and in good standing.

It earns 3 miles per dollar spent on eligible Turkish Airlines purchases through Turkish-owned channels; 2 miles per dollar spent on eligible dining, grocery, entertainment and lodging purchases; and 1 mile per dollar spent on all other purchases. Eligible benefits include cardholder access to Turkish Airlines lounges worldwide, priority check-in and boarding on Turkish flights to and from the U.S. and 125 status miles per $500 spent each statement cycle, up to 5,000 miles per calendar year.

The information for the Turkish Airlines Miles&Smiles Premier card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

You can also transfer rewards directly to Miles&Smiles at a 1:1 rate from four programs with transferable currencies: Bilt, Capital One, Citi ThankYou Rewards and Rove.

Here are some of the best welcome bonuses available that you could transfer to Miles&Smiles:

Marriott Bonvoy points transfer at a 3:1 ratio, with 5,000 bonus Miles&Smiles miles earned for every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred. You can also convert 5,000 Choice Privileges points to 1,000 Miles&Smiles miles.

Hotel transfers generally offer less value and are best saved for topping up a specific award.

Related: Your complete guide to earning Marriott Bonvoy points

You can fly Turkish Airlines-operated flights to earn reward miles based on your fare class, Miles&Smiles elite status level and flight distance.

As a Star Alliance member, Turkish lets you earn Miles&Smiles miles on partner flights, including Lufthansa, United Airlines, Air Canada and Swiss.

Members can also earn miles and status miles on eligible AJet flights, though AJet awards are unavailable. Outside of Star Alliance, eligible Azul Brazilian Airlines and Olympic Air flights earn both, while Gol Airlines and Oman Air only earn redeemable miles. Awards are available on Azul, Gol and Olympic Air.

There are different earning charts for each partner airline. So, check whether your fare class earns miles and see how many miles you’ll earn before entering your Turkish frequent flyer number on a partner reservation.

The Miles&Smiles program has a comprehensive list of other earning partners available here. It includes (but is not limited to):

Miles expire at the end of the third full calendar year after they are processed; activity does not reset the clock. Before expiration, you can pay $20 per 1,000 miles to extend them by three years. Expired miles cannot be restored.

Related: How to keep your points and miles from expiring

Miles&Smiles uses fixed one-way charts. Turkish-operated flights have capacity-controlled Promotion Award Tickets and more expensive Award Tickets with broader availability. Partners use a separate region-based chart with special rates for direct same-country flights and mainland U.S.-Hawaii awards.

Below are some current one-way examples, excluding taxes, fees and surcharges:

Connecting Turkish itineraries are charged per segment. For example, a New York-to-Istanbul-to-London itinerary in promotional business class costs 65,000 miles plus 25,000 miles for the Europe 2 segment for a total of 90,000 miles one-way when both segments have promotional space available.

Check the current Turkish Airlines award charts before transferring because prices can change without notice.

If you want to book an award ticket only operated by Turkish Airlines, you can get to the award booking engine from the Turkish homepage by clicking the “Award Ticket” checkbox.

This will require logging in to your Miles&Smiles account and then going to the award ticket booking engine. There, you can enter your origin, destination, dates, class of service and number of passengers.

After selecting a flight, you’ll see the flight details, the aircraft type and the award space labeled as promotional or regular pricing, which will match the published award charts.

The following page will give you the total flight cost, including taxes and fees, even if you don’t have the required miles in your account. Expect to pay around $300 in taxes, fees and surcharges for a one-way business-class ticket to Istanbul.

Partner awards are harder to book. Follow these steps:

You can also use miles for upgrades on eligible Turkish Airlines tickets, Cash&Miles bookings, seat assignments, extra baggage, selected lounge access, taxes through Tax&Smiles and purchases through Shop&Miles.

Cash&Miles is a paid-ticket option rather than an award ticket, which are much easier to find. It lets you cover up to 50% of the fare, excluding taxes, with miles on eligible Turkish-operated tickets booked through the Turkish website or app, and you will still earn miles according to the paid fare rules. It is not available on codeshare or partner flights.

The best way to redeem Turkish miles is for award flights. While other options may be available in the program, booking Turkish Airlines- or Star Alliance-operated flights will usually give you the most value.

Note that while you can book Turkish Airlines-operated flights and most partner-operated flights online, it is difficult to find the cheapest promotional award tickets operated by Turkish Airlines without clicking through day to day. You may wish to use an external tool like Seats.aero to easily find the cheapest rates across 12 months.

Miles&Smiles is worth considering if you can tolerate its frustrating website. No program is best at everything, but Turkish still has useful fixed-price awards.

Logging in to your account on the website can be challenging, especially if you have a non-Turkish phone number registered. However, if you can get past that quirk, you can take advantage of solid redemption opportunities like 65,000-mile Turkish business-class awards between North America and Istanbul and 15,000-mile domestic partner economy awards.

A U.S. branded credit card and partners like Rove now also make it even easier to earn miles, but no-notice devaluations reinforce the rule to transfer only when you're ready to book.

Farley throws out several prices in the video. In her written caption, she puts coach at more than $1,200 per person roundtrip and the $3,300 option was for “basic business class.” In fact, it was domestic, so the actual nomenclature was first class, rather than business. That comes to $1,650 apiece up front, or $1,760 each if they want to know who they’re sitting next to.

I guess paying over $1000 per ticket isn’t good enough now. @united wants you to pay an additional $55 per person to choose your seat. Mind you, people that are 1K still have to pay an additional $55 to $200 round trip just to pick your freaking seat that you’re already spending over $3000 on for one couple… I can’t even comprehend this level of greed omg

Farley remembers $1,500 for two to Miami during Covid, when domestic fares hit a record inflation-adjusted low. She posted on Black Friday, and Thanksgiving flights are mostly full.

United introduced basic first class this fall. Buy United First Base and you get whatever seat United assigns you at check-in unless you pay separately for a seat assignment. (You also get one fewer checked bag, and changes come with a fee.) According to United’s chief commercial officer Andrew Nocella, most passengers buy up.

After $3,300 it’s reasonable to expect you’re done paying and won’t be nickel and dimed. As for what the seat itself is worth, she presses an imaginary recline button. “Boop. That’s it. That’s all you get. You get a little boop.” Domestic first class is a little more space, it is not luxury. Just this week a United passenger who said he’d paid $4,500 for first class wondered whether the airline had gone to an airplane graveyard to furnish its 737.

Farley says she’s giving up on United 1K after 15 years. She has a point about how much harder United is making it to stay loyal. Someone who qualifies today with 60 flights and 22,000 qualifying points will need 32,000 points starting in 2027. That’s a 45% increase for the customer who’s actually on the plane 60 times a year.

Farley says she was speaking up for ordinary Americans. Some commenters said they could barely afford to fly coach to see family. Quite a few roast her for complaining about first class.

One commenter recommended Spirit for $54. I liked Spirit’s Big Front Seat enough to fly my family to New York in it. But Spirit shut down in May. That commenter eventually admitted she was trolling.

Farley’s solution is to start a nonprofit and she has a name for it, Woww Airlines, though there actually was a WOW Air. It flew from Newark until it went out of business in 2019.

Its seat selection policy is still online. They charged extra to sit together, too.
