#5987. Universities, schools nationwide use Thanksgiving as chance to promote 'Day of Mourning' and decolonization

Loudoun County parent Rachel Pisani joins 'Fox & Friends' to express outrage over school lesson plans teaching children that Thanksgiving is a 'Day of Mourning.' Pisani argues the 'woke' curriculum teaches children to hate their country.

Thanksgiving is a day of celebration and spending time with family for the vast majority of Americans, but for several students on college campuses across the country, the national holiday is a source of anguish that is being expressed in the form of protests and counter-programming events.

On Nov. 18, George Washington University hosted an event called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration" that was described as a chance for students to examine Thanksgiving, Christmas and Independence Day through an intersectional lens, including experiences of "belonging, exclusion, cultural erasure, and historical harm."

"Through facilitated dialogue and shared reflection, students will engage in meaningful conversations about historical memory, social responsibility, and the complexities of celebrating within a diverse society," the student life event description read.

At the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee, the American Indian Student Center & Electa Quinney Institute for American Indian Education hosted a Nov. 17 event called "AlterNative Giving," which was described as "a community gathering that offers a meaningful alternative to the traditional Thanksgiving narrative. Instead of focusing on colonial histories, we come together to honor Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and giving."

TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN ‘MISSES CORE IDEOLOGY' AND MUST TARGET LINGERING DANGER ON CAMPUSES, WATCHDOG WARNS

A modern recreation of the first Thanksgiving in the autumn of 1621 at Plimoth Patuxet Museums (formerly Plimoth Plantation) in Plymouth, Mass. (Courtesy of Kathy Tarantola/Plimoth Patuxet Museums)

Salem State University promoted an event that labeled Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" and told students the land they are being educated on was stolen from Indigenous people.

"The land occupied by Salem State University is part of the traditional and ancestral homeland of the Massachusett tribe," the school’s website posted. "We acknowledge the genocide and forced removal of the Massachusett tribe and their kin from their summer home in Nâmkek."

CALIFORNIA COLLEGE LECTURER REMOVED AFTER ERUPTING AT STUDENT OVER QUESTION ON NATIVE AMERICANS

A review of university calendars found several examples lamenting the downsides of Thanksgiving, including Occidental College, which said the holiday is a "reminder of settler colonialism and its devastating impact on Indigenous individuals, communities and tribes."

The Pratt Institute lists "National Day of Mourning" as an occasion for Indigenous remembrance and reflection, and the University at Albany lists the holiday as "National Day of Mourning/Thanksgiving."

George Washington University hosted an event on Nov. 18 called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration." (iStock)

The colonial messaging around Thanksgiving isn't limited to universities but is also occurring at elementary and high schools, including in Loudoun County, Virginia, where a parent recently pushed back in an interview with Fox News about school lesson plans teaching children that Thanksgiving is a "Day of Mourning."

On its website, the San Diego County Office of Education explained that "November is Native American Heritage Month, a time to honor the diversity, history, and living cultures of Native peoples. It is also the month when Thanksgiving is observed in the United States, a holiday that carries very different meanings for different people, including many Native communities."

Oregon’s Bethel School District links to a "Decolonizing Thanksgiving: A Toolkit for Combatting Racism in Schools" on its official Equity, Access & Inclusion webpage. Listed under teaching resources, the toolkit appears alongside material about honoring Native peoples on Thanksgiving.

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

Earn up to $4,300 in travel value when you spend $120,000 in your first 4 months as a cardholder

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 100,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

Call it a la carte pricing or just nickel-and-diming. Either way, it's not in your head.

U.S. airlines collected about $7.4 billion in baggage fees in 2025, and that's before you pay to pick a seat or buy a snack onboard. As a benefit to cardholders, a handful of credit cards will cover some of those fees for you. However, each credit works differently, and restrictions can make some much easier to use than others.

Here's a closer look at the best credit cards with airline fee credits and how to use them.

*The information for these cards has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

The annual fee definitely raises some eyebrows, but if you use the card's benefits, you can easily justify its cost.

How the airline fee statement credit works: Every calendar year, Amex Platinum cardmembers can receive up to $200 in statement credits toward airline incidental fees charged by one qualifying airline selected in advance from the following list:

The easiest way to think about this benefit is as a cushion for the extras that come with a trip, not the ticket itself. Common qualifying expenses include checked or overweight baggage fees, change fees, seat-selection charges, airline lounge passes and inflight food or beverages.

Airfare, seat upgrades, award tickets, gift cards and mileage purchases or transfer fees do not qualify. Also, bundling a fee into a single transaction with your airfare purchase may not trigger the statement credit.

Other key perks: The Amex Platinum card offers access to the American Express Global Lounge Collection for eligible cardmembers, including Centurion Lounges and participating Priority Pass™ lounges. It also earns 5 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with airlines or through American Express Travel®, on up to $500,000 in these purchases per calendar year, which pairs nicely with airline fee statement credits.

Enrollment is required in advance for some benefits.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum card.

The is best suited to business owners who travel frequently enough to use its airline, lounge and Pay with Points benefits.

How the airline fee statement credit works: The Amex Business Platinum's airline incidental statement credit works like the Amex Platinum statement credit mentioned above. Each calendar year, you'll get up to $200 in statement credits for eligible spending with your selected, qualifying airline. Enrollment is required.

Other key perks: The Business Platinum card includes other perks for frequent flyers, including a Clear+ membership statement credit of up to $219 every calendar year after enrollment (subject to auto-renewal). The card also offers exceptional airport lounge access and hotel elite status benefits.

Plus, when you use Pay with Points for an eligible flight booked through American Express Travel® with the same selected qualifying airline, you can get 35% of those points back, up to 1 million points back per calendar year. For some benefits, enrollment is required in advance.

To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Business Platinum Card.

The is most compelling for travelers who regularly fly American Airlines.

How the airline fee credit works:  Each calendar year, cardholders can receive up to $200 in statement credits across up to two selected Splurge Credit merchants. American Airlines is one of the eligible choices. The credit applies to airfare as well as fees and incidentals for greater flexibility. Just keep in mind you'll need to select American Airlines as one of your Splurge credit merchants before making a purchase (exclusions apply).

Other key perks: Frequent American flyers can also use four Admirals Club passes each calendar year, while a Priority Pass Select membership adds broader lounge access. The card also offers up to $300 off one prepaid hotel stay of at least two nights booked through Citi Travel each calendar year.

To learn more, read our full review of the Strata Elite.

The is best for Hilton loyalists who can use both its hotel benefits and a flight statement credit spread throughout the year.

How the airline statement credit works: The Hilton Honors Aspire provides up to $200 in statement credits every calendar year (up to $50 each quarter). The statement credits apply to flight purchases made directly with an airline, through AmexTravel.com or in the Amex Travel App™. Because the statement credit comes in $50 quarterly installments, though, you'll need an airline purchase each quarter to get the full $200.

Other key perks: The hotel benefits do most of the work in justifying this card's annual fee. Cardmembers receive Hilton Diamond status, a free night reward each account anniversary and up to $400 in Hilton Resort statement credits each calendar year, provided as up to $200 semiannually.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Honors Aspire.

If transfer partners aren't a necessity for you and you're in the market for a premium travel card, consider the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite.

How the airline fee credit works: The Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite card offers up to $300 in airline incidental statement credits each calendar year. While you don't need to choose just one airline, the benefit works only with U.S. airlines and only on flights originating in the U.S.

Unfortunately, you can't use this credit with Allegiant Air or Sun Country Airlines.

Other key perks: On top of the airline fee credits, you'll receive up to $150 annually in lifestyle credits for streaming services, food delivery, fitness subscriptions and ride-hailing services, plus up to $120 in statement credits toward Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fees every four years.

And, no other card offers the same Priority Pass flexibility: Cardholders can enroll up to four people in their own memberships with guest access, even if they aren't authorized users or traveling with you.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite.

If high annual fees aren't for you, the is right up your alley. In fact, its airline credit is worth more than its annual fee.

How the airline fee credit works: Receive up to $100 annually in airline incidental statement credits, subject to the same coverage and airline restrictions as the Premium Rewards Elite card above.

Other key perks: The Bank of America Premium Rewards card also provides up to $100 in statement credits every four years for your Global Entry or TSA PreCheck application fee, plus travel insurance protections. That gives travelers a practical set of benefits without forcing you to commit to more expensive cards.

To learn more, read our full review of the Bank of America Premium Rewards card.

The has the smallest airline credit here, but also one of the lowest annual fees.

How the airline credit works: You'll receive a one-time $50 statement credit after making your first airline purchase of at least $50 during each annual credit period. Any airline-coded charge counts as long as it's $50 or more, including airfare or fees. That means purchases from international carriers can count, too.

Other key perks: This card is also popular because it earns 5 points per dollar spent at hotels and 4 points per dollar spent with airlines without requiring you to make your purchase through a card booking portal.

To learn more, read our full review of the Wells Fargo Autograph Journey.

The Ritz-Carlton card is a special case: it isn't open to new applicants, but eligible Chase Marriott cardholders may be able to product change into it.

How the airline fee credit works: You can receive up to $300 in airline fee credits per calendar year. Unlike other cards, where the credits are applied to your account automatically, you'll need to manually request the credit within four billing cycles of an eligible purchase.

Eligible fees include checked bags, inflight purchases (including Wi-Fi), airline lounge passes or memberships and seat upgrades.

Other key perks: You'll enjoy a Priority Pass Select membership along with unlimited complimentary access to Chase Sapphire Lounges, each with up to two guests per visit. Authorized user cards can be added at no additional fee and also receive their own Priority Pass membership.

This card also provides a free night award worth up to 85,000 points, given on each account anniversary (certain hotels have resort fees).

To learn more, read about how you can still get the Ritz-Carlton card.

These credits reset on a schedule, so one slip can mean losing the full value. Here's what to watch out for, with a couple of examples for each:

If the restrictions above put you off, several of the top travel rewards credit cards offer broader travel credits that may be easier to use.

Both the (see rates and fees) and (see rates and fees) come with $300 in travel credits every year. These credits apply automatically to airfare, hotels, public transit and other qualifying expenses paid for with the card.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve and the Sapphire Reserve for Business.

With the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card, you'll receive a $300 annual travel credit. The caveat is that the credit only applies to bookings made with Capital One Travel, but you can use it toward flights, hotels, vacation rentals and rental cars. The card's annual fee is $395.

The Capital One Venture X Business also offers an annual $300 travel credit valid on flights and other travel bookings, though with this card you'll need to book through Capital One Business Travel.

The Capital One Venture Business has a lower $95 annual fee and offers a smaller $50 annual credit for bookings made through Capital One Business Travel.

To learn more, read our full review of the Venture X card, Venture X Business and Venture Business.

Holding a credit card with an airline fee credit is a great way to avoid paying for things like checked bags, flight changes and inflight purchases. But how much value you get depends on how easy the credit is to use.

If you want an airline credit that's easy to use, start with the cards that cover airfare: the Citi Strata Elite (if you fly American), Hilton Aspire and Autograph Journey.

If you're willing to do more homework, you might get more value through American Express, Bank of America or the Ritz-Carlton cards. They only cover incidental fees, though in today's market most travelers pay for these often enough to maximize that type of credit.

For anyone who thinks tracking rules is a chore, a broader travel credit like that of the Chase Sapphire Reserve is a better bet.

#5985. Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

The draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

The new office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

Britt, R-Ala., said the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

“This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she said in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”

The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide said.

The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

Britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

Senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring

It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

“If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

#5984. Ink Business Preferred Review—100,000 Points And Great For Justing Starting A Business Rewards

I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

The Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (See rates and fees) can be one of the most useful cards for a business that buys online advertising, ships products or spends heavily on travel. It earns 3 transferable points per dollar in those categories, has a $95 annual fee, and currently has an offer to earn a 100,000 point initial bonus. It’s also a way to make points earned on no annual fee Chase business cards more useful.

The current initial offer is 100,000 points after $8,000 in purchases within three months. The $95 annual fee isn’t waived the first year. Those bonus points are worth $1,000 as cash back. Transferring them to the right airline or hotel program can produce more valuable travel, but the cash option gives you a straightforward starting value without a particular award redemption. The purchases made to earn the bonus generate their own points. If all $8,000 earns the ordinary 1 point rate, you’d have at least 108,000 points after earning the bonus. Chase says the initial bonus may be unavailable if you’ve ever had this card. Don’t assume a former cardholder qualifies again merely because 24 months have passed. The bank also considers factors relating to the business. And while 5/24 can generally apply to getting approved for this card, it doesn’t add to your 5/24 total once you are. This is a business card, including for eligible sole proprietors and side businesses. Chase flags opportunities for those with side hustles and freelanding and gigs like ride share, tutoring, babysitting and selling vintage clothing online. Getting a small business card can be one of the most helpful things someone can do when they are first starting a business, because Chase flags the help this is in keeping business and personal expenses separate. The Spending Categories Are The Main Reason To Keep It Ink Preferred earns 3 points per dollar on the first $150,000 in combined purchases each account anniversary year in these categories: Travel. Shipping. Internet, cable and phone services. Advertising purchased from social media sites and search engines. That $150,000 is one shared limit, not $150,000 for each category or each employee card. It also follows the account anniversary year, not January through December. A business putting $50,000 into eligible search advertising would earn 150,000 points from that spending. Using the entire $150,000 combined category allowance produces 450,000 points. That’s substantial earn for a $95 annual fee card. Other purchases, and purchases above the combined cap, earn 1 point per dollar. Qualifying Lyft purchases earn 5 points per dollar through September 30, 2027. Transferring Points To Airline And Hotel Points In addition to spending points through Chase’s portal directly for travel, you have the option to move points to a variety of airline and hotel loyalty programs. Star Alliance: United MileagePlus, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Air Canada Aeroplan oneworld: British Airways Club, Iberia Plus, Cathay Pacific Asia Miles, Qantas Frequent Flyer SkyTeam: Air France KLM Flying Blue, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Non-alliance: Southwest Airlines Rapid Rewards, Aer Lingus AerClub Hotel: World of Hyatt, Marriott Bonvoy, IHG One Rewards Since October 1, 2026, Ink Preferred points transfer to Hyatt at 4:3 rather than 1:1. Chase Sapphire Reserve® (See rates and fees) retains 1:1 Hyatt transfers. If you have a Reserve account, you can combine your Chase points there before transferring to get that better rate. Pairing It With Other Chase Cards The no annual fee Ink Business Cash and Ink Business Unlimited can complement Preferred. Cash earns 5 points per dollar on the first $25,000 in combined eligible office supply store and internet, cable and phone service purchases each account anniversary year. Unlimited earns 1.5 points per dollar on ordinary purchases. Eligible rewards from those accounts can be combined into Ink Preferred and transferred to travel partners. You don’t have to put all your spending on Preferred to make its annual fee worthwhile. A phone bill may earn more on Ink Cash. Online advertising may belong on Preferred. Purchases with no bonus category may belong on Unlimited or another card earning a stronger everyday return. The Protections Are Useful For A Small Business The cellphone benefit covers eligible theft or damage up to $1,000 per claim when you pay the monthly bill with the card. It has a $100 deductible and a maximum of three claims per 12 months. For a business paying multiple eligible phone lines, that’s a reason to consider the card even when another card offers a slightly higher earning rate on the bill. Rental car collision coverage is primary when renting for business purposes, with up to $60,000 in coverage for eligible vehicles. Trip cancellation and interruption protection can reimburse covered prepaid expenses up to $5,000 per traveler and $10,000 per trip. The card also offers purchase protection and extended warranty coverage. Employee cards have no additional annual fee, and you can set individual spending limits. There are no foreign transaction fees. There’s also complimentary DashPass for at least 12 months when activated by December 31, 2027, plus a $10 monthly promotion on a qualifying nonrestaurant DoorDash order while eligible. T How I’d Value The Ink Business Preferred $95 Annual Fee At the cash back redemption rate, 3 points per dollar is a 3% return. Transfers to miles can be worth far more. There’s no question in my mind that the initial bonus is worthwhile, and a great enticement to get the card. Keeping it depends on whether you either use it as your hub for other no annual fee cards (and so their points can become transferable by moving them into the Ink Preferred account) or you spend in the card’s bonus categories. #5983. Democrats, Republicans find rare common ground when asked what they're thankful for

House lawmakers on both sides of the aisle spoke to Fox News Digital about what they are most thankful for as they get ready to celebrate Thanksgiving with their families.

An ocean of ideological differences separates Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill, but they're largely in agreement over one thing this Thanksgiving, and it's usually miles away from Washington, D.C.

"I'm thankful for family," Rep. Eric Burlison, R-Mo., told Fox News Digital. "It's what drives me to keep going, to keep doing this, keep fighting for the country."

Families across America are gathering for Thanksgiving, kicking off a holiday season that's meant for reflection and refocusing on things that matter most. And members of Congress who spoke with Fox News Digital about that special day are no different.

The U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 10, 2026. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"You know, elections can be a bumpy road in many ways, and it's easy to take a shot at somebody who's running — we put ourselves out there. But it's the family, really, and I'm grateful that my wife and my three kids who are in their 20s are so supportive," Rep. John Mannion, D-N.Y., said. "So that's what I'm thankful for."

Reps. Randy Fine, R-Fla., and Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., singled out their children.

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

"I'm very grateful to how great my boys are doing despite the challenges of this job, and just my whole family for putting up with all of this and being there for me," Fine said.

#5981. Delta Flight Attendant Hoped Nobody Would Ask For Coffee — Then Passengers Were Too Afraid To Ask

A Delta Air Lines passenger boarding a Thanksgiving morning flight from Atlanta to Nashville says one flight attendant asked another if she was going to make coffee. The answer was “hell no and I hope the passengers don’t ask for coffee.” Then she noticed a passenger heard her. Later, the same flight attendant came through asking if anyone wanted something besides water. The passenger said water was fine. The flight attendant smiled and asked, “is that because of what I said earlier?” The answer was “yep.” The passenger says the people around them laughed, and so did she. Accidentally overheard flight attendantby u/ITGuySince1999 in r/delta One reader guessed the crew base from the story alone. “Your ATL-based flight crew thanks you for your loyalty.” They got it right. Another reader described putting the coffee packet in the tray, closing the handle and pressing brew. “So easy a pilot can do it.” The passenger put departure at 9:30 a.m. That fits Delta 1155, a Boeing 717 scheduled for 9:34 a.m. Atlanta to Nashville is 214 miles. Delta doesn’t schedule a drink service in coach on flights under 350 miles, but first class still gets full service. It’s also possible the two flight attendants were talking about coffee for boarding. One commenter who works flights says they have to pour out what’s left before takeoff. Another flight attendant figured that was a perfectly good use for a ten-cent bag of coffee. Since September, Delta has told crews to collect even the paper cups before pushback. I’ve heard the boarding pay argument before. An American Airlines passenger in 1B once overheard a flight attendant say she’d stopped doing predeparture drinks because of the contract which didn’t (yet) calculate pay based on boarding time. On Alaska Airlines, a first class passenger actually asked for coffee and got told “we don’t work for free.” Delta became the first major airline to introduce boarding pay in June 2022. They pay half the hourly flight rate for scheduled boarding time. She shouldn’t be griping in the galley within earshot of passengers, but I do give her credit for asking about the passenger’s reason for choosing water. As for whether the passenger even wanted coffee, they said a cup “would have been welcome and much appreciated” and they’ll take their caffeine any way they can get it. When another reader asked if they’d actually planned to order one, their entire reply was “I hate coffee.” Topics on this pageDelta Air LinesFlight attendantAlaska AirlinesAmerican AirlinesAtlantaBoeing 717Nashville+5 more More From View from the Wing

Later, the same flight attendant came through asking if anyone wanted something besides water. The passenger said water was fine. The flight attendant smiled and asked, “is that because of what I said earlier?”

The answer was “yep.” The passenger says the people around them laughed, and so did she.

Accidentally overheard flight attendantby u/ITGuySince1999 in r/delta

One reader guessed the crew base from the story alone. “Your ATL-based flight crew thanks you for your loyalty.” They got it right. Another reader described putting the coffee packet in the tray, closing the handle and pressing brew. “So easy a pilot can do it.”

The passenger put departure at 9:30 a.m. That fits Delta 1155, a Boeing 717 scheduled for 9:34 a.m. Atlanta to Nashville is 214 miles. Delta doesn’t schedule a drink service in coach on flights under 350 miles, but first class still gets full service.

It’s also possible the two flight attendants were talking about coffee for boarding. One commenter who works flights says they have to pour out what’s left before takeoff. Another flight attendant figured that was a perfectly good use for a ten-cent bag of coffee. Since September, Delta has told crews to collect even the paper cups before pushback.

#5980. FLASHBACK: Two presidents pulled off secret Thanksgiving surprises for US troops — see the moments

Melania Trump delivers a powerful message of gratitude to military families during a visit to Fort Rucker ahead of Thanksgiving. She honors the profound sacrifices made by military spouses and children while their loved ones are deployed across the globe. She expresses deep appreciation for their strength and resilience in keeping their homes full of love.

Under a cloak of secrecy, two American presidents made surprise Thanksgiving visits to war zones, bringing a taste of home to U.S. troops serving thousands of miles from their families.

Sixteen years apart, President George W. Bush celebrated with American troops in Iraq in 2003, while President Donald Trump served Thanksgiving dinner to service members in Afghanistan in 2019. Both visits were carried out under tight secrecy, catching troops by surprise as they spent the holiday far from home.

Trump secretly traveled to Bagram Airfield in Afghanistan on Nov. 28, 2019, when he served turkey, posed for photos and thanked American troops for their sacrifices amid the ongoing war.

INSIDE TRUMP’S INTIMATE MEETING WITH NATION’S BRAVEST SOLDIERS DURING WHIRLWIND TEXAS TRIP

President Donald Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to U.S. troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019, in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

"There's nowhere I'd rather celebrate this Thanksgiving than right here with the toughest, strongest, best and bravest warriors on the face of the Earth," Trump told the troops at the time, later adding, "And you don't even know how much the people of our country love and respect you."

The visit came as roughly 12,000 American troops remained in Afghanistan more than 18 years after the U.S. invasion.

ARMY VET LAWMAKER MARKS ABBEY GATE ANNIVERSARY WITH BLISTERING MESSAGE FOR BIDEN-HARRIS: 'ABJECT FAILURE'

President Donald Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to U.S. troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019, in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

During the visit, Trump met with Afghan President Ashraf Ghani to discuss efforts to end the war and told American troops that the Taliban wanted to reach a deal with the United States. He said his administration was reducing America's military presence in Afghanistan while pursuing a political solution to the more than 18-year conflict.

Less than two years later, President Joe Biden oversaw the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from Afghanistan in August 2021.

WOUNDED MARINES RELIVE THE HARROWING KABUL AIRPORT ATTACK IN EXPLOSIVE NEW FOX NATION DOCUMENTARY

Trump serves Thanksgiving dinner to U.S. troops at Bagram Air Field during a surprise visit on November 28, 2019, in Afghanistan. (OLIVIER DOULIERY/AFP via Getty Images)

The withdrawal unfolded as the Taliban rapidly seized control of Afghanistan, culminating in the fall of Kabul and a frantic evacuation at the city's airport.

Sixteen years earlier, Bush pulled off a similar Thanksgiving surprise in Iraq, secretly flying into Baghdad International Airport on Nov. 27, 2003, to celebrate with American troops just eight months after launching the U.S.-led invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein's regime.

GEORGE BUSH WELCOMES TOP OFFICIALS TO HIS HOME STATE FOR 9/11 REMEMBRANCE ON 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF ATTACKS

President George W. Bush helps serve Thanksgiving dinner at the Bob Hope Dining Facility, Baghdad International Airport, Iraq, during a surprise visit with troops, November 27, 2003. (U.S. National Archives and Presidential Libraries)

Bush stunned hundreds of service members when he appeared at their Thanksgiving dinner, emerging to cheers and applause before helping serve a traditional holiday meal and posing for photos with troops stationed far from home.

"I can't think of a finer group of folks to have Thanksgiving dinner with than you all," Bush told the troops at the time.

"We're proud of you," he added. "Today, Americans are gathering with their loved ones to give thanks for the many blessings in our lives."

News of his trip was not even released until Air Force One had already left Iraq.

US FACES ANOTHER MAJOR MIDDLE EAST TROOP WITHDRAWAL, BUT THREAT REMAINS

President George W. Bush carries a platter of turkey and fixings as he visits US troops for Thanksgiving in Baghdad, Nov. 27, 2003. Bush made the Thanksgiving visit to troops in Baghdad under the greatest secrecy and security. (ANJA NIEDRINGHAUS/AP POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Bush's visit came as American forces battled a growing insurgency following the fall of Saddam Hussein's government earlier that year. Despite Bush's declaration in May that major combat operations had ended, U.S. troops continued to face deadly attacks as the military worked to stabilize the country.

Just weeks later, U.S. forces captured Saddam Hussein in December 2003.

#5979. Democrats nominate Jeffries to be House speaker, a historic first

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., flanked by House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., and House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., hold a press conference in the Capitol after the House Democratic leadership elections on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries won a closed-door vote of the Democratic caucus Wednesday setting him up to be the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a historic step that follows Democrats’ staggering election wins earlier this month.

Jeffries, who had called for a recorded vote of the more than 250-member caucus that will serve in the next Congress despite facing no announced opponent, won decisively, 251-11. The margin suggests Jeffries will easily surpass the necessary 218 votes he will need on the House floor when the full chamber votes in January.

“It's a high honor and a distinct privilege to stand before the American people today as a Democratic nominee to be the next Speaker of the United States House of Representatives,” Jeffries said at a press conference following the election.

While Jeffries celebrates his win, he has continued to put an emphasis on unity before he faces what has been deemed the toughest job in Washington. Democrats’ massive majority will give him some margin for maneuvering as he balances the priorities of a complex caucus ranging from moderates to progressives.

“Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other,” Jeffries responded when asked about the 11 defections and what they mean for the next Congress. “Fight MAGA extremism, and to get big things done for the American people, and that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on January 3rd.”

Seven of the 11 members who intended to vote against Jeffries released a statement saying that conversations with leadership are still “ongoing” and that there is “work to be done,” but noting there has been “meaningful progress.” The seven included Reps.- elect Darializa Avilia Chavelier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donovan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” they wrote. “We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations.”

Newly elected House Democrats will meet with former President Barack Obama Wednesday night, where party unity will also be a likely topic.

“This is the beginning of a new bargain, a new politics where hard work is honored and where people's voice is paramount, and where we have more confidence in the future than nostalgia for the past,” House Minority Whip Katherine M. Clark, D-Mass., said at the press conference.

Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., who made history two decades ago as the nation’s first female speaker, arrived for the vote chanting “Hakeem Jeffries!”, reflecting party leaders’ desire to start the long morning of balloting on a positive note.

Jeffries' nomination followed the election of current Democratic Caucus Vice Chairman Ted Lieu, D-Calif., to serve as the caucus chair in the next Congress. Separate votes followed Wednesday morning, keeping Jeffries' leadership team intact: Clark, as the new majority leader and Democratic Caucus Chairman Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., as majority whip.

At his news conference, Jeffries noted that Clark was also making history as the first woman ever to serve in the position. Aguilar will also be the first Latino to serve as majority whip.

“We've been looking at people's talents, not a particular gender or race, and I think that's a good thing,” outgoing Rep. Steny H. Hoyer, D-Md., a former majority leader, told reporters ahead of the election.

“I think Hakeem Jeffries is going to be a good speaker,” Hoyer continued. “He has the confidence of the caucus, and he has a good leadership team that is close knit and very organized.”

Jeffries expressed confidence in the weeks leading up to his securing the top Democratic spot in the House, brushing aside questions about incoming members who had said they remained “undecided” ahead of the election.

Pelosi was nominated for speaker by acclamation ahead of her first election to the position in 2007. But Jeffries’ allies portrayed his decision to move forward with a recorded vote as a show of strength after a group of incoming progressives had floated forcing a recorded vote in the internal leadership race.

The entire leadership team will be tested despite their numerical advantage over Republicans by the same internal tensions facing Senate Democrats, where current Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., is being challenged for leadership of the majority by Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md.

Jeffries said Tuesday that the approach to the caucus vote mirrored the caucus’ 2018 transition from minority to majority, giving members an opportunity to weigh in on who was best positioned to lead based on their “track record, experience and vision.”

Jeffries has already outlined some of his top priorities of his speakership such as a hefty healthcare agenda, immigration legislation, and a multitude of investigations into the Trump administration.

He also signaled Wednesday another area where his party’s restive base is likely to close ranks: oversight.

“House Democrats will hold the crooks accountable, not for partisan reasons, but for patriotic ones,” he said at his news conference.

Like a cross between British colonial ambitions and a cultural crossroads cast in amber, George Town in Malaysia’s coastal state of Penang is a veritable living time capsule filled with colorful shophouses, bustling hawker stands dishing up sizzling char kway teow and tourist throngs posing for selfies with whimsical street art.

Little seems to change in this historical port city, not least of all because of its UNESCO World Heritage Site inscription in 2008. So it’s something of a rarity for a new hotel to open, let alone one that makes its home in a historic Chinese clan compound complete with a stunning temple that dates to 1906.

But that’s part of what makes the Soori Penang so special. It literally could exist nowhere else in the world, and it was only the owner and architect Soo K. Chan’s family ties (on his mother’s side) to the Khoo Kongsi Temple compound where he spent part of his childhood that made the entire project possible.

Staying here puts visitors in the heart of historic George Town, while architectural features that blend antique and contemporary sensibilities, immersive cultural programming and a gregarious staff (who can just as easily show you to their favorite stands for the famous local tamarind-infused asam laksa as recommend Michelin-rated restaurants) all combine to create a truly unique experience inspired by this singular setting.

Here’s what it’s like staying at the Soori Penang and why it is one of the most exciting hotel openings of the year.

Related: Amex's newest hotel transfer partner is a sleeper hit

All the accommodations at the Soori Penang are in traditional shophouses, giving them a particular flow.

The spaces are long and narrow (though still a spacious 1,076-1,184 square feet) with a central skylit space anchored by a burbling fountain, whose granite basin was inspired by traditional Malay rice mortars.

Traditional shophouses though these may be, with features like heavy shutters and wooden doors with blocky draw bars, the look is sleek and contemporary these days with dark stone flooring and pared down wooden furnishings, including a large built-in sectional with neutral-toned upholstery, as well as a wall-mounted 65-inch flatscreen.

Nods to the compound’s heritage include stone plinths with lion sculptures standing guard and wall-mounted replicas of the carved granite window from the Khoo Kongsi Temple featuring motifs of longevity and prosperity.

In addition to the complimentary minibar of nonalcoholic drinks and local treats like cashews and candied nutmeg (spirits are chargeable), on any given day, you’ll also find a bowl of seasonal fruits like crisp rose apples, juicy longans or crimson dragonfruit.

Bedrooms at the back feel ultraprivate thanks to closing shutters and feature colonial-inspired touches like curved wicker headboards inviting you to just sink into the white-sheeted beds.

Guests will find straw hats and bags for their use during their stay in the combined closet and bathroom area beyond, which also features limestone tiling, translucent alabaster sinks and enormous walk-in showers stocked with Byredo Bal d’Afrique products and a Dyson hairdryer.

George Town is a culinary hotspot thanks to the melting pot of cultures that has passed through here and set down roots, so you’ll likely spend your days and evenings out in the city enjoying everything from handmade samosas to gourmet, Michelin-starred, multicourse meals.

While at the hotel, though, you can count on a hearty breakfast (included in most rates) served in the guests-only restaurant, with items like kaya toast, eggs benedicts, plenty of fresh fruit and local specialties like haker-style wanton mee noodle soup with charsiew pork, or Penang koay teow th’ng noodle soup with fish balls and duck.

The all-day menu features items like sandwiches and salads in addition to local dishes, available both in the indoor dining area as well as out in the courtyard during fine weather.

Here are some of the Soori Penang's other amenities:

The Soori Penang is part of Leading Hotels of the World and nightly rates currently start at $905 or 10,086 Leaders Club Points.

Leaders Club recently became a transfer partner of American Express Membership Rewards. Points transfer from Amex at a 4:1 ratio, so 10,086 Leaders Club points would require 40,344 Amex points. Even better, if you have or , you can enroll for automatic Leaders Club Sterling elite status, which confers perks including:

Related: Redemptions with Leading Hotels of the World require taxes and fees — here's how to know how much you need to pay

This is a historical building complex, so guests with accessibility requirements should enquire directly with the hotel about their needs. That said, common areas and rooms are all accessed via step-free paths, though doors are not automatic.

The Soori Penang is one of the most distinctive new hotels to open in 2026 thanks to its unique heritage and location, not to mention the stunning design of its generous suites. It is the perfect home base for exploring George Town’s sometimes hectic streets, and all the more accessible thanks to the fact that you can book a stay using Leaders Club points transferred from American Express Membership Rewards. For travelers who crave a mix of history, culture, personality and design, the Soori Penang should be top of the list for an upcoming stay.

#5977. Strobe Talbott, former deputy secretary of state and Brookings Institution president, dies at 80

Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state who once worked at Time magazine, died at age 80.

Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state whose deep expertise on the Soviet Union shaped U.S. foreign policy before he went on to lead the Brookings Institution, died Thursday at the age of 80.

Talbott’s son, Devin Talbott, said his father died peacefully after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, The Associated Press reported.

An Ohio native, Talbott began his journalism career as an intern at Time magazine while studying at Yale and Oxford, where he was roommates with future President Bill Clinton. Clinton later joked that his job in their shared apartment was to make Talbott breakfast every morning.

NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL

Strobe Talbott, president of the Brookings Institution, right, and Wolfgang Ischinger, chairman of the Munich Security Conference on Security Policy, left, participate in a news conference in Berlin on July 16, 2008. (AP Photo/Franka Bruns)

While at Time, Talbott was tapped to translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former Soviet leader ousted in 1964, which earned him a full-time role at the magazine.

Over a 21-year career there, he focused on U.S.-Soviet relations, led the Washington bureau, and wrote as a foreign affairs columnist.

In 1994, Talbott joined the Clinton administration as deputy secretary of state, helping guide U.S. relations with Russia and other post-Soviet states.

In a statement, Bill Clinton said no one was better suited to advise him on Russian affairs than Talbott, noting that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton also relied on his counsel.

TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT?

Strobe Talbott, president of the Brookings Institution, speaks during a news conference in Berlin on July 16, 2008. (AP Photo/Franka Bruns)

"He was analytical, completely devoted to diplomacy, and on the level," Bill Clinton said. "With his expertise, we made real progress building trust between two former adversaries — moving beyond decades of confrontation to reduce the nuclear dangers future generations would inherit and build a Europe where more people could live in freedom and peace, including through the expansion of NATO and resolving ethnic conflicts in the Balkans. Together we laid the groundwork for greater cooperation while putting Russia on a path to democracy."

"Sadly, its current leader has taken the country in a different direction," Clinton added, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

President-elect Bill Clinton and Strobe Talbott of Time magazine talk privately as they walk along the beach on Hilton Head Island, S.C., Jan. 2, 1993. (AP Photo/James Finley)

He described Talbott as a "good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," and said, "Hillary and I will miss him very much."

After leaving government, Talbott served as president of the Brookings Institution from 2002 to 2017 and chaired the State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board.

President Bill Clinton during his last State of the Union Address before Congress. (Douglas Graham/Congressional Quarterly/Getty Images)

He is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren. His first wife, Brooke Shearer, died in 2009; he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

#5976. Dems express ‘points of anxiety’ over Trump’s summit with Putin and Xi

President Donald Trump prepares to shake hands with Russian President Vladimir Putin as China's President Xi Jinping looks on before the welcome banquet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Iori Sagisawa / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

Some Senate Democrats have heartburn about President Donald Trump’s planned Thursday meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, but Republicans counter by saying he could get the Russian and Chinese leaders to budge on a list of issues even as he appears politically weakened at home.

Trump arrived Wednesday in China’s Shenzhen economic zone on the banks of the Pearl River ahead of a high-level summit that was ostensibly slated to focus on paring each countries’ nuclear arsenal. But before he left, Trump signaled the three-way talks also likely would include the artificial intelligence race, Moscow’s bloody war with Ukraine, global trade and his standoff with Iran.

The U.S. commander in chief’s tendency to sound deferential to Putin and habit of referring to Xi as a personal “friend” concerns many congressional Democrats. But Trump’s GOP allies on Capitol Hill, despite this month’s midterm election losses, still describe him as a dealmaker who has a chance to use his final years to bend Putin and Xi toward U.S. interests.

Rick Scott, a Florida Republican who sits on the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said Tuesday he was hopeful that Trump could make some progress on at least one issue with the Russian and Chinese leaders.

“As we all know, China and Russia want to destroy our way of life,” he said. “But it would be great to reduce … nuclear stockpiles and make sure we're not going to ever get attacked.

Still, Scott sounded skeptical about two world leaders Trump has tried to keep close during his two terms. “But do I trust Xi or Putin? No, they're a bunch of liars.” Asked if he worries Trump might trust them too much, Scott replied: “I don't think he trusts him any more than I do. … I'm glad the president's trying. Hope springs eternal. But do I actually really believe something good's going to come out of it? I don't.”

Outgoing House Armed Services Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., said part of Trump’s talks on Thursday “should be to make sure the world is a safer place, to make sure we don't have aggressive behavior like Russia in an unprovoked attack against Ukraine.

“They ought to be talking about how they don't do those sorts of things, how they don't threaten their neighbors, how they don't try to intimidate through the assertion of force that they ought to be able to work together to make sure we assure a safe globe,” said Wittman, who lost his reelection race earlier this month.

That comment came one day after Trump told reporters as he left the White House for Asia that he sees Putin “backing down a little bit” in his conduct of the war with Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher. I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly,” Trump said Monday. “I think he's backing down.”

Those kinds of deferential remarks about the Russian leader are a big reason why some Democrats have heartburn about Thursday’s meeting.

Senate Armed Services member Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said Tuesday that she’s concerned about the Shenzhen summit because “I’m not sure what’s going to pop out of [Trump’s] mouth next — especially for a meeting with two guys he clearly likes.”

Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., also a member of the Armed Services and Foreign Relations committees, said he has “high hopes” for the trilateral meeting — but “maybe not high expectations.”

“I have some points of anxiety. I'm nervous about any discussion about Ukraine that doesn't involve the Ukrainians. And, so, some of the advance to this is like, ‘We're going to talk about ending the Ukraine war.’ You can't do that without Ukraine at the table,” Kaine said. “So the desire to bring about more peace and stability, that's a good thing to talk about. But no conditions about Ukraine and ending that war without them at the table? Not so sure about that.”

During remarks Tuesday on the Senate floor, Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer criticized what he described as Trump’s misplaced priorities.

“Enforcement of the new rules restricting China’s access to our most sensitive AI chips should start today,” the New York Democrat said, adding that Trump should focus more of his Asia swing on securing commitments from U.S. allies to block China from gaining an upper hand in the AI technology race.

Trump touted just that on Tuesday during remarks in Manila at a U.S.-Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit in the Philippines.

“Since I returned to office, we've made major trade deals with Malaysia, Cambodia, Indonesia, as well as Japan, South Korea, and almost everybody, frankly, at the table,” he said. “And we've made many other vital agreements across the region spanning energy, critical minerals and technology.”

But on Wednesday, Trump appeared to have pivoted to the trip’s main event.

He stood beside Xi at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen and smiled as Putin approached. Trump extended his hand and shook Putin’s as the Chinese leader looked on.

Scott, a Trump ally in the Senate, said Tuesday he sees the president “trying to build relationships to try to make sure we don't end up at war [because] he doesn't like war.”

Trump signaled Monday that he might press Xi for details on an alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, costing the AI mogul his job as the company’s president and CEO. He also said he could bring up Nvidia’s sales of sophisticated microchips that many lawmakers — Republican and Democrat — want to ensure remain in the U.S. for domestic AI development.

The administration’s response to the turmoil at Nvidia, with Trump even suggesting he'd support Huang returning as CEO, is a rare area where Republicans have expressed concern publicly. House Energy and Commerce Committee Chair Brett Guthrie, R-Kent., wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Wednesday seeking information about “the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips, the effect of which has a broad impact on America’s race with China to artificial intelligence (AI) dominance and the ability of U.S. companies to set global technology standards.”

Heather Williams, director of the Project on Nuclear Issues at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, wrote this week that for the three leaders, the “path is fraught with challenges.”

“Putin could diplomatically outmaneuver the Trump administration and make any progress on nuclear issues dependent on undermining Western support to Ukraine,” she wrote in an analysis for the Washington, D.C.-based think tank. “Even the optics of Trump and Putin negotiating while the war continues and as Russia ramps up missile strikes on Ukrainian civilian targets could be interpreted as undermining U.S. values.”

#5974. How to spot real Black Friday savings this holiday season amid the affordability squeeze

University at Buffalo marketing professor Dinesh Gauri shares his tips for scoring the best Black Friday prices, from researching deals ahead of time to taking advantage of online shopping and in-store pickup options.

Black Friday deals are everywhere, but a sale price does not always mean real savings.

With budgets under pressure, amid a persisting affordability crisis and rising fuel prices with the raging Iran conflict, shoppers are looking for ways to stretch their money during the holiday shopping season this year.

The forecasts point to a season of cautious spending. Visa Business and Economics Insights expects holiday sales to increase 4.5% from last year — but after accounting for higher prices, the actual increase in what shoppers buy is projected to be just 1.1%.

That makes it all the more important for shoppers to know what they’re paying for and whether a sale is truly a deal.

"It's still a good time to shop. It's just that you just have to be a little bit more careful," Dinesh Gauri, a marketing professor at the University at Buffalo, told Fox News Digital when discussing holiday and Black Friday shopping.

7 HOLIDAY SHOPPING SCAMS TO WATCH FOR THIS SEASON

Dinesh Gauri, a marketing professor at the University at Buffalo, recommends checking price histories and setting a budget before shopping for Black Friday sales. (Irfan Khan/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images)

Gauri revealed that shopping during Black Friday does not always produce the best deal — especially when it comes to essential technology like cell phones.

He advised shoppers to set a budget and research prices before making a purchase, especially for big-ticket items.

"Have a number in mind and do your research before you go about spending the money," he said, recommending price-tracking sites and extra promotions.

Gauri cited higher gas prices compared with last year as a potential pressure point for consumers, particularly those considering larger purchases.

While the average price of a gallon has risen from approximately $3 in November 2025 to $3.64 per gallon this November, according to AAA, the surging price of diesel is what is impacting the cost of nearly all goods for Americans.

GOOGLE'S NEW AI SHOPPING CART TRACKS DEALS ACROSS STORES

Tariffs are another potential source of price pressure. A New York Fed analysis found that about 26% of tariff increases from 2025 had been passed on to consumer prices. Retailers may also respond to higher costs by raising prices or reducing package sizes.

Gauri said some retailers have done both, a practice known as shrinkflation.

"The package size is getting smaller, even though the price might be the same," he said. "You’re shaving off, let’s say, 10% of the product."

Shoppers are expected to use holiday discounts to stock up on essentials as well as gifts, Adobe Analytics projects. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

Gauri said Black Friday promotions now often begin during Thanksgiving week and run through Cyber Monday, giving shoppers more time to compare prices online and in stores. The shift from doorbusters that once drew shoppers to stores before dawn the Friday after Thanksgiving means consumers can now research deals, order products and arrange for pickup or delivery.

To make sure a discount is worthwhile, Gauri recommended using price-tracking websites and Amazon’s price-history feature to check what an item has cost in recent months. "Consumers tend to overspend sometimes because they do not remember what an item previously cost," he said.

He also advised shoppers to compare prices across retailers and check each store’s price-matching policy before making a major purchase. Some retailers exclude Black Friday specials from those policies, he said.

Black Friday promotions can offer real savings, but shoppers should compare prices to make sure a markdown is actually a deal. (Mike Kemp/In Pictures via Getty Images)

Gauri cautioned that Black Friday is not always the best time to shop.

"For cellphones, Black Friday doesn’t get you anything special," he said, adding that the best deals on phones or plans often come in October, around new product launches and carrier promotions.

Still, shoppers may find Cyber Week discounts useful for stocking up on everyday essentials.

Adobe Analytics projects online sales of clothing basics will run 210% above the September average, while personal hygiene products will be up 150%. Baby products, pet supplies and household cleaning items are also expected to see a boost.

With budgets under pressure, Gauri advised shoppers to set a spending limit before heading into the holiday sales.

Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

#5973. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#5970. From Hollywood mogul to Biden-Harris insiders, Democrats turn to familiar faces to shape their next chapter

National Review columnist Caroline Downey and Democratic strategist Al Mottur join 'The Faulkner Focus' to discuss Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory in Michigan. The panel discusses Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's rising influence and the impact on the 2028 Democratic primary.

On the heels of the blue wave in the 2026 U.S. midterms, incoming Democratic leaders are tapping an eclectic mix of political veterans, business executives and entertainment figures to help shape their transitions into power.

From a Hollywood mogul and former Biden administration officials to figures with ties to Republican leaders, the appointments offer an early glimpse into the people Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern — and the experience and connections they hope to bring into their new administrations.

Several incoming Democrats are turning to familiar faces from the Biden administration. In New Mexico, Gov.-elect Deb Haaland tapped former Biden presidential speechwriter Felicia Salazar and former Interior Department official Joan Mooney for her transition team, while California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra selected Arsenio Mataka, who previously served as his senior counselor at the Department of Health and Human Services under Biden, to direct policy for his transition team. In Ohio, Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton tapped Elisabeth Hire, a former aide to then-Vice President Biden, as a transition co-chair.

Haaland's campaign and Becerra's campaign each did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

A sign points to a vote center during the in-person early voting period in California's Proposition 50 special election on Oct. 27, 2025 in West Hollywood, California. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)

The transition teams will help incoming leaders prepare to take office, including identifying potential administration officials, shaping policy priorities and laying the groundwork for their first days in power. The selections also offer a window into the experience, relationships and perspectives newly elected Democrats are turning to as they prepare to govern.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., tapped Egyptian-American lawyer Brenda Abdelall as the director of his transition team, Politico Playbook first reported in early November. Abdelall previously claimed that Zionists were "controlling" much of U.S. politics, The Washington Free Beacon reported Nov. 6, though Harris' 2024 presidential campaign said at the time that the remarks did not reflect Abdelall's current views.

"The Zionists have a strong voice in American politics," Abdelall told the New York Sun during a conference for the American Muslim Council in 2002, the Free Beacon reported. "I would say they're controlling a lot of it."

Abdelall previously served as the assistant secretary of partnership and engagement at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. She also directed the Kamala Harris 2024 presidential campaign's outreach to Arab American voters, Reuters reported.

U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed speaks at the Michigan Democratic Party convention, on August 29, 2026, in Lansing, Michigan. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS

El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Roxie Richner told Fox News Digital on Nov. 9 that Abdelall "comes to the role of transition director with decades of experience leading teams at the highest levels of politics, including the Biden-Harris administration."

"While at the Department of Homeland Security, Brenda worked to implement the nation’s first National Strategy to Counter Antisemitism and frequently spearheaded efforts to counter the rise of hate crimes and violence across the country," Richner added. "The transition team is committed to building a team that reflects the great diversity of Michigan and ensuring that the El-Sayed office serves all communities across the state."

El-Sayed is set to assume office on Jan. 3, 2027.

DEMOCRATIC SENATOR-ELECT CALLS TRUMP 'UNSERIOUS FOOL' WHILE DEFENDING COMBATIVE POLITICAL STYLE

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, speaks at the Michigan Democratic Nominating Convention in Lansing, Mich., on Aug. 29, 2026. (Anadolu via Getty Images)

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Democratic Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms announced Nov. 6 that filmmaker and actor Tyler Perry would serve as one of 10 co-chairs of her transition team, dubbed "Georgia's Promise," WBAL-TV reported. Perry has long been known for his philanthropic efforts, including supporting underserved communities and charitable causes across Georgia. Bottoms lauded Perry as "an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community and owns Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta," WDSU reported.

Victorious Georgia Democratic gubernatorial candidate, former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, speaks onstage during her election night watch party at the Atlanta Marriott Marquis on Nov. 3, 2026 in Atlanta, Ga. (Megan Varner/Getty Images)

EX-BIDEN OFFICIAL WINS GEORGIA DEM PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR IN BID TO END PARTY'S LOSING STREAK

The news that Perry will serve on Bottoms’ Georgia transition team has sparked some criticism due to the entertainment mogul facing two active lawsuits accusing him of sexual assault and misconduct, allegations his attorneys have denied, Variety reported Nov. 6.

Perry has denied all sexual assault and harassment allegations made against him, People reported on March 3.

Maxscene, a division of Tyler Perry Studios, did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Bottoms previously was an executive producer on Netflix’s "Miss Governor," a 2025 political comedy sitcom produced by Tyler Perry Studios, per online film database IMDb.

Other prominent figures that have been tapped for Bottoms' transition committee include Home Depot co-founder Arthur Blank and former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance Roz Brewer, WBAL-TV reported.

Bottoms’ campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

Bottoms is set to take office on Jan. 11, 2027.

Democratic Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson's transition team includes Mark Penley, a former deputy attorney general who reported outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton to the FBI, and Erin Epley, who served as lead attorney in Paxton's impeachment, The Houston Chronicle reported Nov. 16.

Johnson also tapped Amanda Crawford, a former appointee of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, and Thaddeus Cleveland, a Republican sheriff from Terrell County, as part of his transition team, according to the Chronicle.

Johnson's campaign did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Democratic Gov.-elect David Crowley is also turning to the world of professional sports, tapping Alex Lasry, a former senior vice president of the NBA's Milwaukee Bucks, to serve on his transition team, Wisconsin Public Radio reported Nov. 11.

Lasry, the son of former Bucks co-owner and billionaire businessman Marc Lasry, helped oversee the franchise's operations during its rise to the 2021 NBA championship and played a key role in developing Milwaukee's Fiserv Forum arena. #5969. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

The cost gap is wide: Heathrow puts expansion at about £49 billion ($65.2 billion), while IAG, owner of British Airways and the airport's biggest customer, says it should be no more than £30 billion ($39.9 billion), with IAG CEO Luis Gallego calling the current plan "unaffordable and doomed to failure" in a letter reported by The Times. The committee also said the plan leans on sustainable aviation fuel and carbon removal that isn't yet at the scale needed — the Department for Transport has cut its 2050 SAF uptake forecast to 30% from 50%. Heathrow's own projections have landing charges rising from £25.28 ($33.13) per passenger to as much as £60 ($80) by 2034.
